title: Does China Own Apple? With Patrick McGee
summary: The launch episode, and a statement of method. Eisman spends an hour on how Apple physically makes things, and arrives at an argument about national security rather than about the stock.
discussed: Apple's near-bankruptcy in spring 1996, closer than the standard Jobs story admits
The shift from Apple owning factories on three continents to roughly nine countries in 2000 and then almost entirely China
Tim Cook's contribution framed as manufacturing genius rather than product innovation
How Apple bought the tooling, designed the machines and trained the workforce, running factories it did not own
The Chinese suppliers Luxshare, Goertek and BYD displacing Taiwanese firms inside the supply chain
Xi Jinping's 2013 pressure on Apple and Apple's counter-argument that it contributes to indigenous innovation
Why moving to India fails, since the component ecosystem itself sits in China
learned: Manufacturing know-how is a transferable asset, and transferring it is harder to reverse than transferring money
A supply chain can become a strategic encirclement. McGee's Go analogy is that you win by removing your opponent's moves, not by checkmate
Concentration risk hides inside companies that look diversified. Components come from many countries but are assembled in one
When a company has no good options, saying so plainly is more useful than proposing a fix
notable: Business ties unbreakable, political ties untenable. The situation is not in equilibrium, and nobody knows how it breaks.

title: Stablecoin and Instability with Trump and Musk - The Friday Market Wrap!
summary: An early wrap that sets the template: index stats, a walk through the week's news, then a mailbag answer that turns into a framework. Here the framework is his complacency warning.
discussed: Steel tariffs doubled to 50%, and the US and China each accusing the other of reneging
Tesla registrations in France down 67% year over year
Private equity monetisations stalling as the IPO window stays shut, with institutions seeking secondary exits
Meta's twenty-year nuclear deal with Constellation Energy as the start of a trend
The Fed finally lifting the Wells Fargo asset cap after seven years
Circle's IPO at 31 dollars trading to 107 within two days
learned: Markets correct on the possibility of a recession, then rally back until an actual recession arrives
His World War One analogy: nobody wanted the war, but reciprocal treaties triggered it. Trade can work the same way
Bitcoin trades opposite its own stated thesis, rising with NASDAQ rather than against fiat risk
Two contradictory headlines can follow the same jobs print, which is a reason to read the data yourself
notable: He compares the moment to 2007, when the economy looked fine while the underlying credit was already rotten, while explicitly declining to predict calamity.

title: A Skeptic's Guide to Cryptocurrency and Stablecoins
summary: Eisman opens by calling himself a crypto skeptic rather than a hater, then hands a fintech strategist his single objection and lets him answer it at length.
discussed: The correlation between Bitcoin and NASDAQ split into three eras, before 2019, the pandemic, and after the crypto winter
The separation between a coin as an asset and the underlying technology as payment rails
Why ubiquity and liquidity, not technology, decide which coins matter
Exactly how a stablecoin works: dollars in, treasuries held in custody, one-to-one backing, no capital appreciation
Why network fees rather than the coin are where value would accrue
Visa Plus and Visa Direct as the interoperability layer challengers have to beat
The regulatory split, with most assets heading to the CFTC as commodities
learned: A payment technology has to beat the incumbent on the whole job, not on one fee line. The network fee is about 12 basis points of a roughly 3% merchant cost, so attacking it is not worth the build
Remittances, not retail payments, is where stablecoins have a real opening
Vertical payment businesses like Toast build a moat by solving an industry's whole back office, which is harder to commoditise
Eisman's pattern recognition: every few years someone pitches disintermediating Visa and Mastercard, and returns later working with them
notable: He discloses owning Visa for years and calls it the best business model he has seen.

title: Safe to Stay Invested? Decoding 2025 Stock Charts
summary: A working tutorial in technical analysis, with Eisman pressing on whether charts are a philosophy or a tool. The answer he accepts is a tool, and he adopts it.
discussed: What a technical strategist actually does: trend, momentum, sentiment and intermarket relationships
Why head and shoulders patterns are mostly head fakes
Base building after a collapse, and the UnitedHealth counterexample where a base broke lower
The equal-weight index as a health check on breadth
Percentage of S&P stocks at one-month highs as a durability measure
Consumer discretionary versus staples as an economic barometer
Levered ETFs at roughly 100 billion dollars, twelve times larger long than short at the January peak
Why long-duration bonds failed to work after the Fed began cutting, breaking a pattern back to 1975
Private equity and private credit stocks failing to recover with the rest of financials
learned: Sentiment is a contrarian tool. When every metric aligns bullish, plan the exit
Index concentration masks internal deterioration, so look through to breadth
Active managers face a structural problem: risk limits stop them owning enough of the largest names
The charts flagged trouble in private credit stocks months before the news did
notable: Sohn reads the private asset managers as distributive across the board, and Eisman connects it to a closed IPO window and impatient institutions.

title: Market Resilience Amid Multiple Challenges - The Friday Market Wrap!
summary: A quiet week that Eisman uses for the most important mailbag answer of the early run, on whether incompetence causes crashes.
discussed: Chinese exports to the US down 35% in May, matching a logistics guest's earlier forecast
Rare earth monopolisation as China's equalizer in trade talks
Warner Brothers splitting in two, with Netflix at 520 billion against Warner's 26 billion
Apple's developer conference passing without a meaningful AI announcement
Israel striking Iran as the episode is recorded
learned: How he actually detected the housing bubble: a Moody's securitisation database showing early delinquencies month by month, read like a Rosetta Stone
Incompetence does not cause bubbles. If it did we could screen for it. Minsky's rational irrationality does
Chuck Prince's dancing line explains why executives cannot act against their own incentives
On regulation, the question is never whether but how much, and there is no formula, only iteration
notable: Incentives trump ethics almost every time. The maxim he returns to for the next fourteen months.

title: Are We Building an AI Future We Can't Power?
summary: A structural tour of the data centre stack with Cisco's head of investor relations, framed as a trip back to 2015 to see what changed.
discussed: The 2015 landscape before trillion-dollar market caps, when public cloud was still displacing enterprise data centres
How CPUs and GPUs differ in practical terms, using a spreadsheet analogy of rows and columns
The networking layer, NVLink aggregation, and why the interconnect matters as much as the chip
That much enterprise data is stored but not usable without reformatting
Cisco's own position across switching, security, observability and collaboration
learned: The constraint on AI is shifting from chips to power and interconnect
If people who cannot code can now produce software, the moat around software companies may be thinner than assumed. Eisman flags this in June 2025, well before the software selloff he later covers
Hardware may outperform software precisely because software's defensibility is now in question
notable: He says plainly that he is struggling with the software moat question, an early sighting of what becomes the SaaSpocalypse thesis.

title: Earnings, Geopolitics, and Sectors - The Friday Market Wrap!
summary: With earnings season over, he explains the rhythm of the market calendar, then uses the empty week to lay out his first full statement on private credit.
discussed: Why the weeks between earnings seasons trade on macro themes alone
The Iran conflict driving headline-to-headline trading
Renewable incentives being cut, with Enphase down from 340 dollars to 35 and First Solar from 285 to 140
Homebuilders losing the benefit of mortgage rate buy-downs, with Lennar down from 185 to 105
The explosive growth in business development corporations and private credit funds
learned: His causal model for credit: in 2008 the credit blowup caused the recession, which is unusual. Normally a recession comes first and exposes bad credit
He expects the normal order this time, so private credit will reveal mistakes rather than cause them
The reason he will not call private credit a bubble is the absence of any credit-quality data, in direct contrast to the securitisation data he had in 2006
Solar is a policy-dependent trade, and he does not expect a rally while the incentives are gone
notable: He names a trade war as the only thing he can see causing a recession, a view he holds for most of 2025.

title: Is Capitalism Flawed? Fixing and Regulating Free Markets
summary: A book conversation that doubles as Eisman's fullest statement of his own political economy, conducted with a critic of capitalism he clearly respects.
discussed: Why Cassidy traced criticism of capitalism back to its origins rather than starting after the Cold War
Left and right converging on anti-globalisation, which Cassidy calls a crisis of legitimacy
Mercantile capitalism and the monopoly power of the East India Company at both ends of the trade
Marxian declining-rate-of-profit theory and why it failed
Keynes's demand formula and why it was designed to save the system rather than replace it
Minsky on instability as an internal product of stable periods
Eisman's own claim that risk-weighted assets, not the repeal of Glass-Steagall, enabled the leverage behind 2008
learned: The useful debate is not free markets against socialism but where on the spectrum to sit, since both extremes are unserious
Capitalism's flaws come from people, not from design, so they recur rather than get fixed
Regulatory capture is real but cyclical, and post-crisis regimes do get teeth
Populist economic nationalism can be politically coherent while remaining economically incoherent
notable: Eisman argues that even capitalism's critics concede the counterfactual, which he later uses against listeners who read the K-shaped economy fatalistically.

title: Bullish Signs Continue - The Friday Market Wrap!
summary: Both indices hit 52-week highs and Eisman explains the round trip from the February peak through the April 8 low. The answer becomes one of his standing mental models.
discussed: The year reviewed: all-time highs in February, a sharp correction to April 8, then a rally back
Nvidia's 69% revenue growth as proof the AI story is early
Tech and tech-related stocks passing 40% of the index, a concentration no other country approaches
Mastercard and Fiserv launching a stablecoin, with Visa expected to follow
Nike rallying 15% on green shoots despite weak fundamentals
Zohran Mamdani winning the Democratic primary, hitting New York real estate names
learned: Markets price the ultimate outcome immediately, then wait to see if it arrives. The error in April was expecting tariffs to hit the economy instantly
Regulatory capture is real but moves in waves rather than one direction
Buy the dip is a religion he largely subscribes to, with one named exception: a genuine trade war
New entrants usually fail against Visa and Mastercard because the incumbents already own trusted global networks
notable: He states the belief that anchors his bullishness: the US economy is more dynamic than at any time in his lifetime.

title: How CEOs Build Empires, Or Blow Them Up
summary: A three-analyst panel naming good and bad chief executives in financial services, with roughly a century of combined coverage in the room. The most quotable episode of the early run.
discussed: Jamie Dimon's record of fixing Bank One, then JP Morgan, then Chase in sequence
The accountability and transparency the panel calls shocking in the best sense
John Kanas selling North Fork to Capital One in 2005, before the blowup
Citigroup trading at three times book while JP Morgan sat at 75% of book in 2000
The recurring anatomy of failed banks: concentrated risk, balance sheets growing too fast, no controls, high-risk lending
Texas banks in the 1980s, Northeast banks in the 1990s, Washington Mutual and Wachovia in 2008
Lloyd Blankfein named as the most overrated
Brian Moynihan offered as the rare bad-to-good turnaround
Marianne Lake flagged as the likely Dimon successor
learned: Good chief executives build teams, hold them accountable, and go against the grain while absorbing criticism for it
Bad ones share a specific fingerprint, and it is a balance sheet fingerprint rather than a personality one
Avoiding dilutive acquisitions and buying cheap in distress is a marker of the best operators
Growth in tangible book value per share over ten to fifteen years is the scoreboard that survives cycles
Great leaders produce successors, which is itself a test of the leader
notable: Eisman's own summary elsewhere: a chief executive who stays too long becomes good, mediocre and bad in sequence.

title: Jobs Shock, Bank Buyback Boom & AI Talent Wars | The Friday Market Wrap!
summary: A technical wrap that teaches bank capital from first principles, prompted by the annual stress test results.
discussed: Payrolls at 147,000 against 106,000 expected, ending hope of a summer rate cut
The ten-year yield stuck in the same range since October 2022, which he calls directionless
Meta poaching OpenAI talent with very large signing bonuses
Foxconn recalling Chinese engineers from Indian iPhone plants, stalling Apple's diversification
Stress capital buffers falling across the board, with Goldman down nearly 300 basis points
learned: Capital ratios divide common equity by risk-weighted assets, not by assets, and the stress capital buffer is the binding constraint on large banks
Regulators should not ratchet the test forever, because enough deleveraging makes banking uneconomic
His defence of calling Hank Greenberg a bad chief executive: AIG was his largest short in 2005, and Greenberg built both the powerhouse and the decentralised structure that sank it
Fifteen years to merge 200 operating systems is the real cost of a decentralised empire
notable: For the first time since the crisis, he says, regulators are turning friendlier to banks, while stressing this is nothing like pre-2008 leverage.

title: Don't Get Fooled Again: Pulitzer Winner Warns of Wall Street's Dark Side
summary: Two people who were reporting and shorting the same companies in the 2000s compare notes. The register is moral as much as analytical.
discussed: Her 2002 Pulitzer for exposing conflicted Wall Street analysts during the dot-com era
Her recurring theme: practices that harm many people and benefit a small group on the inside
Household International, Enron, WorldCom and the road to Sarbanes-Oxley
AIG's disputes with Goldman over credit default swap pricing, and how circular the marks became
Fabrice Tourre as a junior salesman who became the face of a firm-level problem
How little changed after 2008 despite trillions in losses and mass foreclosure
Private equity bankruptcies beginning as the rate and IPO environment turns against the model
Private equity firms taking on pension liabilities, leaving retirees dependent on them
learned: Incentives ran the length of the chain. Countrywide loan officers earned two to three times more for a subprime loan than a prime one
State-based insurance regulation is a structural weakness, since a national insurer answers to whichever state it is domiciled in
Eisman's discipline in his own words: he would not short the planet without data, and the private-equity-into-insurance story is compelling but currently dataless
notable: He tells her that explaining how finance actually works to ordinary people could not be more crucial, which is effectively the podcast's mission statement.

title: Big Beautiful Bill, Write-Off Revolution & Tariff Tempest | The Friday Market Wrap!
summary: A wrap that hands most of its runtime to a policy analyst, because a 900-page bill had just become law. The most investment-relevant policy episode of 2025.
discussed: Tariff threats against fourteen countries, plus copper at 50% and Brazil at 50%, with the market ignoring all of it
The five themes in the bill: permanent individual tax cuts, the president's campaign promises, business investment incentives, spending cuts and a five trillion dollar debt ceiling rise
100% immediate expensing for factories built in America, and for capital goods, made permanent
R&D expensing restored for domestic research
Medicaid growth slowed rather than cut, with effects starting in 2028
Orphan drug carve-outs from inflation-reduction price controls
learned: Clifton's framing that Eisman adopts: the bill sterilises the tariffs rather than stimulating growth. Read the two together or you misjudge the deficit
The Congressional Budget Office scores the bill at 3.4 trillion added and the tariffs at 2.8 trillion raised, leaving the deficit near 6.2% of GDP rather than exploding
America has entered austerity for the first time in thirty years, measured by interest cost against tax revenue
Policy changes create two distinct winner sets: those who sell the goods and those who buy and expense them
notable: Eisman's own aside on conspiracy theories: the important conspiracies are the unspoken ones that develop over time, like an entire sector's ethos of lending badly.

title: Why the Market's Surging Despite the Headlines
summary: A market strategist walks through why the year confounded everyone, and Eisman uses him to test his own worry that the market has priced trade risk at zero.
discussed: Equity inflows in the 99th percentile of all history going into January, a sentiment warning
The 65-day rally off the April low ranking fourth best in history, alongside 2009, 2020 and 1982
Credit conditions described as remarkably benign
Deregulation as a reason to prefer Goldman over Apollo and Blackstone, since regulation protects incumbents and deregulation helps challengers
Homebuilders correlating tightly with regional banks
Gold sentiment described as excessive
Bitcoin surviving three separate 90% drawdowns
learned: Having the headlines in advance would have lost you money, which is the argument for listening to price rather than predicting news
The market is consistently smarter than any individual, and the best response is to listen
Anything that survives three 90% drawdowns is a survivor, whatever it eventually becomes
Verrone's line that Eisman adopts permanently: the market is my favourite economist
notable: Eisman names his precise discomfort: he thinks the US economy is great, and worries the market is treating trade-war probability as zero.

title: Earnings Season Kickoff, Bank Earnings & Nvidia China Greenlight | The Friday Market Wrap!
summary: He opens by disclosing a breast cancer diagnosis, deliberately, to make men aware the disease is not confined to women. Then he teaches bank valuation and works through earnings.
discussed: The diagnosis, caught early, with treatment expected over several months
An oncologist squash partner spotting a skin irritation he had ignored for months
Return on tangible common equity and price to tangible book as the two metrics that drive bank valuation
JP Morgan, Goldman and BlackRock earnings, with advisory revenue up 71% signalling an M&A recovery
Progressive's premiums up 18%, which he calls remarkable at that size
learned: A bank with a higher return on tangible common equity earns a higher multiple of tangible book. Those two numbers explain most bank valuation
Why he invests only in the United States: tech is 31% of the S&P alone, and over 50% including tech-adjacent names, which no other market approaches
His own education arc. He joined Neuberger knowing financials, spent years learning technology and industrials, and that study changed his view of the whole economy
notable: He tells men to get unexplained breast symptoms checked, and credits his friend with probably saving his life.

title: The Secrets of the Short Seller: How the Pros Spot Trouble
summary: The first of two consecutive short-selling masterclasses. A boutique researcher walks through winners, losers and the rules she now refuses to break.
discussed: An airline short built on a Freedom of Information Act request and a whistleblowing mechanic
Stellantis from 20 dollars to 9, built on calls to 100 to 300 dealerships
How stimulus cheques turned subprime borrowers into paper-prime borrowers, then reversed
Negative equity freezing the trade-in market and stranding dealer inventory
SolarEdge and Enphase advertising sub-1% failure rates while installers reported nearer 40%
California's NEM 3.0 stretching solar payback from seven years to twenty
Reddit and DraftKings as losses, both cult stocks
Carvana covered at 4 dollars, then rising above 300
learned: Never short a cult, because cultists care about things you consider irrelevant and buy on them
Never short purely on valuation, and never short a stock at a 52-week high. Wait for one missed earnings
Never short a roll-up before its anniversary, since acquisition accretion masks the problem for about a year
It is always the management. Investigate every board member, where they worked and why they left
Watch receivables, warranty expense and liabilities. The balance sheet tells the story
Eisman's ranking: a pure microeconomic short is best, one with macro or political overlay second, a politically dependent short last
notable: Her partner's test for whether a thesis will work: the fundamentals may be bad, but does anybody care?

title: Meme Stock Resurgence: Warning Signs or Just Noise? - The Friday Market Wrap!
summary: A 113-company earnings dump, used to illustrate why identical industries earn wildly different multiples, and to announce the masterclass series.
discussed: The Japan deal at 15% rather than the threatened 25%, plus a 550 billion dollar investment fund
Verizon and AT&T trading below their year-2000 levels despite 180 to 200 billion dollar market caps
T-Mobile at 22 times earnings against AT&T at 12 and Verizon at 9
Everyone in cable and wireless attacking everyone else's business, leaving Charter without growth
GE Vernova at 86 times 2025 earnings, justified by scarcity since only two companies make gas turbines
Tesla earnings down 23% and revenue down 12%
Meme stocks under 5 dollars spiking on social buzz and short squeezes
learned: Multiples reflect story and growth, not industry. Three wireless companies with similar assets trade at wildly different valuations
Electrical power is the binding constraint on AI, and removing solar subsidies raised the value of gas turbines
Scarcity value is a legitimate reason for a rich multiple when only two suppliers exist worldwide
Tesla taught Chinese manufacturers to build electric vehicles, and they now build them better and cheaper
notable: He announces the financial literacy and 2008 crisis lectures, and asks listeners to send topics they want covered.

title: The Secrets of the Short Seller Part 2: The Blueprint for Strategy & Survival
summary: The second short-selling masterclass, and the more structural of the two. Safalow supplies a market-structure framework before discussing a single company.
discussed: The four Ps: passives, processors meaning quants and algos, pods, and positioning
How multi-strategy pod risk management forces violent unwinds on a 3% to 5% drawdown
Gamma squeezes, and why dealers must buy the underlying as calls are bought
Fresh Pet: store saturation near 28,000 of a 32,000 to 35,000 addressable base, rising acquisition costs, no third-party study of the product's benefit
Trupanion and the insurance rate spiral, with premiums up 400% to 700% over a decade yet loss ratios still above target
Kinsale compared to ITT Educational, both revered financially, both serving customers other providers refuse
Shutterstock and title insurers as set-and-forget shorts
learned: Every great short rallies 50% to 100% against the trend three to five times on the way down, which is the hardest part to survive
Rank short types by durability: secularly challenged first, then fad, then cyclical, then fraud, because frauds persist for a decade
Carry both kinds. High-maintenance shorts are war, set-and-forget shorts on quiet decline often deliver the better return on time
Where passive ownership dominates, valuation is nearly irrelevant and flows decide the price
The IKEA effect is real in research. A thousand pages of work on one name does not make the position right
notable: Safalow's short ideas have generated about 27% annual alpha since inception, yet he notes Pepsi alone produced roughly 200% over five years as a simple secular short.

title: How Tariff Deals, Pharma Shocks, & Mega Mergers Redefined the Market - The Friday Market Wrap!
summary: Tariff diplomacy dominates, and a weak payroll print with a large downward revision changes the Fed conversation.
discussed: The EU deal at 15%, which he reads as Europe mostly caving, with Germany most exposed as the largest exporter
India threatened at 25% plus penalties over Russian oil purchases
July payrolls at 73,000 against 104,000 expected, with June revised from 147,000 down to 14,000
PayPal down from nearly 300 dollars in 2021 to 67, with payment volume growth slowing
Microsoft revenue up 18% at a four trillion dollar market cap
Meta showing AI translating into better monetisation
learned: A four trillion dollar company growing revenue 18% would normally be astonishing, and only looks ordinary beside Nvidia's 69%
Payments outside the Visa and Mastercard duopoly is a brutal business where everyone attacks everyone
His sell discipline stated plainly: hold while the thesis is intact, largely ignore valuation, and sell when the story changes rather than when the multiple moves
notable: He previews the venture capital episode by flagging a claim he says is not written about anywhere: venture entered a depression in 2022.

title: Venture Capital Revealed: Behind the Schemes They Haven't Told You
summary: A co-founder of RRE Ventures describes a venture depression that began in 2022 and, he argues, is largely absent from public coverage.
discussed: Founding a fund in 1994, the month Netscape shipped
How cloud removed the fixed costs of servers, racks and licences that once made a pivot impossible
The 2017 to 2021 period, which his partners judged worse than 2000 on valuation
Vanilla term sheets with no board seat as a marker of the top
Pay-to-play recapitalisations diluting non-participating investors roughly ten to one
Why venture firms die slowly rather than quickly, continuing to claim they are in business while deploying almost nothing
Tokenisation of real estate cash flows as his next area of study
learned: Venture accounting lets firms carry marks that public markets would have repriced, so distress stays hidden longer
The sector is bifurcated. AI, crypto and blockchain attract capital while everything else stays frozen
Illiquidity is the through-line connecting venture, private equity and private credit. Getting in is easy and getting out is the problem
Both venture and private equity are broadening from institutional to retail investors, which is when the public starts to care
notable: Eisman uses this episode repeatedly afterwards as the first sighting of the exit problem he later tracks through private credit.

title: Tariffs Are Back, Apple's Big Bet, and AI's Real Impact - The Friday Market Wrap!
summary: Recorded from the road. Sector tariffs arrive, and Eisman applies real scepticism to a headline investment promise.
discussed: Switzerland threatened at 39% and improving its offer, India raised from 25% to 50%
Pharma tariffs threatened to escalate to 150% then 250% to force domestic factory building
100% semiconductor tariffs, waived for companies building in the United States
Apple pledging another 100 billion dollars, reaching 600 billion over four years
Vertex down 20% on a failed pain drug despite fine revenue and earnings
Eli Lilly down 14% despite beating and raising, on disappointing obesity pill data
Super Micro down 18% while Arista rose on more proprietary products
learned: Effective total tariff rate heading to roughly 13% to 14%, per his go-to policy analyst
In pharma and biotech the pipeline matters more than current earnings, which is why beats can be punished
Investment pledges deserve arithmetic. Apple invests around 55 billion a year in China, so the promised US figure needs context before it is taken at face value
Proprietary products defend margins. Commodity servers do not
notable: He says the president appears to take corporate investment announcements at face value when more scepticism might be appropriate.

title: Steve Eisman Shares the Real Story Behind Predicting the 2008 Crash
summary: The role reverses and CNBC's Melissa Lee interviews him. The most complete first-person account of his career and the Big Short trade in the whole run.
discussed: Why he is structurally bullish: after 2014 he studied technology and industrials and revised his view of the economy
His Oppenheimer coverage spanning investment banks, Fannie, Freddie, Sallie Mae, credit cards and the subprime lenders
Turning negative on subprime lenders in early 1998
Shorting New Century, Countrywide and Washington Mutual as equities, with borrow costs as high as 25%
Moving into credit default swaps because the equity shorts were illiquid and expensive
The single metric he cared most about in a securitisation: the share of no-doc and low-doc loans
Visiting Aames Financial in the 1990s and finding the chairman personally on the loan committee
Why what happened to Greece cannot happen to the United States while treasuries have no alternative
learned: He describes living The Man Who Shot Liberty Valance, a candid note on being credited for a call
Reserve currency status alone is not the protection. The banking system's plumbing runs on treasuries, and no alternative exists yet
He owns Apple unhedged while acknowledging it is fully captive to US and China relations, an honest statement of a position held despite a known risk
notable: Asked about the industry's hunger to call the next crisis, he suggests people want a movie made about them.

title: The U.S. Sets an Unprecedented AI Chip Agreement with China | The Friday Market Wrap!
summary: An end-of-quarter reflection that doubles as his clearest statement of how he reads an earnings season.
discussed: Nvidia permitted to sell certain chips into China under an unprecedented arrangement
UnitedHealth halved from its 2024 peak above 600 dollars, with Berkshire disclosing a new position
Arista beating strongly while Cisco beat only slightly
The MLP collapse as a case study in paradigm shifts
learned: His earnings-season method: he is not a trader, and uses quarterly reports as a thesis check rather than a trading trigger
Revenue is harder to manage than earnings, so a revenue miss is the more serious red flag, especially for growth stocks
Decide in advance which numbers matter, and listen to conference calls for what is not said
Paradigm shifts are hard to see because management and investors are both too invested, financially and emotionally, to read the signs
Balance sheets matter as much as income statements, which the MLP investors learned the hard way
notable: He ranks AI stories by how proprietary the product is, which is why he separates Nvidia and Arista from Super Micro and Dell.

title: Industrial Sector Explained: Data Center Growth & Rise of Vertiv | The Real Eisman Playbook Ep. 21
summary: JP Morgan's industrial analyst, best known for years of scepticism on GE, on how data centres turned a thematically dull sector into a historic investment cycle.
discussed: Data centres upgraded from a ferocious to a historic investment cycle
The scale check: data centres are only about 5% of US private non-residential construction, so the growth rate matters more than the base
Hyperscaler capex of 300 to 400 billion a year plus utility capex in the hundreds of billions
Vertiv with roughly 80% data centre exposure, more than Nvidia by revenue share
Cooling demand rising exponentially as chip density climbs from about 100 kilowatts toward 200 and beyond
A 300 gigawatt US data centre pipeline of which only about 35% is funded
GE Vernova still losing a billion dollars in wind while power demand carries the rest
learned: The AI trade extends well past chips into transformers, distribution and grid equipment
New chip architectures every couple of years push hyperscalers toward outsourced thermal design rather than in-house teams
Autos and process industries are not participating, so the capex cycle is narrower than it appears
Tusa's old GE critique: the balance sheet sat in financial services while the earnings were reported from the industrial side, and the sell-side incentive structure discouraged asking about it
notable: Peacock today, feather duster tomorrow, peacock again. Tusa's line for the cyclicality of industrial reputations.

title: Powell Says Nothing & Markets Cheer, Amazon Wins & Target Loses | The Friday Market Wrap!
summary: He opens by explaining exactly how he makes the show, then uses retail market caps to show how completely the sector reordered itself.
discussed: His process: he starts writing Monday, builds a script through the week, and writes every word himself
Palantir down 20% from its high while still up over 100% on the year
Amazon at 2.4 trillion, Walmart at 810 billion, Costco at 434 billion and Target at only 45 billion
Target reporting badly and naming an insider chief executive, disappointing the street
Home Depot reaffirming weak guidance, with sales up 3% and earnings down 2%
learned: Seasonal rules like selling in May are mostly noise. He shows the arithmetic of having sold on 30 May and missing a 9% to 13% move
Monthly Fed pronouncements matter little unless the Fed turns genuinely aggressive. Everything else is tinkering
His Jim Cramer point about 2008: the crisis was never about rates, it was about the financial system, and rate cuts cannot fix a broken system
The existing-home market is frozen because owners refinanced at 3% to 4% and will not sell into a 6.5% market while they still have jobs
notable: Target's market cap was once roughly three times its current level, which he offers as a caution about assuming today's leaders are permanent.

title: Tesla vs Waymo: Who Will Win the Robotaxi Race? | The Real Eisman Playbook Ep. 22
summary: TD Cowen's auto analyst on why Tesla earnings fell about 57% from the 2022 peak while the stock stayed flat, and whether autonomy can justify the gap.
discussed: Over-earning in 2022 at roughly 4 dollars a share and 25% gross margin, off a single ageing platform
Why a vehicle remains an emotional purchase, so software updates do not substitute for redesigns
Chinese manufacturers matching then exceeding Tesla on speed of development
EV penetration around 7.5% of new sales, with a pull-forward expected before credits expire
Waymo at over 250,000 weekly fully autonomous rides against Tesla's very limited service
Why solving autonomy in Manhattan differs completely from solving it at 3am in a quiet suburb
GM as his top overall pick, Aptiv as top supplier
learned: A metric can be right for the wrong reason. Growth over market was read as pure secular EV demand when mix and trim were doing much of the work
Design variety expands demand. Two vehicles on one platform can sell to buyers who would reject either alone
Tesla's case now rests on autonomy and cheaper product rather than on current deliveries
notable: Eisman stays on the sidelines and says so, offering his own purchase of a Tesla as the barometer for autonomy actually working.

title: Trump vs The Fed, U.S. Takes 10% Stake in Intel, Cracker Barrel Cracks | The Friday Market Wrap!
summary: A long wrap covering an attempt to remove a Fed governor, a government equity stake in Intel, and a full ranking of sector performance.
discussed: Mortgage fraud allegations against Fed Governor Lisa Cook and the attempt to fire her for cause
The US taking a 10% equity stake in Intel via Chips Act funds, with the commerce secretary signalling more such deals
Semiconductors leading all subsectors, followed by real estate management on CoStar and CBRE
Diversified financials up 10%, with Goldman up 31%
Food staples and retail lagging, with Target down 28%
Salesforce and Adobe falling in a bull market where tech outperformed
learned: His test for industrial policy is symmetry. Ask how you would feel when the other party holds the same equity stake and steers the company toward its agenda
Defensive stocks keep underperforming while the economy holds up, so their weakness is information about growth
Subsector analysis reveals what sector analysis hides. AI is already producing losers inside the winning sector
When iconic software names fall during a tech rally, the market is pricing a moat problem rather than a cycle
notable: He admits he raised Cracker Barrel's logo reversal purely so he could say Cracker Barrel cracked.

title: Steve Eisman Answers YOUR Investing Questions | The Real Eisman Playbook Episode 23
summary: A scripted mailbag episode that turns into the most personal statement of method in the run, covering what he reads, how he researches and why he sleeps better investing only in America.
discussed: Why he avoids business books and reads history, psychology and politics instead
Richard Posner as his formative influence, having read roughly 35 of the judge's 40 books
How Posner's 1974 antitrust book taught him that ideas matter and that disciplines can be reframed
The pre-Dodd-Frank alphabet soup of regulators and how banks played them against each other
Quantitative easing inflating the Fed balance sheet with debatable effect on the real economy
Holding cash, and how his view changed as his confidence in the economy grew
The MLP collapse revisited, including a call where management could not answer a cost-of-capital question
learned: His research loop: form a thesis from fundamental work, then pay for outside data that can confirm or destroy it. He paid for the Moody's securitisation database precisely for that
Leverage without capital retention is dangerous, the specific flaw that broke the MLPs
He recommends the CFA course over any book for anyone wanting to run money
Having predicted the end of the world once, he is in no hurry to predict it again, and sees no evidence for it
notable: His closing advice is about sleep. He once woke at 3am to check a global portfolio and could never get back to sleep. Investing as a passion is fine, as a preoccupation it is a signal to change your style.

title: Google Wins Antitrust Case, Is AI The Next Bubble? | The Friday Market Wrap!
summary: He opens with a correction to his own error, then works through Google's antitrust win and the first serious articulation of his AI bubble worry.
discussed: Correcting himself: the Fed was created by the Federal Reserve Act of 1913, not a constitutional amendment
An appeals court rejecting the emergency-powers basis for tariffs, with a Supreme Court appeal expected
Google winning the antitrust case outright, which he attributes partly to AI competition making search look less dominant
Two of the three overhangs on Apple clearing at once
Buffett opposing the Kraft Heinz breakup while Berkshire holds 27.5%
Salesforce beating but guiding weakly, down almost 6%, and flat over five years despite being up nearly 6,000% since 2004
Lululemon missing a shift in silhouettes
learned: Correcting a factual error on air, promptly and without hedging, is part of how the show builds trust
The AI worry stated cleanly: if scaling ever-larger models is losing steam and returns disappoint, investment slows and a painful digestion period follows, as in 2001
Retailers eventually miss a fashion inflection, and they all do, which is the structural risk in the sector
notable: He notes reports that the newest model release was not much better than its predecessor, the first appearance of the scaling question that becomes his central AI risk.

title: Steve Eisman's Masterclass on Financial Literacy | The Real Eisman Playbook Episode 24
summary: A formal solo lecture in eight parts, and the single most useful episode for a non-professional investor. His stated aim is to teach the language of investing, which he calls the entrance fee to the club.
discussed: Market corrections, and why his own answer differs completely from 2007 when he told people to go to cash
Why he believes another crisis of that kind is unlikely after Dodd-Frank deleveraging, while a recession is always possible
Long-term investing: buy the indices, use SPY for lower risk tolerance and add QQQ for more, invest on a schedule and do not market time
Thesis creep explained through a worked Capital One example
Shorting, short squeezes, and why forced covering by risk managers makes them worse
Valuation methods by sector: price to earnings, EV to EBITDA, price to tangible book for balance-sheet-dependent financials
Sector weights, and how reclassifying Meta, Google and Amazon would lift tech from 31% to over 40%
How interest rates hit growth stocks hardest through the discount rate in a discounted cash flow
learned: Thesis creep is the bane of every investor. When the thesis breaks, you were wrong, and holding on because the stock is now cheaper is a different decision pretending to be the same one
He does not much like discounted cash flow because it needs too many variables, while admitting it is in principle correct
Safety sectors still exist but several are less safe than they were, since cable and traditional media stopped being defensive
Most professionals fail to beat the averages over long periods, which is the honest case for indexing
notable: Every profession is a club with its own language, and mastery of that language is the entrance fee. That is his stated purpose for the whole series.

title: Oracle's Massive AI Forecast, Hot IPOs Explained | The Friday Market Wrap!
summary: Oracle misses on both lines and the stock takes off, because the backlog number rewrites the story. He then grades the new IPO class.
discussed: Oracle missing earnings and revenue, then disclosing remaining performance obligations of 455 billion, up 359%
How that backlog converts into forward infrastructure revenue guidance
CoreWeave described as the strongest story of the recent IPO vintage
Circle's revenue being interest earned on the treasuries backing its coins, making it highly rate-sensitive
Buy now pay later names with intense retail followings and untested credit
learned: A backlog can matter more than the quarter. Investors bought the obligation schedule and ignored two misses
A business whose earnings track short-term rates does not deserve a technology multiple
Buy now pay later credit has never been tested by a recession, and he expects investors to exit the whole group when recession fears return
The market's default assumption has flipped. Once a new thing had to prove itself, now it is assumed to be the next big thing until disproved
notable: He walks through beta as a portfolio tool while explicitly refusing to advise a listener to add leverage through it.

title: Trump's Battle with the Fed Explained | The Real Eisman Playbook Episode 25
summary: A former Dallas Fed president, now Goldman vice chairman, on what actually happens inside Fed meetings during political pressure. Eisman calls himself a professional critic and Kaplan the man in the room.
discussed: Growth at 1.25% to 1.5%, with unemployment low only because labour supply has fallen
Tariffs as a short-run headwind even if they eventually raise growth
Whether political pressure is discussed at Fed meetings, which Kaplan says it is not
Kaplan's dissent on aggressive forward guidance during COVID, when he argued the neutral rate would drift up
Why he would not build an operation that is only competitive behind a tariff moat
Consolidation among roughly 4,150 US banks, only about 80 of which hold more than 20 billion in assets
learned: Doing the deal is the easy part. Integration is where mergers are won or lost
Large banks hold a widening structural advantage in technology spending and deposit gathering, which is the argument for regional consolidation
When an entire group disagrees with you, the first thought should be that you are wrong. Kaplan's point is that occasionally you still are not
Eisman's own long-standing call for a regional bank M&A wave gets its fullest airing here
notable: Eisman's framing of the difference between them: he was an analyst and fund manager, which makes him a professional critic, while Kaplan was in the room where it happens.

title: Are Stablecoins the Next Big Thing? Luigi Mangione Terror Charges Dropped | The Weekly Wrap
summary: A solo wrap built around a stablecoin primer: the opportunity is real in cross-border payments, but consumer payments are a fortress stablecoins probably cannot storm. He opens on the Mangione ruling and the Kirk assassination, arguing markets stay peaceful because everyone accepts a final arbiter.
discussed: A New York judge dismissing state terrorism charges against Luigi Mangione, with murder and weapons charges remaining
The Charlie Kirk assassination as evidence of how polarized discourse has become, contrasted with market Reddit rage that never turns violent
Circle going public June 4, 2025 at 31 and trading at 140, which put stablecoins on everyone's radar
Cross-border payments routing through three to five banks, the process stablecoins could streamline first
Why consumer payments resist disruption: the merchant pays the 2.5 to 3% fee, Visa and Mastercard take only about 15 basis points, and rewards lock consumers in
Tether as the sector's reputational risk: the largest stablecoin company, not US-based and unregulated
Mailbag on valuing loss-making tech with DCF supplemented by price to sales
learned: A payment system where the consumer pays nothing upfront is nearly impossible to disrupt on price; you have to bribe consumers away from rewards they already get free
Attack the clunky corridor first. Cross-border and remittances, not consumer checkout, is where stablecoins can win
How companies are valued within a sector is set by consensus, what he calls the mafia; accept the terms of debate or do not play, but do not argue with them
An unregulated offshore giant can damage the reputation of its regulated US competitors; Tether risk is Circle risk
notable: His answer to why market rage never turns violent: unlike politics, the market is a final arbiter everyone concedes makes the final decision.

title: Breaking Down the United Healthcare Disaster: What’s REALLY Going On? | Real Eisman Playbook Ep. 26
summary: Baird's managed care analyst, who was in the auditorium at UnitedHealth's investor day when Brian Thompson was murdered, walks through how the most hated company in the world went from PR noise to genuine fundamental cracks. The core of the bear case is Optum Health, the crown jewel, being structurally impaired by V28 risk model changes the company still has not offset.
discussed: The timeline: Thompson murdered in December at the investor day, the stock falling from about 600 to around 440 by February on PR alone, recovering to 600, then breaking on first quarter results in April
UnitedHealthcare's three insurance pillars: Medicare Advantage, Medicaid and commercial, with Medicare Advantage the biggest earnings driver
Optum Health as the crown jewel: converting 90% of roughly 10 million Medicare Advantage members at 10 to 15% margins could double enterprise earnings over a decade
The V28 risk model revisions phasing in equally across 2024 to 2026, which removed thousands of ICD-10 codes that mapped to payable condition categories
The disclosure problem: a roughly 3.3 billion dollar gain from selling stakes in Optum businesses, about 3 dollars of 27 dollars in 2024 EPS, mentioned only vaguely in the 10-K
Baird's underperform: bull case of 257 against a stock at 305, on a 14 to 15 times multiple he calls the new normal versus the old 20 times
learned: Separate PR noise from fundamental cracks. The first 20 to 25% drawdown was noise; the April quarter was not
Optimized clinic models have no slack. When reimbursement rules change, tightly staffed value-based care has very limited offsets, which is why the South Florida models disappeared
When a company's entire year of earnings growth comes from a gain on sale disclosed as a vague line item, treat management confidence with suspicion
Eisman's own rule surfaces again: without dramatically improved disclosure, the stock is very difficult to recommend regardless of valuation
notable: Ha's bull case implies 15% downside, and after marketing across the country he has found a definitive zero healthcare investors positive on the name.

title: The Wild West of Crypto: Chaos, Shenanigans, & The AI Revolution | The Friday Market Wrap!
summary: Framed by his upcoming Andrew Ross Sorkin interview on 1929, he argues crypto today rhymes with the unregulated shenanigans and leverage of that era. He then maps the AI trade into themes of winners and losers and flags a tiring market under the surface.
discussed: Monday's crypto selloff of about 10% in some coins on no news, traced to the offshore structure of trading
Binance handling roughly 40% plus of global crypto spot volume after migrating from China to Japan to Malta to the Cayman Islands, which he calls a big bunch of red flags
Market breadth deteriorating: less than 60% of the S&P 500 above its 50-day moving average near all-time highs
AI hardware winners: Nvidia, Broadcom, Arista Networks, Amphenol, maybe Cisco, and CoreWeave, the data center manager public since March
The consensus that AI guts consultants and traditional software: Gartner down 49% and Accenture down 32% this year
Morgan Stanley's estimate of 2.9 trillion dollars in data center spending through 2028, 1.4 trillion funded by hyperscaler cash flow and the rest by debt of every flavor
Nvidia's new vendor financing making an otherwise healthy funding story less clean
learned: History rhymes too often. The 1929 mix of no regulation, manipulation and crazy leverage maps directly onto offshore crypto today
US-regulated crypto firms hold the high ground on leverage limits, which makes them safer and less competitive at the same time
A market at highs with shrinking breadth is consolidating at best and tiring at worst
That half of the AI buildout is funded from operating cash flow of large famous companies is what keeps the story healthy; watch the other half
Too little regulation gives you a casino, too much stalls the system; his job is measuring the odds between them

title: The AI Revolution: Winners, Losers, & The Future of Tech | The Real Eisman Playbook Episode 27
summary: Wedbush's resident tech bull calls this a fourth industrial revolution and an unprecedented capex buildout, and Eisman lets him run through the whole board: Apple, Tesla, Palantir, Nvidia and the derivative plays. Two bulls, but Eisman keeps forcing the how questions under each thesis.
discussed: The ATCO saga: Ives named chairman on Monday, a 250 million dollar private placement to buy Worldcoin, the stock riding from 145 to 80 to 40 and back up
Apple's elephant in the room: no AI story until it doubles down on the Gemini partnership, despite a roughly 8.5 out of 10 iPhone cycle
Hyperscaler capex adding up to 300 to 350 billion dollars, and Nvidia growing revenue 55% year over year at a 4 trillion dollar market cap
Power as the biggest constraint on the buildout, with his thesis of small nuclear reactors powering data centers
Palantir as Karp being the Musk of the enterprise: software behind every three-letter agency now moving commercial
Tesla versus Waymo on autonomy: Waymo's cars costing 200,000 to 230,000 dollars in five cities against Tesla's scale at 30,000 dollars per vehicle
Second, third and fourth derivative plays: MongoDB, Snowflake, GE Vernova, Nebius, and Spotify in his top 30 as a consumer AI monetization bet
learned: The AI trade moves in derivatives: once the buildout layer is priced, follow the breadcrumbs to data mining, power and consumer use cases
Enterprise is where AI spending is today; the consumer wave is the next leg, which is how names like Spotify sneak into an AI list
Scale is the autonomy argument: whoever produces millions of cheap autonomous vehicles owns the market and everyone else pays rent
Ives got vicious institutional email for his early Palantir call, a reminder that the most profitable calls often draw the most abuse first
notable: Eisman opens by contrasting their outfits, his stayed sport jacket against the tech analyst's Wild West look, then congratulates Ives on the ATCO chairmanship mid-episode.

title: U.S. Consumers Are Collapsing: Cars, Credit, & the Chaos Ahead | The Weekly Wrap
summary: A wrap with a returning guest: Lakshmi Ganapathi of Unicus Research lays out the case that the prime consumer was a stimulus-era illusion now unwinding through auto loans and credit cards. Eisman frames it with his math showing the US economy barely grows once AI capex is stripped out.
discussed: The government shutdown that the market completely ignored, with the S&P and Nasdaq at all-time highs

His GDP arithmetic: 29.18 trillion in 2024, 1.8% expected growth of about 530 billion, against roughly 400 billion of AI infrastructure spend, leaving under 50 basis points of growth for everything else
Stimulus checks inflating credit scores so subprime borrowers looked prime, meaning ABS pools labeled prime hold effectively subprime auto loans
The used car market bifurcating: only older cars under about 10,000 dollars moving, with dealers and banks modifying loans to avoid taking losses
Credit card debt up roughly 50% from third quarter 2020, about 400 billion dollars of additional balances, while issuers cut credit lines as student loan defaults drop scores 100 to 200 points
Her warnings on meme stock Opendoor, and the abuse she gets from retail holders for making them
learned: A credit score is a snapshot, not a truth. Government transfers can make a borrower look prime long enough to get a loan he cannot service
Watch what securitization data says about the consumer monthly; it leads the official statistics
When the only used cars that move cost under 10,000 dollars, the consumer is telling you something the headline GDP number is not
Retail investors trusting a famous fund manager's endorsement is not diligence; her Opendoor warnings are aimed exactly at that reflex
notable: Asked what critics say, she reports being called dumb and accused of shorting Opendoor, then explains compliance bars her from trading her own calls at all.

title: Inside the AI Chip War: From Nvidia’s Dominance to Intel’s Turmoil | The Real Eisman Playbook Ep 28
summary: Bernstein's semiconductor analyst, 18 years on the beat since three weeks after Bear Stearns failed, walks the whole chip landscape: an AI trade that is ripping while everything else is lackluster. The throughline is that a digestion period is a 100% certainty eventually, just not now, not next year, and maybe not 2027.
discussed: The Nvidia origin story of this cycle: ChatGPT in November 2022, then the May 2023 earnings call he titled the big bang
Why a capex digestion phase is inevitable but invisible on the horizon, with Jensen Huang and Broadcom's Hock Tan pointing past 2027
AMD's data center GPU business at 5 billion dollars from zero, impressive but small against Nvidia's roughly 100 billion, and the bull case of 5% of a claimed 500 billion TAM
The China argument: export bans forcing Huawei to build purportedly leading-edge chips at SMIC, risking a robust competitor that eventually exports

Reported proposals for a one-to-one rule pairing every foreign chip purchase with a US-made one, plus possible tariffs on semiconductors inside devices, roughly 500 dollars of chips in a 1,000 dollar smartphone
Intel's collapse: Gelsinger's build-it-and-they-will-come foundry losing about 13 billion dollars last year, and the outlandish February 2022 target of 120 billion in revenue by 2026
Why he likes Lip-Bu Tan's underpromise-and-overdeliver approach while refusing to call the turnaround
learned: Hyperscaler capex has always built and digested in cycles; the question is never whether digestion comes, only when, and betting on the date has been a losing trade for three years
Reasoning models and agentic AI multiply compute per query, which is the demand-side answer to the digestion worry
Export controls cut both ways: restricting sales to China forces China to become creative, in every sense of that word
A TAM speech is not a business. Every internet company promised 2% of a trillion; watch shipped revenue instead
A CEO who enters a turnaround declaring everything already fixed is telling you the turnaround has not started
notable: On whether Lip-Bu Tan can save Intel: he is doing absolutely the right things, and the honest answer is call me in three or four years.

title: AI’s Real Life Impact: Inside the Human Cost of the Tech Boom | The Weekly Wrap
summary: A mailbag-heavy wrap anchored by a letter from a listener named Max, whose daily experience with clumsy AI tools punctures the euphoric capex narrative. He repeats his tale of two economies math and calls the Fifth Third purchase of Comerica the start of his regional bank M&A wave.
discussed: The week's headlines: the AMD deal with OpenAI, gold crossing 4,000 dollars an ounce for the first time, and the government still shut down
Fifth Third buying Comerica at about 80 dollars, only 10 dollars above its 1998 price, which he reads as the Trump administration encouraging regional bank consolidation
His estimate that 1.8% GDP growth this year is almost entirely large-cap AI capex, leaving the rest of the economy barely growing
Max's letter: AI tools that are clumsy, imagine things and create more work, while employees are more or less forced to use them
Housing advice from the mailbag: illiquid, seven-year or longer cycles, and hidden costs from closing fees to insurance
Retirement allocation: taking required minimum distributions at 73 and buying treasuries or high-grade corporates rather than selling appreciated index funds and paying roughly 30% capital gains
learned: The AI capex frenzy must eventually generate strong returns on investment; right now it is so early that anyone can literally say anything
One frustrated employee's letter is a better check on the euphoric AI narrative than another sell-side report
Never sell an appreciated asset and pay 30% tax to buy a 6% bond fund; fund bond purchases from money already being forced out, like RMDs
Match stock sales with equal gains and losses; taxes are the hidden factor that hurts otherwise good decisions
notable: He puts a listener named Max at the center of the episode, working double time to clean up after the AI tools his employer forces on him.

title: Inside America’s Economic Divide: AI, Tariffs, & The Fed | The Real Eisman Playbook Episode 29
summary: CNBC's senior economics reporter pushes back on Eisman's framing, insisting the market and the economy are different questions, then works through the K-shaped economy, tariffs and Fed history. The episode ends far from the ticker, in Liesman's stories from 1990s Russia, where nobody understood what a price was.
discussed: Eisman's twitch: 1.8% growth on 29.18 trillion of GDP is about 530 billion, roughly matching the 400 billion plus of hyperscaler AI spend, so the economy ex-AI is flat

Josh Brown's line that the momentum will continue as long as the momentum continues, and the parallel to Henry Blodget, who was right about the internet changing the world and wrong for investors anyway
Auto loans as the last bill a stressed consumer skips, and why used car weakness therefore matters
Tariff damage papered over by AI: Orvis closing stores and laying off, fly-fishing importers hit on both the import tariff and metal content
Greenspan running Fed communication through a single reporter, John Barry, before the FOMC statement arrived around 1994
His years covering Russia: the US government paying accounting firms millions to write Russia a universal legal code, and oil output reversing a 20-year decline within two years of privatization
learned: Do not conflate the market and the economy; they are separate pies divided on different logic and different clocks
A technology can change the world, create dynastic wealth and still lose money for the investors who bought the story at the top, the Blodget lesson
Watch the payment hierarchy: when the car loan, the bill people pay first, comes under stress, the consumer is genuinely stretched
Markets are not natural. Liesman's Russia stories show the price mechanism is a learned institution, not an instinct
notable: The missile factory director asked for 200 million dollars to make rifles; asked how he knew it was a good business, he answered that before the revolution, Russians created great rifles.

title: The Bank Stock Rout: Separating Facts From Fiction | The Weekly Wrap
summary: Bank earnings kick off the season against a backdrop of tariff whiplash, and he argues the credit scare is a normal cycle, not 2008. The distinction he draws is between visible commercial deterioration and the kind that actually causes a recession.
discussed: Trump's Friday threat of 100% tariffs on China sending NASDAQ down 3%, unwound by a Monday Truth Social post saying it will all be fine
JPMorgan's $170 million loss on the Tricolor fraud bankruptcy, which he calls tiny for a bank that size
Commercial non-accrual loans up 33% year over year at JPMorgan and 119% at Citi, with no problems at Wells Fargo
Jamie Dimon's phrase too small to succeed, and why Dodd-Frank and soaring technology costs favour the big banks
Fifth Third buying Comerica two weeks earlier at around $80 per share
Progressive as the champion that emerges in a mature industry by passing efficiency to customers as better pricing
learned: Quarterly reports exist to check the thesis; buy, sell and hold are all three investment decisions, and doing nothing takes as much guts as trading
Some commercial credit deterioration is normal; real deterioration arrives with the recession, not before it
Regional and community banks must merge to carry regulatory and technology costs or go the way of the dodo
In mature industries, reclassified as cyclical or safety sectors, the companies that keep taking share are the ones that convert efficiency into price
notable: His earnings-season image: industries report like herds in the Sahara, and the banks come first like the gazelles.

title: The Next Revolution: AI, Advertising, and the Collapse of Old Media
summary: Two analysts from one of Eisman's favourite research boutiques cover the wreckage of old media: Apple's reprieve in the Google antitrust case, the cable-versus-fiber stalemate, Verizon firing its CEO, and AI ads that may end the agency business. The closing debate is whether AI revenue can ever justify the infrastructure spend.
discussed: The Google payments to Apple, $20 billion a year at roughly 100% margin and about 20% of Apple's operating income, ruled illegal and then left intact at the remedy stage
Why the judge blinked: district judges hate being overturned, and AI's arrival gave him an easy out
Cable versus fiber as technically interchangeable networks, with bears betting 80% of the country gets overbuilt
Fiber overbuilds costing roughly $4,000 per connected home, funded by private equity money pouring in
Verizon firing its CEO and installing board member Dan Schulman, 67, who Eisman says did not do a good job running PayPal
Meta producing a fully finished TV ad from just a brand logo, with the 15 most effective versions A/B tested by the end of the day
Paramount under David Ellison, the Bari Weiss hire as a pitch to Washington, and the case for streaming consolidation
learned: Disruption starts at the bottom, per Clay Christensen: AI ads first empower small brands that could never afford an agency, then the technology climbs
The AI capex bull case is a company paying nearly the full salary of a $125,000 employee for a bot; the bear case is four competitors driving the bot's price below what the infrastructure needs
When there is no counterfactual you can dream any dream; the honest position on AI returns is humility
A regulated industry's structure can be the story: legacy Bell-system norms explain why Verizon reached for a 67-year-old insider
notable: The verdict on who has to justify the entire AI buildout: it is really on Sam Altman's shoulders to prove this makes sense.

title: The K-Shaped Reality: AI Booms While Housing & Tesla Struggle | The Weekly Wrap
summary: He splits 89 reporting companies into two economies: AI and everything else. The AI side prints spectacular numbers while Tesla, managed care and housing-adjacent names deteriorate, the K-shaped economy in one earnings week.
discussed: Apple hitting an all-time high on iPhone 17 sales up about 14% versus the 16, market cap just below $4 trillion
GE Vernova, the turbine maker feeding AI's insatiable electricity demand, up around 80% this year
Amphenol's third quarter: sales up 53% in total and 41% organically, EPS up 87% year over year
Tesla revenue up 6% only because buyers rushed the expiring $7,500 EV credit; net income down 37% to $1.4 billion with zero guidance
The FICO price war after the FHFA required lenders to accept VantageScore, with the credit bureaus striking back
Molina reporting $1.84 versus $3.90 expected on exchange medical costs, cutting 2025 guidance by 26%
learned: A K-shaped economy shows up in earnings before it shows up in macro data: sort the reports into AI and everything else and the split is stark
Revenue pulled forward by an expiring subsidy is not growth; Musk gave no December-quarter guidance because he could not
Starting a price war is one thing; starting one against the three companies that supply your competition (the bureaus behind VantageScore) is another
A safety stock can be turbocharged into a growth stock when its end market explodes, as Amphenol shows
notable: He notes the date: October 24, exactly 96 years after the 1929 crash began, teeing up the Sorkin interview.

title: Inside the Data Center Boom: Understanding the Massive Infrastructure That Supports AI
summary: MoffettNathanson's digital infrastructure analyst maps the data center landscape from first principles: who the hyperscalers are, why most of the buildout happens in private markets, and what a GPU is actually worth. Unusually for a coverage universe, most of the space he analyses is not publicly traded at all.
discussed: Why only Digital Realty and Equinix remain public: the capital required and years of negative cash flow spooked public shareholders
A data center defined as a warehouse for computers, with the four hyperscalers being Amazon, Microsoft, Google and Meta
The REIT problem: paying out cash flow as dividends forces constant trips to the capital markets to fund growth
Equinix as the connectivity hub, with cloud on-ramps he compares to on-ramps to the Jersey Turnpike
Bitcoin miners repurposing power-rich, latency-insensitive sites for high performance computing
GPU economics: CoreWeave depreciates chips over six years, and its OpenAI deal runs five years with two one-year renewals
Cogent's conversion of the old Sprint network into a wavelengths business against Lumen and Zayo
learned: Judge an AI infrastructure deal on its unit economics, not on a headline multiple of spend
Tight power supply is the industry's pricing stick; lifting the constraint helps volumes but pushes returns back toward the cost of capital
The economic life of a GPU is genuinely unknown, and the most sophisticated buyer signing a five-plus-two year lease is the best evidence available
Hyperscalers will build in oddball markets that third-party developers avoid, because developers fear the re-leasing risk 10 to 15 years out
notable: When Del Deo mentions Bitcoin miners pivoting to high performance computing, Eisman replies that the sentence was definitely in English but he is not quite sure he understood it.

title: Andrew Ross Sorkin on the Crash of 1929 & The Parallels We See Today | The Real Eisman Playbook
summary: Sorkin spent eight years in archives, some boxes never indexed, reconstructing 1929 with the room-where-it-happened detail he brought to 2008, except everyone in this book is dead. The conversation keeps circling one theme: elites who believed they ruled the world did not see the paradigm shift coming.
discussed: Why he wrote it: Americans have only a vague idea that something very bad happened in 1929
Stock pools as normalized pump and dump, run by the era's biggest names, who circulated written circulars about it; he compares it to the Davos guest list colluding today
Jack Morgan knowing he was not his father and installing Thomas Lamont, a former journalist, as the real power behind the scenes
Ferdinand Pecora, the little-known lawyer from Queens on $250 a week, whose hearings shamed the uber-WASPs though nobody went to jail
The Fed of 1929 seeing too much speculation but fearing for its own existence if it raised rates, then failing to flood the system with liquidity in 1930 to 1933
Eisman's own 2008 mistake: assuming the government knew how bad it was, disproved by the scene where officials learn AIG is in trouble and have no idea
learned: The crash formula is credit plus leverage plus FOMO, and the policy failure is hesitating on the front end and withholding liquidity on the back end
The hardest thing a person lives through is a paradigm shift; masters-of-the-universe confidence is precisely what blinds them
Never assume the authorities have read the research; in both 1929 and 2008 the people in charge understood less than the market's analysts
Humility can be strategy: Jack Morgan's genius was knowing he needed someone else to play his father's role
notable: Eisman's framing: Too Big to Fail was Lord of the Rings, and Sorkin has now written the prequel, in the wrong order, so he never has to write a sequel.

title: The AI Boom Rolls On: AI Partnerships Pay Off as Stocks Soar & Meta, Google & Microsoft Go All-In
summary: A Halloween wrap where every AI partnership announcement makes a stock soar and the big three all raise capex, yet the market punishes Meta and rewards Google for the same behaviour. His explanation is return on invested capital: cloud businesses earn on AI spending now, Meta has to build products first.
discussed: The US-China agreement landing as only a one-year truce after markets hit all-time highs on the outline of a deal
The Fed's second 25 basis point cut, with Powell warning a December cut may not happen
Nvidia reaching $5 trillion in market cap while Apple and Microsoft breach $4 trillion; Europe's largest stock is not even at $500 billion
The announcement effect: PayPal as a ChatGPT payment engine, Nvidia's $1 billion Nokia stake for 6G, and Qualcomm's Humain deal, where he flags Humain hedging across Nvidia, AMD and Qualcomm
2025 capex: Meta in the low $70 billions, Microsoft $80 billion, Google above $90 billion; all three beat, yet Meta fell 7% and Microsoft 4% while Google rose 7%
Fiserv down over 40% in a day after new management said the company had been masking its problems
UnitedHealth's Optum Health margin at 1% versus 8.3% a year ago, and Eli Lilly's $7.02 against a $5.69 estimate
learned: Identical capex headlines get opposite receptions because ROIC differs: cloud AI spending generates revenue today, product-building AI spending is a promise
In a mania, any partnership announcement is greeted with joy, but read the capacity numbers; the details still matter
Payments is a dangerous space because things change fast, and a company can mask deterioration for years before it surfaces all at once
Peacock today, feather duster tomorrow: Chipotle shows how quickly the hottest stock in a sector loses the crown
notable: His offer to the market: if anyone is listening, he is happy to become the spokesperson for anyone in AI, maybe his stock will soar.

title: Inside the Cannabis Comeback: How One Company is Beating a Broken Market | The Real Eisman Playbook
summary: A first for the show: interviewing company management, Glass House Brands, a sub-billion-dollar California cannabis grower that actually makes money in an industry left for dead. Eisman discloses he is a recent shareholder and frames the position as speculative, prompted by Trump's Truth Social posts on cannabis.
discussed: The setup: the 2018 boom priced in Biden-era legalization that never came, leaving the sector starved and oversupplied
Second quarter profitability: 53% gross margin, roughly 18% EBITDA margin, and normalized returns on equity in the mid to high teens
Production costs around $100 per unit in California, the lowest-price and most competitive market in the country
The ICE raid on their farm and hiring Julie Myers Wood, the former Bush-era ICE director, to make the workforce audit-proof
Federal Schedule I status and what rescheduling would change
Trump's two Truth Social posts on medical cannabis and his public support for Florida's Amendment 3 adult-use measure, against DeSantis
The asset: about 165 acres with 120 acres of greenhouse, only two of five greenhouses productive so far, and export prices five to six times California's
learned: Look at sectors everyone has abandoned when the political weather shifts; Eisman's model is FanDuel and DraftKings before sports betting normalized
Winning in the most competitive, lowest-priced market is transferable; the inverse is not, like training at altitude
In a broken industry the survivor is the cost leader, not the best story
Management quality shows in crisis response: their answer to an ICE raid was to hire the former ICE director and invite scrutiny
notable: Farrar's line on expansion once other markets open: it is going to be like throwing a knife into a pillow.

title: Cracks Beneath the AI Boom: Is the U.S. Economy Heading For a Downturn? | The Weekly Wrap
summary: With the government shutdown blacking out official statistics, private data points to a cooling labour market and the K-shaped economy sharpens: the top 10% of households drive nearly half of consumer spending. He argues that makes the economy unusually exposed to a stock market correction.
discussed: The Challenger report showing the most announced October job cuts in over 20 years, sending stocks down and bonds up on Thursday
Cap-weighted indices masking narrowness: the S&P 500 up roughly 16% and NASDAQ up about 23%, flattered by the largest names
The Mamdani effect on New York property: SL Green already down 25% this year and talk of Wall Street firms eyeing Dallas
Arista growing EPS 25% and still falling, because in-line guidance is not enough at over 40 times 2026 earnings
Apollo beating on revenue and earnings yet down about 20% this year on private credit worries after Tricolor and First Brands
FICO guiding fiscal 2026 to $38.17 against a $39.19 consensus after raising score prices from $5 toward $10, with the FHFA pushing an alternative
learned: When official data goes dark, markets trade on single private data points, which amplifies volatility
Concentrated consumer spending means the wealth effect runs in reverse: a big market correction could take the whole economy with it
At 40 times forward earnings, beating estimates is table stakes; only raised guidance keeps the stock up
A monopolist that raises prices too far invites both customer revolt and its regulator to sponsor a competitor, which is how FICO got greedy
notable: He closes with a financial literacy explainer of the money multiplier, walking a $100,000 deposit through the banking system: it sounds like magic, but that is how we want it to work.

title: The Private Credit Panic: Why Wall Street's Big Winners are Now Losing | Real Eisman Playbook Ep 33
summary: Evercore's Glenn Schorr, who covers what Eisman calls the good, the bad and the ugly of finance, explains why the alternative asset managers are having a terrible year in a bull market. The core puzzle: secular growth stories keep raising record money while their stocks fall, and either the tight high-yield market or the falling manager stocks has to be wrong.
discussed: Blackstone down 15%, Apollo down 25%, KKR down 21% and Blue Owl down 33% in 2025 despite record fundraising
The contradiction of Goldman at $800 and tightening high-yield spreads while private credit stocks get shot
Private equity mechanics: seven to ten year fund lives and a good outcome of 2 to 2.5 times invested capital
Why Apollo takes the credit-fear beating: roughly half its balance sheet is its own insurance book
Praise for Jane Fraser breaking eggs at Citi after 15 years of mess, exiting hobbies and 2%-share consumer markets
Tokenization, which Eisman says not one in two million people can explain in plain English
The decline of traditional asset managers: more mutual funds than stocks, then index funds and ETFs at 5 to 15 basis points
learned: Technology eventually comes for every industry; for asset management it arrived as the index fund and the ETF
When two markets price the same risk differently, one of them has to give; watch the disagreement, not either signal alone
Traditional managers got fat and happy in the hay days and let the alternatives build private markets uncontested; not one invested in it
A back book of legacy products can drag on a firm for a decade even while new businesses hum
notable: On what Goldman would be had it skipped consumer and just raised funds 10 years ago: don't shoot me David if you're watching this, but we'd call them Morgan Stanley.

title: The Shutdown Ends, Burry's New AI Warning & Disney Stumbles | The Weekly Wrap
summary: Eisman opens by telling newer viewers about his breast cancer diagnosis and chemotherapy, then walks through the end of the shutdown and takes on Michael Burry's depreciation argument. The through line is that in this tape, high-flyers cannot disappoint on any metric, actual or perceived.
discussed: Eight Democratic senators crossing over on Monday to end the shutdown, with funding only through January 20
Burry's claim that stretched depreciation schedules will overstate Meta's earnings by 21% and Oracle's by 27% by 2028
Fitch data showing more subprime borrowers at least 60 days delinquent, another sign of the strained low-end consumer
CoreWeave's Q3 revenue of roughly 1.44 billion, up 134%, against a consensus of no profits until 2027 and a 47 times 2027 PE
Paramount's 17 billion market cap versus Netflix at 475 billion, with the Warner Brothers dance ongoing
A hot stablecoin name at roughly 70 times 2026 earnings, where the real question is who wins dominant market share
learned: Even granting Burry's math, a depreciation argument does not change cash flows; the debate is about the quality of reported earnings, not solvency
