At 47 times earnings two years out, a company cannot disappoint in any way; the multiple prices in perfection
David and Goliath can fully swap places in an industry; Paramount versus Netflix proves scale advantages migrate
In payments and stablecoins, market share, not this quarter's numbers, decides who deserves the multiple
notable: He announces mid-chemotherapy hair loss, says he is starting to wear a hat, and moves on to the shutdown in the same breath.

title: Inside Publishing's Big Shakeup: AI, TikTok & the Battle Ahead | The Real Eisman Playbook Episode 34
summary: An episode born from a conversation with his wife Valerie: two literary agents and a publisher on how book publishing changed over 20 years and what AI does next. The verdict is that the platform now precedes the book, and publishing is recalibrating the way music already has.
discussed: Why a nonfiction author now needs social media numbers before a deal, even the world's leading expert on an important topic
Romantasy readers driving deluxe print editions with etched end papers and maps after starting in self-published ebooks
Hybrid publishing's 70/30 profit split versus the traditional 10 to 12% royalty on cover price
Eisman's ChatGPT test: essays on morality in the voices of Alasdair MacIntyre and Richard Posner, produced in 30 seconds
No decade-scale cultural phenomenon in publishing in five years, nothing like Oprah's club or Harry Potter
Agents as fiduciaries weighing a modest advance against a real marketing commitment
learned: Distribution flipped: audiences are built first and monetized through books, the reverse of the old order
Publishing is tracking the music industry, where content margins collapsed and the money moved to community and events around the person
AI raises the bar rather than abolishing it; plot, pacing and characterization arriving together is the concert that is hard to mimic
People increasingly buy books because of the author, not the content; the individual is the brand
notable: The ChatGPT essays blew him out of the water: work that would have taken him a month of rereading arrived in 30 seconds, and he calls them excellent.

title: NVIDIA'S Explosive Growth Can't Hide the Market's AI Panic | The Weekly Wrap
summary: Nvidia posts accelerating 62% revenue growth at a 4.4 trillion market cap and the market still cannot hold its nerve. Eisman spends the week on why great numbers no longer calm an AI-anxious tape, leaning on Niall Ferguson's railroad analogy.
discussed: Nvidia's EPS of $1.30 versus $1.25 expected and revenue of 57 billion, up 62% versus last year and accelerating from 56%, all without China
Emotional trading: corrections Monday and Tuesday, a Wednesday rally, then a fade after the after-hours pop
Ferguson's parallel to the railroad crashes of 1873 and 1893, when overlapping lines competed returns away
Target down 4% on EPS with a new CEO refusing to say when sales turn, the stock down 39% this year
Tricolor, then First Brands, and now another credit blowup in the sequence he is tracking
A mailbag question from his high school classmate Mark on whether 2 and 20 is fair or sustainable
His FrontPoint years, 2004 to 2011, investing in Indian banks and real estate
learned: The railroad pitfalls map to AI: it may prove an upgrade of Google rather than a miracle, and overlapping LLMs may compete returns down
When the largest company on earth accelerates growth and the market still sells off, the anxiety is about the cycle, not the company
Two and twenty creates asymmetric incentives; the manager shares the upside and bears none of the downside
Emerging-market bull runs with insane IPO multiples read the same in every country; he made and lost money in India and learned humility
notable: Nvidia sang an operatic aria whose music the market at first seemed to really enjoy, and then the anxiety returned anyway.

title: Why It's So Difficult For Companies to Go Public: A CFO Explains the Process | The Real Eisman Playbook Episode 35
summary: Amy Butte, CFO of newly public travel platform Navan and CFO of the New York Stock Exchange for its 2006 IPO, dismantles the idea that going public is hire some bankers, bing bang boom. The real work is building financial processes reliable enough to repeat without mistakes, and it takes years.
discussed: Becoming NYSE CFO in January 2004 and getting the IPO done in March 2006, a two-year rebuild
Her admission that the Exchange's financial process was a plug, which is what auditors actually care about
The four things going public buys: a branding event, forced maturation, easier capital access and acquisition currency
Taxes as golf putting: a third of your score, and nobody practices it until it hurts
Navan's claim of running on less than a tenth of the customer support staffing of an Amex GBT, thanks to AI
The roadshow from the other side: portfolio managers mapping the company onto their own investment thesis
Hiring smart non-coders to build on Navan's AI framework for its next-generation product, Edge
learned: Auditors care about one thing: do you have a process that produces reliable numbers over and over without mistakes
Not every company needs every benefit of being public; NYSE needed maturation and currency, not branding
IPO pricing is a matching problem; the question is how the story fits each buyer's existing thesis, not whether the story is good
AI-era operating leverage shows up first in support headcount ratios, not in the product itself
notable: The sign-off: Eisman wishes her luck with the company, and Butte answers with best of luck to you and your health.

title: Google Surges Past OpenAI and AI Faces a Bigger Crisis That Could Break the Boom | The Weekly Wrap
summary: A Thanksgiving-week rally erases the prior week's AI correction while the competitive ground shifts under OpenAI. Eisman introduces his binding constraint framework, borrowed from bank stress tests, and argues the constraint on AI is electric power.
discussed: The market recovering last week's 2% to 3% losses on dovish Fed governor comments, back near all-time highs
Dell's quarter: EPS up 17%, revenue up 11% but a slight miss, and a 31.5 billion Q4 sales guide versus 27.6 billion expected
Gemini 3 leapfrogging ChatGPT, with Sam Altman's memo admitting we have some work to do and expecting rough vibes
The binding constraint concept from the Fed's annual bank stress test, transplanted to AI
Texas power math: proposed projects equal to consumption of over 150 million homes on an ERCOT grid serving 30 million
A European viewer's twice-rejected permit application for a simple consumer product, with a 30-page business plan
learned: Every industry has a binding constraint that governs everything else; for banks it is stress-test capital, for AI it is power
The second railroad catches up: OpenAI's lead looked structural until Gemini 3, and perceived moats in AI are measured in months
Novel power solutions, nuclear included, are becoming part of the AI investment case rather than a footnote
Europe's sclerosis is procedural; no one says no, they just never say yes, and capital goes elsewhere
notable: His correction of the week: the US produces roughly 4,200 terawatt hours, not terawatts, and he stands corrected.

title: Steve Eisman Reflects on 2008, The Big Short & Today's K-Shaped Economy | The Real Eisman Playbook Episode 36
summary: A recorded October 29 event at Case Western Reserve University, hosted by housing analyst Ivy Zelman, where Eisman retells the financial crisis for a hundred students and fields their questions on today's market. The crisis story he tells is a debt story, not an equity story, ending in what he calls the biggest fraud in human history.
discussed: His path from Harvard Law and a federal clerkship to Wall Street
Credit default swaps tying bank balance sheets into a spiderweb, and AIG's roughly 50 to 70 billion of swaps sold to the street
Underwriting standards loosening from 2002 until the 2006 standard was can you breathe
Zelman blaming Greenspan's 2004 endorsement of ARMs for the option-ARM and negative-am era
Citigroup levered about 35 to 1 pre-crisis versus about 10 to 1 now, which he calls the distance from Pluto to the sun
Silicon Valley Bank as a rates and business-model failure, not a capital problem
A student pressing him on AI driving roughly half of GDP growth, which he thinks understates it
learned: The crisis lived on the debt side of planet Earth; equity investors watching stocks missed where the risk sat
When results keep beating expectations year after year, standards loosen; prosperity itself degrades underwriting
Bank leverage, not bank size, is the systemic variable, and on that measure today's banks are basically safe
He no longer considers housing an investment; matching inflation is the best case
Sell-side rewards writing and speaking; buy-side is a quieter skill of just picking stocks and making money
notable: His sole contribution to The Big Short: overruling his wife's pleading to tell Adam McKay the cab line should be schmuck, not asshole. Schmuck is in the movie.

title: The Housing Market is Broken: Why Homes Are Unaffordable & What It Takes to Fix It | The Weekly Wrap
summary: After dismissing the Fed-cut rally as tinkering, Eisman devotes the wrap to housing: affordability is the most stretched in decades and nothing that fails to attack local supply rules deserves to be taken seriously. He closes with a primer on active ETFs versus mutual funds.
discussed: The S&P 500 up 3.7% and Nasdaq up 4.9% in the holiday week, recovering the AI correction as Fed governors bless a December cut
Bitcoin down from 125,000 in late September, barely participating in the equity rally
Salesforce's mixed quarter under the AI Grim Reaper, rescued by better Q4 revenue guidance for a 4% Thursday pop
Public builders' share of new homes at about 50%, double the 25% of 2001
Entry-level buyers needing 60% of income for the monthly payment, worse than before the financial crisis and beaten only by the late 1970s
Property taxes and insurance rising from 5% to 7% of income since 2000
His fix list: cut local regulation, impact fees and permit times, allow smaller homes, and have Washington threaten state and local funding
learned: A 25 basis point cut here and there is tinkering; the market cares, but in the long run it does not matter
Housing affordability is a local supply problem; federal gestures that skip zoning and permitting cannot begin to solve it
America still builds homes one at a time on site while Sweden builds in factories; the production model itself is antique
All else equal the actively managed ETF beats the mutual fund on taxes, disclosure and cost, but stock picking trumps structure
notable: His test for any housing plan: until the federal government threatens to cut off state and local funds over supply rules, the problem is not even beginning to be dealt with.

title: Inside the Industrial Comeback & AI’s Power Crisis with Nigel Coe | The Real Eisman Playbook Ep 37
summary: Wolfe Research's industrials analyst maps a sector split in two: pockets of fast growth wherever a company touches the data center, and no growth anywhere else. The conversation lands on power as the binding constraint on AI, with data centers migrating to wherever they can plug in.
discussed: His coverage as the successor companies of the old GE and ITT conglomerates: aerospace and defense, electrical equipment, HVAC, industrial automation
Eaton lagging because legacy businesses drag; its class eight truck units down roughly mid-teens this year
Honeywell breaking up after Elliott Management pushed to spin out aerospace, its biggest division
Data centers built by 2028 that may not get plugged in, so siting shifts to Texas and the Midwest where power exists
Gas turbines, the large ones producing 400 megawatts, back in demand after the market was left for dead in the renewables shift
3M as a classic CEO-change margin story under Bill Brown after years of PFAS liabilities
The ISM Index sub-50 for three years, now about 48; his housing-inflection picks are Lennox International and Stanley Black & Decker
learned: The best industrial stories of his career have been CEO-change margin-improvement stories, not end-market calls
Flexibility beats consistency: his most impactful sell at 250 became one of his better buys after upgrading around 90
Short cycle industrials have been stagnant for three years; the 2026 question is whether investors will pay up for cyclicality before the Fed eases
After stocks run 100% to 300%, the question shifts from the story to how much more multiple expansion is possible
notable: Eisman's compressed version of the power problem: they'll get this stuff built by 2028, the question is whether they can plug it in.

title: Netflix & Paramount’s WBD Fight Heats Up + Oracle Falls as AI Doubts Grow | The Weekly Wrap
summary: Oracle disappoints and the Warner Brothers fight turns hostile, and Eisman uses both to sketch the emerging risks to the AI trade. His bet on the media brawl: the odds favor Paramount, and Netflix shareholders should be nervous.
discussed: The Fed cutting 25 basis points on a 10 to 3 vote, with Powell signaling future cuts will be tougher and his chairmanship ending
Oracle at the center of the AI debate because, unlike Google, it cannot fund AI demand from cash flow
Netflix's announced purchase of Warner Brothers, and Jeff Bewkes's 2010 Albanian army dismissal of Netflix
Paramount's higher hostile bid, backstopped by a syndicate including Jared Kushner's private equity firm
One commentator's estimate that big tech needs 2 trillion in AI revenue by 2030 to justify the capex
2025 GDP growth of about 2% coming almost entirely from hyperscaler AI capex
Home Depot guiding 2026 EPS growth of 0 to 4% against expectations of 5%
learned: Warner Brothers has been bought and sold many times and only the executives ever benefited; culture, not price, is the risk in this deal
The longer a regulatory delay runs, the more management gets distracted, which itself changes the odds
If scaling ever-larger models loses efficacy, hyperscalers slow chip purchases and the whole virtuous cycle reverses
Strip hyperscaler capex out of 2025 and there is no GDP growth at all, which is how much the economy leans on one trade
notable: A listener named Sebastian, a software engineer, reports he can no longer conceive of doing his job without AI, and that the senior engineers are the most eager adopters.

title: Steve Eisman's Masterclass on the 2008 Financial Crisis (Part One) | The Real Eisman Playbook Ep 38
summary: Part one of a two-part lecture on the financial crisis, covering the first two of four interlocking causes: too much leverage and the subprime blowup. Eisman builds it from first principles, starting with why a bank cannot function without leverage, then narrates his own short from the inside.
discussed: The four causes: leverage, a large asset class blowing up, systemic institutions owning it, and derivatives tying balance sheets together
The bank thought experiment: 1 billion in equity, a 1% ROA, and why ROE equals ROA times leverage
Subprime's history from the first pure-play IPO in 1992 (the Money Store, Aames Financial) through 20 billion of loans in 1993
By 2006, roughly 600 billion in annual volume, about 20% of the US mortgage market, on collapsed underwriting
Monthly securitization data from the ratings agencies as the tool that let him watch credit deteriorate in real time
Why he shorted securitizations rather than stocks: borrow cost on names like New Century ran as high as 20% a year
The March and April 2007 head fake, when tax refunds made credit data look temporarily better
learned: Banks are the one business where the cost of goods sold, loan losses, is unknown at the point of sale
Leverage is like the porridge in Goldilocks: too little and banks cannot recycle deposits, too much and the system breaks
An entire generation of bank CEOs mistook leverage for genius; a $50 million paycheck is proof against self-doubt
Knowing the seasonal pattern in consumer credit let him add to shorts into the 2007 rally instead of covering
Once the buyer strike hit, the chain was mechanical: no securitization sales, no loan purchases, no refinancing, soaring defaults
notable: He ends on a deliberate cliffhanger: by late summer 2007 the crisis was already inevitable, and the reason why is part two.

title: Steve Eisman's 2025 Wrap Up: 4 Themes Defining the Market Today | The Weekly Wrap
summary: The year-end review: an S&P up 16% and NASDAQ up 20%, a 19% tariff drawdown, and a 37% rally off the April bottom. He organizes the whole year around four themes and then reads them out of the performance of all 11 S&P sectors.
discussed: The timeline: up about 1% by February 19, Liberation Day tariffs April 2, down 19% through April 8, then the AI-led recovery
The four themes: the K-shaped economy, AI revolution or bubble, private credit fears, and consumer affordability
Nvidia's third quarter revenue growing more than 60% as the one number that settles whether AI demand is real
Power as the structural constraint on AI growth, with LLM scaling doubts as the intellectual one
Tricolor and First Brands as private credit warnings even though neither loan originated in private credit
GE Vernova up over 100% on gas turbines while housing-tied Carrier fell 22%
Staples up only 2%, with Clorox, Campbell, and Kimberly Clark down 36%, 32%, and 28%
learned: Unlike subprime, where monthly securitization data let anyone watch credit rot, private credit offers no data, so no firm conclusion is possible
Defensive stocks did not just lag the AI story; tariffs squeezed margins while consumers pulled back, a double hit
A sector table tells the theme story better than the index: the same AI trade explains both the winners and the losers
Cash can work for you without risk, his closing point for retail investors after a euphoric year

title: Steve Eisman's Masterclass on the 2008 Financial Crisis (Part Two) | The Real Eisman Playbook Ep 39
summary: Part two covers the final causes, Wall Street's own subprime holdings and credit default swaps, then runs from the September 2008 collapse through Dodd-Frank, Silicon Valley Bank, and his predictions for the Trump-era regulatory turn. The ending is a reversal: the man who shorted the banks now argues for a bank merger wave.
discussed: Why Wall Street kept the excess paper: 600 billion of annual origination produced more securitizations than investors could absorb, so firms bought their own AAA product
Credit default swaps explained through a GE example, and AIG having sold about 80 billion of CDS when it hit trouble
The September 2008 sequence: Fannie and Freddie seized September 7, Lehman down September 14, Bank of America taking Merrill, AIG two days later
Clayton Mortgage checking roughly 10% samples of loan files, about 500 files per billion-dollar pool, as underwriting went to hell
Dodd-Frank creating the vice chair of financial supervision, the first head bank regulator the US ever had
Silicon Valley Bank as a mark-to-market and concentrated-deposit failure, not a capital failure, and regulators fighting the last war anyway
JP Morgan's deposit share rising from 7.4% in 2008 to over 12% as compliance and technology costs made the big bigger
learned: Incentives trump ethics every time; securitization heads knew the loans would blow up and planned to buy the paper back for pennies
Every crisis in history combines leverage, a blown-up asset class, and concentrated ownership; derivatives were 2008's only genuinely new ingredient
Unrealized bond losses hide in book value until the bonds are sold, which is exactly the accounting that let SVB's problem build
Regulation aimed at safety concentrated the industry: only large banks can afford compliance and technology, so deposits migrate to them
He has changed his mind: the system now needs many bank mergers so more banks can afford the technology arms race
notable: On the securitization bankers who said the loans were legal: after these meetings, I felt like I needed to take a shower.

title: Steve Eisman Reacts to Scenes From The Big Short
summary: Eisman walks through the scenes of The Big Short one by one and separates what happened from what the screenwriters invented. The film gets the emotional truth right even where it invents dialogue, and he ends by conceding that the angriest version of himself on screen was the accurate one.
discussed: Mark Baum being Eisman with the name changed, Ryan Gosling's Jared Vennett being Greg Lippmann of Deutsche Bank, and Vincent Daniel, Porter Collins and Danny Moses keeping their real names
His single contribution to the script, telling Adam McKay that he would have said schmuck rather than a harsher word, which made the final cut without a credit
The taxi argument with his wife never happening, but capturing the real anxiety of shorting the entire US housing market while Wall Street called them lunatics
The Las Vegas securitization conference in January 2007 with roughly 5,000 people at the Venetian, where they met everyone to test whether they were wrong
Credit default swap pricing being quoted by the dealer rather than shown on a screen, which he calls corrupt, and why subprime bond prices rose while defaults soared
Morgan Stanley's internal hedge fund being long the paper and taking a write-off of at least 10 billion in the fall of 2007, one year ahead of the general collapse
The 2015 release of his Financial Crisis Inquiry Commission interview transcript, which changed his own verdict on Steve Carell's portrayal
learned: Go meet the other side of your trade before you size it up. The Vegas trip was a search for disconfirming evidence, and it came back showing the consensus was delusional
A market where the dealer quotes the price and no screen contradicts him is not a market you can trust to mark your position honestly
Prices can move against the fundamentals for a long time. Defaults were spiking while the bonds went up, and the position had to survive that gap
When an institution is on the other side using its own capital, that is information. Morgan Stanley's write-off pre-announced the crisis a year early
Memory sands down conviction. His own contemporaneous transcript was angrier than his recollection of himself
notable: He closes on the same note the film does, that ordinary people pay for Wall Street's mistakes, and says being proved right about it makes him sad rather than superior.

title: 2026 Predictions with Dan Ives and Chris Verrone | The Real Eisman Playbook Episode 40
summary: The resident bull and the market strategist review the whiplash of 2025 and set up 2026. Verrone's discipline anchors it: as long as banks are working and credit is calm, the trend is up, whatever the narrative of the month says.
discussed: The 2025 narrative churn: DeepSeek in January, tariffs in April, ChatGPT eating Google's lunch, then Google eating everyone's
Verrone's sentiment composite hitting the second percentile after Liberation Day, then a 25% three-month rally nobody believed
Eaton flat since roughly April 2024 as investors sort real AI plays from companies that just say AI on calls
The memory super cycle: Samsung and SK Hynix as the trade Asian investors already own
Housing at a decision point, with D.R. Horton sitting on critical support and needing to turn up now if 2026 is the year
Bank of America at 55, with Verrone calling 75 a conservative target and defending Brian Moynihan's record
Private credit growing from 2 trillion in 2020 to 3 trillion today, with First Brands and Tricolor as public-credit canaries
learned: Watch banks and credit, not narratives; both stayed calm through every 2025 panic and the trend never actually broke
Saying AI 30 times on a conference call does not make you an AI play; the market is now separating winners from pretenders
Valuation-centric investors have had to rewrite their resumes repeatedly for missing Mag Seven names, the argument for trend-following in transformational stories
If housing stocks are going to work in 2026, they must move before the fundamentals confirm, because they are anticipatory
The consensus risk list for 2026: power constraints, LLM scaling doubts, and a 10-year yield move back toward 4.5% that would spook speculative names
notable: Eisman accepts the bull case with two exceptions he keeps repeating: energy always takes longer than people think, and the LLM scaling question is the serious one.

title: 5 Long-Term Themes You Need to Understand For 2026 | The Weekly Wrap
summary: With earnings season a week away, he zooms out to five structural themes that explain how the market itself has changed, all downstream of one fact: tech dominance. The history of S&P sector weights becomes an argument about why the consumer no longer moves the index.
discussed: The US taking Maduro and his wife out of Venezuela, arraigned in New York federal court, and the market treating it as a non-event
2025 closing with the S&P up 16% and NASDAQ up 21%
Info tech at 35% of the S&P, versus 28% at the end of 2020 and 21% at the end of 2015
The 2018 defanging: Facebook, Apple, Amazon, Netflix, and Google reshuffled and the communication services sector created
Embedded unrealized tax gains in tech as a force that overrides almost every sell decision, retail and institutional alike
A listener question on PayPal: from a COVID-era high of 289 in August 2021 to 58 at the end of 2025, an 80% decline
The coming week: bank earnings start, plus an interview with Warris Bokhari of Claimable on health insurance denials
learned: The consumer drives 70% of the economy but no longer reliably moves the market; tech does, and the two facts coexist
Embedded tax gains create structural buy-and-hold pressure: nobody sells winners unless the rug is truly pulled
Beating a 35%-tech index year after year is structurally hard for any manager who will not concentrate the same way
A stock that soared because of a temporary regime, like payments during COVID, can fall 80% without ever being a scandal

title: The Broken US Healthcare System is Failing Millions of Americans with Warris Bokhari | The Real Eisman Playbook Episode 41
summary: No stocks this week. A British-trained ICU doctor turned Anthem executive, now CEO of Claimable, walks Eisman through why American health insurance denies care, why providers cannot fight back, and why he built a company to appeal denials. Eisman frames it with the Mangione trial: the murder was wrong, and the system is still broken.
discussed: Bokhari's route: son of two disabled parents in England, anesthesia and ICU training, then biotech, GE, Apple, Anthem, and Amazon
The four-part system, commercial insurance, Medicare, Medicaid, and the ACA, and why all four have problems
Defining deviancy down: mass claim denial, once the villainy of the movie The Rainmaker, now standard practice most patients never appeal
Sutter Health as the consolidation case study: buy the regional practices, promise nothing changes, then raise prices on a captive network
ACA-era rules that barred doctors from owning hospitals and enriched PBMs, entrenching the corporate side of medicine
Bokhari's own CVS denial of an asthma medication he has taken since 2007, answered with an angry letter to CEO David Joiner
Elizabeth Potter, the Austin breast surgeon called out of surgery by UnitedHealth to be told her patient was denied
Hospitals running 1.5% to 3.5% margins while EMTALA, signed by Reagan, forces them to eat the cost of the uninsured
learned: Denial economics depend on inertia: most people never appeal, so denying everything is profitable even when appeals usually win
Consolidation is the system's survival strategy on both sides; monopoly hospital systems and vertically integrated insurers price against each other and the patient pays
Regulation intended to expand coverage handed structural advantages to insurers and PBMs by prohibiting provider ownership of hospitals
A denial overturned in a day can still be a catastrophe; the patient whose vision never came back won her appeal
notable: Bokhari closes with his medical school professor's eulogy: he did not try to make the world perfect, he tried to make his corner of it a little more perfect.

title: Why Bank Earnings Are Essential to Understanding the Market in 2026 | The Weekly Wrap
summary: Prompted by viewer questions, he pulls back the camera and ties the four themes of 2025 to the five structural themes of 2026 in one framework, then grades the first week of bank earnings. The verdict: fundamentals fine, credit benign, valuations at their ceiling.
discussed: The four 2025 themes: the K-shaped economy, AI revolution or bubble, private credit fears, and affordability
The five structural themes, from tech dominance to index funds taking 60% of equity flows
The Justice Department opening a criminal investigation into Fed Chairman Powell, which the market read as an attack on Fed independence
JPMorgan revenue up 7% with stable credit in both commercial and consumer; investment banking fees down 4% on M&A deals slipping into 2026
No signs of credit deterioration in any category across the reporting banks
Goldman near three times tangible book versus 1.3 times two years ago, levels last seen before the financial crisis
Citi valued above tangible book even though its return on tangible common equity never reaches 10%
learned: Higher return on tangible common equity earns a higher price to tangible book, but bank valuations move within a range, and the range is now at peak
With 60% of flows passive, index funds buy their holdings automatically; when a recession or an AI capex slowdown comes, the same machinery will make the correction fast and furious
The stock market has become unmoored from everyday life; 70% of GDP is consumer driven, yet consumer stocks move the market less every year
Fed independence is a market variable, not just a political one: it underpins the dollar and interest rates
notable: He frames the whole wrap as connecting the dots: one lens through which a year of themes and a decade of structure become a single coherent story.

title: Gary Marcus on the Massive Problems Facing AI & LLM Scaling | The Real Eisman Playbook Episode 42
summary: The leading LLM skeptic explains why scaling has hit diminishing returns and why hallucination is built into how the models work, not a bug awaiting a patch. Eisman treats this as the deepest risk to the AI trade: if Marcus is right, the capex boom rests on a technology that cannot deliver what it promises.
discussed: Marcus's credentials: an MIT dissertation on neural networks and a 2001 book, The Algebraic Mind, that anticipated hallucinations
System 1 versus system 2 thinking: LLMs do fast pattern matching but have never managed slow deliberative reasoning
A tracker of fabricated legal citations finding roughly 300 court cases of lawyers filing made-up references, then 600 three months later
GPT-5's launch on August 7, 2025, sold as doing anything a PhD can do and picked apart by the public within about an hour
The novelty problem: models break outside their training distribution, which he compares to LTCM and the Russian bond collapse
If scale is all that matters, Google wins with its own tensor processing units; OpenAI next needs roughly a hundred billion dollar check that maybe five people in the world can write
Models trained on every chess rulebook and millions of games still make illegal moves, the case for world models and foundational research
learned: Hallucination follows from the architecture: statistical blurring works on average but can never guarantee any particular fact
Claims that one model beats another are task-dependent; there is no definitive ranking, only intuitions from different users doing different things
Models fail hardest on novelty, and markets are where novelty does the most damage
When critics from opposite ends, Marcus and Ilya Sutskever, converge on the view that scaling alone is a dead end, investors should listen
notable: The chess example lands hardest: after reading every rulebook and seeing millions of games, the models still make illegal moves, which Marcus calls just damning.

title: The “Lone Wolf” Effect: Trump, Burry & a Market on Edge | The Weekly Wrap
summary: A shortened wrap, current through Wednesday, built around a new theme he calls lone wolves: contrarian outsiders whose once-dismissed positions now move markets, from Trump on Greenland to Michael Burry on chip depreciation. Tariff escalation and rising yields leave the market on edge.
discussed: Escalating tariffs on eight European countries to pressure Denmark over Greenland, starting at 10% in February and rising to 25% in June
85% of Greenlanders opposing US annexation, turning the dispute into a contest of credibility and ego that is very difficult to handicap
Nvidia's Rubin chip shipping later this year, barely a year after Blackwell began shipping in late 2024
Burry's argument that hyperscalers stretched semiconductor depreciation from 3 to 5 years out to 5 to 6, inflating earnings by billions
Private equity's monetization problem: companies bought at zero rates are hard to exit with rates significantly higher
The 10-year Treasury jumping to 4.3%, pushing mortgage rates back above 6% and hurting homebuilders most
A mailbag question on why index investing would make any market pullback more severe
learned: A chip generation that turns over in about a year makes 5 to 6 year depreciation schedules hard to defend; Rubin's arrival strengthens Burry's math
When a conflict becomes about credibility and ego rather than economics, it stops being possible to handicap, and that is itself the risk
Passive flows buy stocks automatically in index weight on the way up and will sell the same mechanical way on the way down
Lone wolves matter most at the moment their contrarian positions start gaining adherents
notable: His aside that sometimes lone wolves join into packs and create their own society with their own rules, his description of private equity.

title: The Mystery of Stablecoins, Visa, & Fiserv’s Collapse with Ken Suchoski | The Real Eisman Playbook Episode 43
summary: The Autonomous Research payments analyst walks the sector from newest to oldest: stablecoins and Circle, then PayPal, Block and Toast, then Visa, Mastercard and the legacy processors. The backdrop is a brutal year in which only two of the 32 payment companies in his screen beat the S&P 500.
discussed: What a stablecoin actually is: Circle mints USDC against very short US treasuries, about two weeks of average duration
Why Autonomous was negative on Circle at the IPO: roughly 75 times EBITDA for a reserve return rate that tracks the Fed funds rate, so rate cuts hurt
Stablecoins' real edge in cross-border payments: 24/7 settlement with no cutoff times or weekends, against a correspondent banking system that still holds about 90% of the market
The anatomy of a card swipe, from merchant acquirer to network routing to the issuing bank's approve-or-decline decision
Fiserv down 71% on the year, with Clover on one side and issuer processing for banks on the other
Block as two businesses: Square at about 40% of gross profit and Cash App, a neobank for the unbanked, at 60%
PayPal's premium pricing under pressure when merchants get Apple Pay free through Stripe
learned: A stablecoin issuer is really an asset manager; its earnings are short-term interest rates in disguise and deserve to be valued that way
Biometric authentication is a uniquely strong password with a fatal flaw: once someone steals your face or thumbprint, you cannot change it
Lower starting valuations mechanically improve prospective returns; after a terrible year, that is the bull case for quality payment names
Sector carnage does not indict every franchise: both men would still own Visa and Mastercard
notable: The year-end scoreboard read aloud like casualties: Fiserv down 71, Bill down 36, Block down 30, PayPal down 27. Eisman's verdict: it's like a minefield.

title: Silver Goes Crazy, United Healthcare is Falling, & AI’s CapEx is Exploding | The Weekly Wrap
summary: Silver jumps roughly 60% in a single month while the VIX sits at 17, so complacent equity bulls now live side by side with investors betting on the dollar's demise. He works through a heavy earnings week in which AI capex begins to cut both ways.
discussed: Silver surging from $72 an ounce at the end of 2025 to about $115, with gold breaching the $5,000 barrier
The bedrock assumption of commodity trading breaking down as silver traders demand physical delivery
The Fed holding rates steady despite pressure from President Trump, citing a stronger economy
UnitedHealth's real problem: a change in Medicare compensation created a 6% pricing gap and left Optum Health barely profitable in the fourth quarter
GE Vernova orders of $22.2 billion, up 65%, as one of only three companies in the world making large gas turbines
Tesla revenue down 3% and autos down 11%, largely irrelevant at a 200 times 2026 PE built on robotaxi promises
Bank leverage then and now: Citi at 33 to 1 before the financial crisis, roughly 40 to 1 with off-balance sheet items, versus 14 to 1 today
learned: When traders start demanding physical delivery, a commodity market's core assumption fails and the squeeze feeds on itself
Only an actual recession, not fear of one, will break retail's buy-the-dip conditioning
Short-tailed insurance can be repriced quickly and fixed; a regulatory change to Medicare compensation is structural damage that cannot
A market that is simultaneously complacent (VIX at 17) and apocalyptic (gold and silver soaring) is telling you two incompatible stories at once
notable: His flat approval of the central bank under political fire: the Fed showed some backbone.

title: Jason Trennert on Populism, Policy & a Distorted Market System | The Real Eisman Playbook Ep 44
summary: A conversation between two old friends that opens with Trennert's multiple myeloma diagnosis and his search for a kidney donor, then turns to populism distorting markets, above all the price of money. Trennert expects a strong 2026 economy but sees a Fed that has become a participant in the game instead of its referee.
discussed: The diagnosis arriving two weeks before he was to start as assistant Treasury secretary for financial markets; dialysis three times a week while he waits for a matching kidney
The One Big Beautiful Bill injecting roughly $150 billion of tax refunds and stimulus into 2026, plus supply-side provisions behind it
Why populist price-setting is a bad idea everywhere, including setting the price of money and blocking buybacks
The Fed as active participant rather than referee: Trennert would have let Silicon Valley Bank go down
Private equity secondaries always trading at a discount to par, never at the marks
Retail and meme stock power, from Carvana's run from $4 to over $400 to his skepticism of Opendoor
Prediction markets going mainstream: CME's FanDuel deal reaching effectively 50 states within weeks, and Polymarket, a significant Trump family holding, partnering with ICE
learned: The secondary market is the tell on private equity marks: if the holdings were really worth par, sellers would not have to exit at a discount
Suppressing the price of money is price-fixing like any other; the escape valve is higher inflation, a weaker currency, or both
Online virality lets stocks be manipulated faster than ever, true or not, and erodes the whole idea of long-term investing
Unregulated prediction markets are, in Trennert's words, as ripe for insider trading as anything he can think of; regulation is coming
notable: A self-described rock-ribbed Republican, weeks from joining the Treasury, arguing the Fed should have let Silicon Valley Bank fail.

title: Crypto & Silver Collapse, Software Gets Obliterated, & Two Stock Recommendations | The Weekly Wrap
summary: He opens with a personal announcement, his cancer treatments are over, and thanks his wife Valerie Feigen, then covers a rout: silver and crypto collapsing, software stocks obliterated by AI fear, and hyperscaler capex now punished instead of rewarded. He also lays out theses for two stocks he just bought, Charter Communications and Meritage Homes.
discussed: Silver's violent round trip after its run to $115, and a sharp crypto decline with one major name down over 75% from its peak and 29% in a week
ServiceNow reporting genuinely great numbers and falling 10% anyway, dragging all of software; Anthropic's new model releases feeding the fear that AI kills software franchises
The Charter thesis: roughly $121 of estimated 2029 free cash flow per share, an implied 54% yield, less than two times free cash flow, with the cash going to buybacks
Waymo raising $16 billion at a $126 billion valuation, an awkward comp for Tesla's $1.6 trillion robotaxi-and-robotics story
Palantir growing fourth quarter revenue 70% and guiding 2026 to $7.2 billion versus a $6.3 billion consensus
Eli Lilly winning the weight loss wars: EPS of $7.54 versus $6.67 expected and 25% revenue growth guidance
Amazon guiding 2026 capex to $200 billion versus a $146 billion estimate and falling 7% after hours; last year the same announcement would have lifted the stock
learned: When a great quarter sinks a stock 10%, the market is repricing the category's future, not the quarter; software is now guilty until proven innocent
A free cash flow yield above 20% signals suspected bankruptcy; when the balance sheet says otherwise, that gap is the opportunity
Narratives flip without warning: identical capex announcements that lifted hyperscalers last year now sink them
A stock at more than 30 times earnings after doubling in a year cannot afford any disappointment; AMD proved it with a 17% drop
notable: The wrap pauses for gratitude: hundreds of viewer emails through months of treatment, and a thank-you to Valerie Feigen, without whom the podcast would be impossible.

title: Consumer VibeCession & Private Credit Risk with Lakshmi Ganapathi | The Real Eisman Playbook Episode 45
summary: The Unicus Research short seller argues the US consumer is in a vibe-cession: credit data looks fine while invisible costs in insurance, car repair and health care crush households whose wages have not kept up. She expects the cracks to appear in consumer spending in the second half of 2026, before they ever reach the credit statistics.
discussed: The disconnect: Michigan consumer sentiment at a multi-decade low while bank credit metrics stay benign
Earners of $100,000 to $150,000 cascading down into the lower leg of the K-shaped economy
Car repair costs up roughly 45 to 50%, breaking the old rule that consumers could safely borrow to a 30% debt-to-income ratio
19% of buy now pay later users forgetting payments across Klarna, Affirm and PayPal, with BNPL now covering rent and DoorDash
Lenders quietly extending auto loans rather than repossessing, including a reported 100-month car loan on a depreciating asset
The yen carry trade in plain terms: borrow cheap in Japan, buy dollar bonds, credit and equities
Private credit's opacity, with First Brands as the case where nobody saw the problem until it was too late
learned: Credit is now cut silently in real time: BNPL firms underwrite at the point of sale and decline cards without ever saying why
Loan term extension masks deterioration; a repossession avoided is a default deferred, invisible to CPI and credit data alike
Watch spending, not credit metrics; stretched consumers cut expenses before they miss payments, so spending cracks first
Even a short shop has untouchables: her Carvana rule is no shorting the cult
A correct short can still moonshot; her GE Vernova call caught the wind write-off, then watched the stock ride the AI power wave from about 250 to 700
notable: The episode's coinage: not a recession but a vibe-cession, a silent squeeze that shows up in how people feel long before it shows up in the data.

title: AI Panic Spreads, Health Insurers Crack & Retail Keeps Buying | The Weekly Wrap
summary: AI fear has escaped the software group and now torches a new sector every day, while retail keeps buying every dip. He closes with a two-stock lesson in cheap versus broken: Charter yes, PayPal no.
discussed: December retail sales flat against expectations of 0.4% growth, another sign of a mixed consumer
Altruist's AI tax planning tool knocking Raymond James down 9%, LPL 8% and Schwab 7% in a day
CBRE and JLL both down 12%, then CH Robinson down 15%, as AI fears hit real estate services and logistics
Molina's results showing health insurance problems are widespread, not confined to UnitedHealth
T-Mobile beating on EPS but losing its discounter role to a newly aggressive Verizon
A mailbag on measuring portfolio risk through the betas of individual holdings
Charter's 94 billion in long-term debt against a 30 billion market cap, defended anyway
learned: Buying the dip works until an actual widespread recession arrives, and not before
Even profitable hyperscalers like Google will have no cash flow this year because of AI capex
In a panic regime investors shoot first and rarely ask questions, so a group burned by bad news can stay rejected
A portfolio of high-beta stocks can be effectively 121% invested without any margin; beta is how you see it
Cheap is not the test. Charter is an improving story with rising cash flow; PayPal is losing share with no obvious fix
notable: His running refrain for the week: every day is an AI adventure.

title: Daniel Guetta on the Guts of AI, Agentic AI & Why LLMs Hallucinate | The Real Eisman Playbook Ep 46
summary: A deliberate second opinion after Gary Marcus: a Columbia professor who worked at Amazon and Palantir explains LLMs from the inside, embeddings, agents and hallucination included. Guetta agrees LLMs will not reach general intelligence but argues it does not matter, because the products are good enough to disrupt anyway.
discussed: The top four hyperscalers set to spend roughly 650 billion dollars on AI infrastructure
How deep learning in the mid 2010s let models capture the meaning of text as a list of numbers
The Sandy Koufax example: a model answers by finding the words around your question in embedding space
Agentic AI as a chatbot given tools, able to book a hotel or send an email on its own
Why companies whose moat is control of a database, such as commercial real estate data, are vulnerable
His Good Will Hunting analogy for what models know versus what they understand
Models as statistical parrots of their training data, which is why they hallucinate
learned: The first job for a company adopting AI is a fertile environment: IT systems a computer can actually operate
These are calculations and statistics, not magic; understanding the mechanism removes both the awe and the panic
AGI is the wrong bar. Good-enough agentic products can still shake insurance brokers and wealth managers
Eisman's timeline: whether the spending earns its return will not be known this year, perhaps not until 2027 or 2028
notable: Eisman sides more with Guetta than Marcus, then immediately concedes the only question that matters, returns on the hundreds of billions, is unanswerable for years.

title: Flight to Safety Begins, Private Credit Cracks & the Software Bloodbath Continues | The Weekly Wrap
summary: The index is flat but the hood is off: software down 20% this year, staples up 13%, a flight to safety with no fundamental improvement behind it. He also flags a brewing life insurance story he will spend the next fortnight unpacking.
discussed: S&P info tech down 4% and the software subsector down 20% for the year, while staples are up 13%
Homebuilder TPH acquired by Sumitomo Forestry for $47 a share, a 29% premium at 1.3 times tangible book
His Meritage thesis getting outside affirmation from the TPH deal math
Walmart's rare stumble: $2.80 EPS guidance against a $2.96 estimate, 4% same store sales, and still a 50 times PE
Payments consolidating to two long-term investments, Mastercard and Visa, everything else a trading vehicle
Mailbag questions on what a recession does to markets and on private equity owned insurers like Athene
A coming interview with a forensic accountant and former life insurance examiner on hidden risk in the sector
learned: Watch rotation, not the index level; a flat tape can hide a genuine flight to safety
Staples rallied without their fundamentals improving at all, which is what a pure safety bid looks like
Recession and recovery recalibrate an economy; weak balance sheets fail, the Fed cuts, and the survivors emerge healthier
When e-commerce has devastated a sector, investors pay 50 times earnings for anything still working
notable: He teases the life insurance story as increasing investment risk plus hidden leverage, a very important story to tell.

title: George Noble on Gold's Rise, Crypto Doubts & Tesla's Struggles | The Real Eisman Playbook Ep 47
summary: An old-fashioned buyside stock jockey, at it since 1981, bullish on gold, energy and materials and bearish on tech, crypto and Tesla. Eisman lets him run, then pushes back on the gold thesis while agreeing completely on crypto.
discussed: Noble's Fidelity years: launching the Overseas Fund in December 1984 and returning 79% in 1985
Both men on the short side in 2008, both redeemed heavily because they did not gate; 'I was the ATM'
His call that R is for rotation, not recession: out of tech, into energy, materials, gold and silver
Fiat debasement and the risk of a global Liz Truss moment, echoing the UK gilt collapse of autumn 2022
Tesla's 2025 consensus EPS falling from $8 three years ago to about $1.70, with the stock flat for five years
Gross versus net revenue recognition, illustrated with a ticket reseller reporting $120 instead of $20
An engineer's view that OpenAI underprices badly: the $20 a month product does what the $200 one does
learned: Eisman will not short anything that involves a cult, Tesla included, however bad the numbers
When a discussion is all chart and narrative with no fundamentals, you are no longer analyzing a business
As long as there is no alternative to treasuries, betting on the demise of the dollar has failed for 40 years
Crypto was sold as digital gold but trades with tech in every crisis; it is speculation about speculation
notable: Noble's line that young people now have FanDuel and prediction markets, so Bitcoin is for old people; Eisman thought it captured something real.

title: Trump Tariff Turmoil, Private Credit Risk Grows, & AI's Software Fears | The Weekly Wrap
summary: The Supreme Court kills the IEEPA tariffs and Trump rebuilds them within a weekend, so the market barely blinks. The real story is Blue Owl freezing redemptions, which turns private credit from an institutional curiosity into everyone's problem.
discussed: The Supreme Court striking down the IEEPA tariffs; Trump answering with a temporary 15% tariff under Section 122 plus new Section 301 investigations
Bessent's claim that the reworked tariffs leave 2026 revenue virtually unchanged
Blue Owl freezing redemptions while selling 1.4 billion in loans at roughly par to CalPERS, OMERS, British Columbia Investment Management and a fourth buyer
Retail money, 401k plans and policyholder-backed insurers now inside private credit, which is why the freeze matters
Another AI fear week: CrowdStrike down 10%, Visa and Mastercard hit, IBM down 13% on an Anthropic product aimed at its COBOL franchise
First Solar down 15% as commercial solar cracks; Enphase down from $340 in COVID to $46
Mailbags on why tariff news did not sink the market and what edge institutions really have over retail
learned: His three risks to watch: whether AI spending earns a return, private credit's overexposure to software, and the private equity, private credit, life insurance triangle
Private credit sold only to institutions was nobody's problem; sold to retail and insurers, it is everybody's
The private credit model has never been stress tested with valuation doubts, liquidity pressure and a sector disruption hitting at once
For most retail investors the honest answer on edge is that indices beat active managers anyway
notable: He breaks his own format to flag the coming Tom Gober episode up front, calling it truly worth checking out.

title: The Next Financial Crisis? Private Equity, Private Credit & Life Insurance | The Real Eisman Playbook Ep 48
summary: A forensic accountant and former Mississippi insurance examiner walks through how private equity turned life insurers into captive buyers of their own credit paper, then hid the leverage offshore through captive reinsurance. Eisman's verdict: nobody is looking, and it rhymes with the years before the financial crisis.
discussed: Why insurance is regulated state by state while banks answer to the Fed, and how companies play states off each other
Five industry-friendly states, Vermont, South Carolina, Delaware, Arizona and Iowa, granting permitted practices outside statutory accounting
Captive reinsurers as special purpose vehicles with no building and no employees, absorbing liabilities under looser rules
Deferring commissions already paid over 25 years, underfunding future death claims
Athene sharply increasing its exposure to affiliated private credit investments
One company taking reserve credit for 7 billion laid off to three captives whose assets, when visible, fell well short
Why sell-side coverage misses it: Apollo and KKR are covered by asset manager analysts who never read statutory filings
learned: When an insurer buys credit paper from its own private equity parent, there is no arms-length pricing and every incentive to hide risk
Offshore captive reinsurance is leverage you cannot see; the industry is far more levered than it looks
A credit bull market postpones the reckoning without repairing it; the risk compounds quietly
Regulators act after blowups, not before, exactly as before the great financial crisis
The people bearing the risk are policyholders and annuity owners, who have no idea
notable: Eisman's closing image: a slow boiling frog that one day is just going to explode.

title: Iran War Volatility, Private Credit Fears Grow, & Solar Continues to Crash | The Weekly Wrap
summary: The US and Israel bomb Iran and kill Khamenei, and the market closes flat; the narratives that actually move stocks are private credit fraud and forced markdowns. Bitcoin fails the hedge test yet again.
discussed: The weekend strike on Iran killing Ayatollah Khamenei and much of the leadership, with oil, gold and silver up and Bitcoin down
UK private lender Market Financial Solutions, a 2.4 billion loan book, liquidated amid apparent double pledging of assets
Barclays, Apollo, Jefferies and Wells Fargo among the exposed; the third lending fraud in six months after Tricolor and First Brands
TCPC marking a 25 million loan from par to zero, three months after valuing it at 100 cents on the dollar
CMS threatening Elevance with a Medicare Advantage enrollment freeze over risk adjustment data submitted 2015 through 2023
A viewer asking whether he is short the life insurance names; he says simply that he is not
A preview of the Glenn Schorr and Dwight Collins financial services panel
learned: In a genuine crisis Bitcoin correlates with tech stocks; it has never once acted as the hedge it claims to be
Credit problems emerge where the growth was: subprime mortgages before the GFC, private credit now
Frauds like double pledging are discoverable; they grow because private lenders skip the due diligence
Ganapathi's line stands for the whole sector: getting in was easy, getting out is a whole different story
notable: Elevance allegedly submitted its data corrections to CMS on a USB flash drive, every year, that CMS could not open.

title: Private Credit Cracks, The AI “Boogeyman” & Why Crypto is for Boomers | The Real Eisman Playbook Episode 49
summary: Depth and breadth: Evercore's Glenn Schorr, who covers the alternative managers, and Autonomous sales head Dwight Collins on the private credit panic. Schorr's contrarian core is that the equity market is pricing a credit cycle the credit market itself cannot see.
discussed: Blue Owl stocks down 30% to 50% this year, and the canceled fund merger that offered holders roughly 80 cents on the dollar
Private credit at 1.8 trillion, with direct lending concentrated in software because that is where five years of growth went
The distinction between direct lending and the rest of the pie: real estate credit, infrastructure debt, investment grade asset-backed finance
Insurance brokers down 10% to 12% in a day on a Spanish AI insurance app approved on OpenAI's platform
Bank M&A running slower and thinner than hoped, without the 30% premiums of the early 2000s
Stablecoins as a threat to the 29% of US deposits that pay zero interest, and the banks' federal guarantee objection
Software buyouts financed with roughly 75% equity and 25% debt
learned: Credit spreads at all-time tights and private equity stocks obliterated cannot both be right; watch which one blinks
A 75% equity cushion means a great deal must go wrong before the private credit loan itself is impaired
Retail is walking away from direct lending before any actual losses appear, trying to move first
Bank CEOs still like being bank CEOs, which is why the long-predicted M&A wave keeps underdelivering
The old conclusion holds: Visa and Mastercard are the only long-term investments in payments, the rest are trades
notable: Schorr's screen paradox: high yield spreads tighter than ever, every bank CEO upbeat, every broker cheering the capital markets cycle, and the private market stocks getting pummeled. Can all those things coexist?

title: The Iran War Crisis: Ex-CIA Analyst Helima Croft on Oil Shock & Energy Risk | The Weekly Wrap
summary: With war on, traditional equity analysis is suspended; the market trades every Iran headline, and oil breaching $100 on Monday swooned stocks until Trump told CBS the war would end soon. The wrap then hands off to RBC's Helima Croft, a former CIA analyst, on why the administration misjudged the oil risk and what a shutdown does to supply.
discussed: Oil breaching $100 on Monday and collapsing as Trump told CBS News the war would be over soon
Croft's read that Washington extrapolated from Venezuela, where installing Delcy Rodriguez kept goals manageable, and from the June 12-day war that markets faded
Why restarts are not a light switch: Aramco could come back fast, Iraq's creaky infrastructure could not, and LNG liquefaction takes long to cycle
Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline to the Red Sea as the oil market's main comfort if Hormuz stays shut
Croft's CIA start on December 1, 2001 and Iraq as her formative bias
Storage hitting tank tops if the shutdown drags on
learned: In geopolitical crises the market stops discounting cash flows and trades only the events creating the uncertainty
Policy makers anchor on their last two crises; both precedents here argued for a muted oil response, and both may mislead
Supply that shuts down does not restart on command, so the duration of a closure matters more than the closure itself
Mission creep is the real war risk: objectives change, and the adversary gets a vote on the timeline and the cost
notable: Eisman retires the chemo hat on air, his hair growing back, and reveals its provenance: he bought it at The Gap.

title: Mark Cuban Shares His Plan For Fixing Drug Prices in America | The Real Eisman Playbook Ep 50
summary: Mark Cuban explains why US drug prices are a delivery-system problem, not a research-cost problem, and how Cost Plus attacks it with one transparent price of wholesale plus 15% for everyone. The third episode in Eisman's healthcare series, after Michael Ha on insurance and Warris Bokhari on claim denials.
discussed: The PBM scheme: wholesale acquisition cost equals retail, rebates of roughly 400 on a 1,000 drug get pocketed by PBMs, not consumers
Formularies as pay-to-play, with insurer-owned PBMs telling pharma companies that working with Cuban means being cut off
Deductibles as the real barrier: a $1,500 deductible you cannot afford means you have no insurance, which turns providers into subprime lenders
Medical loss ratios gamed through vertical integration, with the biggest insurer running 2,600 subsidiaries and shifting profit pocket to pocket
Cost Plus Wellness contracts published free at costpluswellness.com, with no insurance company in Cuban's own employee plan
Cuban's own portfolio: mostly cash, waiting Buffett-style for the tide to go out on meme-like and AI-labeled names
learned: The US is the only country with PBMs, and their rebate economics are a core reason drug prices are higher here than anywhere else
Different prices for the same drug depending on insurance is the disease; one published price for all is the cure Cuban is betting on
When patients cannot pay deductibles, hospitals lend money they know they will never collect, so credit risk hides inside healthcare delivery
The interests of health insurers are structurally unaligned with patients, which no amount of regulation-tinkering fixes
notable: Cuban's distilled lesson from Shark Tank and the Mavericks is simply: be nice, and your business does better.

title: Private Credit Risks Explained, Oil Surges Above $100 | The Weekly Wrap
summary: With Hormuz still closed, oil above $100 and the S&P down 4% for the year, Eisman uses the fog of war to deliver a primer on private credit, the opaque lending machine now cracking in public. He runs through a list of fresh warnings, from Carlyle's Project Potomac to SoFi's breached securitization triggers.
discussed: Straits of Hormuz closed, China back-channeling passage for Chinese-flagged ships, and Mnuchin denying rumors of federal oil-market intervention
The 10-year Treasury yield rising from 4.0% to 4.3% since the war began, the opposite of the usual flight to safety
Private credit's structure: 80% of direct lending funds private equity buyouts, with an estimated 25% of loans to software companies bought from 2018 through 2022
AI eroding software business models as the sector's concentrated risk
Carlyle's Project Potomac, a collateralized fund obligation pooling LP stakes from multiple funds so new investors buy out old ones
MFS Investment Management as the third lending fraud after Tricolor and First Brands, plus Canada's subprime lender GoEasy
SoFi's 2025 securitization breaching its cumulative net loss trigger, cutting off SoFi's excess spread and threatening its funding model
learned: He dismisses government-intervention conspiracy theories with a simple test: if it were happening, it would leak, and it never has
Private credit stays invisible until problems develop precisely because it is private; the information vacuum is the risk
When a securitization trigger breaches, the lender's economics vanish first, and losing securitization investors can shut off lending entirely
Redemption limits and creative structures like CFOs are signs that money wants out faster than the assets can pay it
notable: A viewer letter about the Cuban interview lets him restate the whole PBM scheme in two minutes, a wrap-as-classroom move.

title: The Only Health Insurance Stock You Can Own with Michael Ha | The Real Eisman Playbook Episode 51
summary: Baird's Michael Ha returns to survey a managed care sector in wrenching decline: risk adjustment crackdowns, flat Medicare Advantage rates, and a sicker Medicaid pool. discussed: Risk adjustment as a revenue multiplier, where coding sicker members lifts the benchmark rate and drops straight to earnings
Medicare Advantage rate notices coming in flat for 2027 when everyone expected roughly 5%, echoing the margin destruction of 2024 and 2025
Medicaid redetermination leaving Molina with a sicker pool, and the 24-to-36-month actuarial lag before state rates catch up
United Healthcare's 2,000-plus subsidiaries and databases that do not speak to each other
PBMs surviving rebate reform through fee-based revenue levers most investors do not understand
Ha's pick ALHC as the one name he loves, and European investors sitting on hundreds of millions in unrealized losses
Breakup tail risk rising from about 1% to perhaps 5% or 10% as Congress stirs
learned: Vertical integration built by acquisition is not integration; these companies are conglomerates of parts that cannot talk to each other, which is why the oligopoly earns no excess rent
When healthy members drop off a pool, rates set on the old population become inadequate everywhere at once
Government-administered pricing repricing on a two-to-three-year lag defines when the recovery trade works: too early is simply wrong
Eisman's bottom line is that it is mostly too early to buy the sector, selectivity or not
notable: Ha opens by wishing Eisman well on his health and calling the show the best financial podcast in the world, before an hour of unrelieved sector gloom.

title: The Iran War is Masking Economic Problems: Why Housing is So Expensive | The Weekly Wrap

The theory that Trump's delays are setting up a US move on Kharg Island, the key to Iran's economy
The country underbuilt since the Great Recession, with builders slow to bring lots and supply back
Median new home prices above half a million dollars, and Meritage's focus on delivering product below that line
Meritage at roughly a 5 billion market cap versus Lennar around 20 billion and DHI up to 45 billion, and why the big three earn higher price-to-book multiples
Off-balance-sheet land banking, its drag on margins, and bringing land on book only when ready to build

Land is the builder's real balance sheet decision: optioned land costs margin but frees working capital, and it is all math on the IRR
Scale earns builders a valuation premium through higher returns on equity, so the mid-caps trade cheap to book
In a headline-driven market, single-stock work like housing is where actual analysis still pays

title: Inside the Iran War with Steven Cook: What’s REALLY Happening? | The Real Eisman Playbook Ep 52

Trump's deliberately vague war aims, his 4-to-6-week claim now entering week four as energy prices bite
Israel folded into CENTCOM after the Abraham Accords, forcing even Qatar to work with it
A Saudi-hosted gathering of 18 foreign ministers issuing tough statements on Iran, with criticism of Israel almost an afterthought
The regime killing an upward estimate of 30,000 of its own civilians in December and January, and why Cook still expects Iranians to be heard from
An Iranian strike missing Dimona by about 12 miles, and Israeli confidence that the enriched uranium is buried beyond reach under rubble
learned: Vague war aims are a dealmaker's choice: they preserve maneuverability at the cost of criticism
Regimes look resilient until they are not; the Iranian revolution unfolded over 15 to 18 months, so quiet streets today prove little
The adversary sets its own timeline and prices its resistance to deter the next intervention, not just to survive this one
Any negotiated end requires verifiable limits on the nuclear program, or the whole war is for naught

title: The Private Credit Reckoning is Coming: Executives Are Mistaking Luck For Genius | The Weekly Wrap

discussed: Q1 ending with the S&P down 4.6% and Nasdaq down 7.1% on war, AI fears and private credit
Trump threatening Iran's energy infrastructure and Kharg Island unless the straits reopen
A Wall Street Journal piece finding software exposure in direct lending well above the 25% estimate, thanks to what he calls data massaging in sector classification
Hedge fund idea dinners breeding herd trades, visible in gold falling while oil and rates rise, which he says makes no sense
Pre-crisis Wall Street pay built on ROE and net income, so an entire generation mistook leverage for genius
A viewer question on GameStop: 6.3 billion cash against 4.1 billion debt on a 10 billion market cap, and why he rejects Michael Burry's buy-something thesis
BDCs versus private funds: the 1980 structure trades SEC registration, two-to-one leverage limits and 90% payout for retail access
learned: Rising rates during a crisis signal that inflation fear has displaced the flight to safety
When funds classify software borrowers as healthcare companies because of their customers, believe the exposure is higher than reported
Executives who have never seen a default cycle radiate the same certainty as 2007 bank CEOs; lack of a track record through a downturn is itself the risk
Buying a stock because management might acquire something good someday is a pipe dream, not a thesis
notable: His GameStop verdict on the Burry argument: buy a stock because they could buy something worthwhile at a good price? Good luck with that.

title: Is Private Credit the Next Systemic Crisis? Steve Liesman Weighs In | The Real Eisman Playbook Ep 53

The unforecastable resilience of the US economy, which contains an oil economy the size of Saudi Arabia inside it
Fed turmoil: Warsh nominated with possible delays, Powell maybe staying, Cook before the Supreme Court, and Kansas City hawks floating policy action to anchor inflation expectations
Why raising rates against an exogenous oil shock troubles Eisman
Liesman's point that private equity may borrow to fund its own equity checks, so true leverage in buyouts is unknowable
Banks levered 12 to 1 versus private credit's 2 to 1, and whether the boom is a sign Dodd-Frank pushed lending too far outside banks
Bank of America card data showing the lower-end consumer hurting, with oil the insult to injury
learned: Opacity itself is the systemic risk: small known losses calm markets, small unknown losses panic everyone who might be holding the bag
If equity beneath private credit loans is itself borrowed, headline loan-to-value ratios understate the leverage in the system
A central bank facing an exogenous supply shock has no good move; watching inflation expectations is all it can do
The K-shaped economy shows up first in bank card data, and the low end that thrived during COVID is now the pressure point

title: Q1 Market Recap: How Private Credit, AI, & War Have Dominated 2026 So Far | The Weekly Wrap

Vance calling the ceasefire a fragile truce, with Iran keeping the Strait of Hormuz closed and disputing whether Lebanon is covered
Blue Owl's OCIC receiving redemption requests of 21.9% and its $3.3 billion tech fund OTIC 41%, both capped at 5%
Carlyle's $7 billion CTAC fund getting a 16% redemption notice; Moody's turning negative on OCIC and the whole BDC industry
Energy at only 4% of the S&P 500 despite the US energy sector matching the size of the entire Saudi economy
Utilities and consumer staples up 7% plus as safety plays in a down quarter
Meritage Homes revisited: recommended in January near tangible book value around $74, with a valuation range of 50% to 1.5 times tangible book

Software modeling reduces to seats times price per seat, and AI now puts both assumptions at risk
A homebuilder bought at or below tangible book value tends to work over time because profitability compounds book value
Nobody could have stopped the subprime crisis by mid-2007; the environment had to change in 2005, when underwriting first rotted and everyone was paid on volume
notable: His answer to whether commentators could have averted 2008: with lenders, Wall Street and the raters all paid by volume, a bunch of podcasters complaining about underwriting would not have been listened to.

title: Catching a Falling Knife: The Truth About Software Stocks Today | The Real Eisman Playbook Ep 54
summary: Baird software analyst Rob Oliver explains how a group built on sticky systems of record and decades of pricing power lost half its valuation to AI fear before anything bad showed up in the numbers. Eisman's verdict: the group is cheap for the first time in its history, and that is not a reason to buy it.
discussed: Why software was great for decades: systems of record, brutal change management, pricing power, and survival through the client-server and cloud transitions
Valuations cut by more than half, leaving software at a huge discount to the S&P for maybe the first time ever
The seat-based revenue model, with both seat growth and price per seat now in doubt
Oliver calling this a golden age of creation, with anyone able to build software and an explosion in domain creation visible at Cloudflare
Whether proprietary-database companies like Moody's or S&P are the best-protected position
Only one company in his coverage reporting on a GAAP basis, which astonishes Eisman
Private equity's software holdings, bought at big multiples, now worth less whatever the checks say
learned: Software investors do not care about valuation; they buy revenue growth, so cheapness reads as a symptom rather than an opportunity
You cannot disprove a negative, and a stock fighting one has no floor until real data arrives
Disruption timelines run long; the iPhone took years to kill the yellow cab, and the AI hit to software revenue could take three to four quarters to even start showing
Eisman's own sticking point is pricing power: when the cost of creating software collapses, revenue growth estimates must come down, and until he knows how far, he will not buy
notable: Oliver's cocktail-party summary of his own coverage group: nobody loves software right now.

title: John Spencer on What the Headlines Get Wrong About the Iran War | The Real Eisman Playbook Ep 55
summary: Urban warfare scholar John Spencer cuts through five weeks of contradictory headlines on the Iran war, arguing the US and Israel are systematically achieving four defined goals without seeking regime change. The market takeaway is that a demonstration of American military prowess this complete changes the calculus in Beijing as much as Tehran.
discussed: The four US goals: no nuclear capability, no ballistic missile program, no exported power, and pressure on the regime's ability to survive, without regime change as an objective
Intelligence penetration including tapping Tehran's highway cameras as sensors to track the supreme leader
B-2 bombers flying from Missouri, roughly 18 hours each way, with seven sent toward the Middle East and six toward Guam as deception
The pilot rescue completed without a single death or injury
A Foreign Policy editor's headline claiming Trump is losing the war, which Spencer rebuts
Iran lobbing missiles at Turkey, Cyprus and Azerbaijan, validating the case for the operation to every neighbor
Twenty years ago an entire corps attacking Baghdad had one drone; the technology gap since then explains what is now possible
learned: Strikes on the Basij and regime communications target the ability to suppress the population, not just military hardware; wars are won by threatening what a regime values most, its survival
Russia and China are taking notes: their equipment just failed the comparison test, and Xi has to rethink Taiwan with a military that has not fought in decades
Deception still decides operations; Sun Tzu's rule held for the B-2 raid
Spencer expects the war to end in more global stability, not less, which is the bullish reading markets keep missing

title: Bank Earnings Are In: Here’s What They’re REALLY Saying About the U.S. Economy | The Weekly Wrap

Using consumer and commercial non-accruing loans, from disclosures like JP Morgan's 28-page supplement, as the cleanest read on credit quality
17 years of benign credit since the financial crisis, and whether the good times are ending

Why lending-centric banks earn less: Goldman, JP Morgan and Morgan Stanley return above 20% while Wells and Bank of America sit at 14% to 16%
A mailbag explainer on credit spreads as the market's fear gauge
Why he avoids giving trade ideas: taxes of 30% plus mean a trade has to be very good to beat holding

Widening credit spreads signal worry, but they are not by themselves a verdict on credit quality

The software fear list is so long, replacement, internalization, dead pricing power, that no clarity is possible for at least a year; predicting the bottom of a group with a broken narrative is brutal
When expectations are high, a good quarter still sends the stock down, as Goldman showed

title: Market Patterns Work and Jeffrey Hirsch Explains Why | The Real Eisman Playbook Ep 56
summary: Jeffrey Hirsch, keeper of the Stock Trader's Almanac his father Yale started in 1966, walks through sixty years of seasonal patterns and which ones still work. The premise is simple: people have patterns, people buy stocks, and even the algorithms are written by people.
discussed: The Almanac's family history: Yale Hirsch, ex-songwriter, launching the book in 1966 out of Indicator Digest in Palisades Park, New Jersey
The midterm election pattern: volatility bottoming around September or October of the midterm year, then rallying through April
The January barometer, which still works, versus the September reverse barometer, retired to the indicator graveyard
Using MACD only to confirm a seasonal entry or exit, work refined with David Aronson around 2008
Bitcoin's failed patterns: it trades like leveraged Nasdaq, so Hirsch asks why not just buy a 2x ETF
Sell in May, but buy in October, his correction to the old saw
A tongue-in-cheek 5-year taco trade cycle: Trump shocks the world in Q1, then negotiates it better through year-end

Keep a graveyard for both losing stocks and dead indicators; if you do not profit from your mistakes, somebody else will
Black swans are by definition unforeseeable; anyone asking a forecaster to name the next one has missed the point
Patterns persist because they encode how people react to war and inflation, and those reactions change slower than the news
notable: Hirsch describing the pre-Excel workflow: lead pages stacked as high as himself in his father's office closet, added up on an adding machine and drawn on graph paper.

title: Is a Recession Coming? What 100+ Companies Are Telling Us | The Weekly Wrap

Blackstone's BCRED, at 81 billion the industry's largest private credit fund, reporting weak new share sales

His closing case that stock-based compensation is a real expense, since the same companies deduct it from their taxes

A monopoly's value can end with one regulator's announcement; watch the FHFA, not just FICO's earnings
Building software internally is easy; maintaining, patching, and staying compliant is the expensive part AI does not remove
User acquisition, not code, is the bottleneck for consumer startups; the VC money flows straight to Google and Meta

title: Apollo's Private Credit Exposure: Chris Edson Weighs In | The Real Eisman Playbook Ep 57
summary: Apollo's global head of originations, Chris Edson, describes a lender with 16 platforms and 4,000 employees that looks nothing like the buyout-shop caricature of private equity. CFOs de-risking borrowing after COVID, the Russia war, the regional bank crisis, liberation day and now Iran

An AI test for any software credit: no moat, no proprietary data, quickly installed means quickly replaced
Honoring only a 5% redemption cap may be contractually fair, but the industry's treatment of exiting investors will define its reputation

Microsoft down despite Azure growing 39%, because 39% was only one point better than expected
Amazon's AWS accelerating to 28% growth from 24% last quarter
Caterpillar's construction industries unit up 38% on AI capex, and Apple beating overall while iPhone missed for the second time in three quarters
