The low-cost provider tends to win a convergence war, which is why one awful subscriber print does not kill the story
At AI-era valuations, meeting expectations is not enough; Microsoft fell on a beat because the beat was too small
Visa remains as good a single read on the consumer as any company reporting

Gold underwhelming through the entire war, having jumped from safe haven to risk asset before a January blow-off

GE plane orders up roughly 80% as a non-recession indicator, with transports breaking out just as street economists raised recession odds
Energy oversold within a long-term uptrend; Eisman says he is thinking about adding, not trimming

When defensive groups get their moment and give it back within two weeks, the market is telling you it does not want to be defensive

Transports breaking out while economists raise recession odds is the tell to trust the market over the forecasts

GameStop's deal to buy eBay, with a prominent holder selling his entire position over the debt it requires

PayPal as a structurally problematic payments company squeezed by Apple and Google Pay
McDonald's growing EPS 6% with 3.8% same-store sales while Shake Shack broke even and fell 30%
Whirlpool's disaster quarter: a 56 cent loss versus $1.70 last year, with guidance slashed to $3 to $3.50

In a bifurcated consumer, scale and value win; the same week can produce a McDonald's beat and a Shake Shack collapse
Software is guilty until proven innocent on AI; even a good Palantir quarter cannot rescue a 100 times multiple
Housing-related names remain the market's dead zone, and earnings keep confirming it

title: FICO's Monopoly is Fading & Consumers Are the Winners w/ Kelsey Zhu | The Real Eisman Playbook Ep 59
summary: The Autonomous financial information services analyst walks through how FICO turned a 60 cent mortgage credit pull into a $10 one and enraged the entire lending ecosystem, which is now rallying behind VantageScore. discussed: Mortgage scoring mechanics: 60 cents per pull times three bureaus times three lenders, with five or six pulls per completed mortgage
FICO pricing rising from 60 cents a pull in 2022 to $10, an increase of more than 1,000%
VantageScore already validated for mortgage underwriting while FICO 10-T is not, giving lenders a live alternative
Widespread confusion among lenders and investors over how to even model FICO's pricing grid and success fee
Verisk as a near-monopoly in property and casualty loss-cost data, serving an insurance vertical built on 30-year relationships
MSCI benefiting from the shift to passive while FactSet suffers from it, since an index needs no analysts
Zhu's underperform on FICO: management insists it will lose no share, and she thinks estimates are far too high
learned: A monopoly that antagonizes every customer at once manufactures its own competition; the whole lending ecosystem now wants FICO to fail
Vertical culture determines pricing power: mortgage players eagerly trial new products while insurance carriers stay loyal for decades
AI is a cost tailwind, not a threat, for data companies with proprietary moats; the market currently prices the whole sector the other way
Narratives swing further than fundamentals: two years ago investors asked if score pricing could reach $50, now they ask if it goes to $1

title: Conspiracy of Credit Part 1
summary: Part one of a three part lecture on private credit. Eisman argues we are in the early stage of the first real credit cycle since 2008, that almost all post crisis loan growth moved outside the regulated banks and behind a veil of secrecy, and that the concentrated bet on software is the rotten core. He expects losses and possibly a recession, but not a systemic repeat, because the banks are well capitalized.
discussed: The Fed forcing banks to delever and to stop making riskier loans after the crisis, which pushed loan growth into private credit and curtailed bank lending to private equity
The banks finding a workaround by lending to the funds instead, with recent data showing roughly 300 billion of bank leverage extended to private credit
Public BDCs being levered at two to one while other private credit vehicles go higher, and an unknown amount of the underlying equity being borrowed too
Blue Owl disclosing first quarter 2026 redemption requests of 21.9% of assets in its roughly 36 billion flagship OCIC fund, with the smaller 3.3 billion OTIC also hit
Retail private credit funds capping quarterly redemptions at 5% to 7% and receiving requests above the cap all year
Sizing the problem against 2006, when 600 billion of subprime was resecuritized into CDOs many times over, versus a roughly 1.8 trillion private credit industry with little resecuritization

A Wall Street Journal analysis on March 30 showing private credit labelled software loans by end industry, so healthcare software counted as healthcare, hiding true software exposure above the estimated 25% of direct lending
learned: Equity is subordinate to debt on the same assets, so equity investors who ignore the credit markets are ignoring the thing that will price them
Markets are clearing mechanisms. When risk is hidden it cannot be priced, and unpriceable risk turns into panic rather than an orderly repricing
Rating agencies are referees, not regulators, and they are always late. When downgrades start arriving, the damage is already done
Concentration is the real risk multiplier. Herd behaviour put a quarter or more of direct lending into one bet, so one wrong assumption hits everyone at once
Relabelling exposure does not reduce it. Check how a lender classifies loans before you accept its industry breakdown
notable: His line for the whole lecture: even expensive, well paid cows prefer to join the herd.

title: A Conspiracy Of Credit Master Class: Part 2
summary: The middle lecture is a fixed income primer built on one claim, that the bond market's complexity is mostly lingo defending insiders. Eisman teaches the terms, the price and yield relationship, the treasury curve, the power of the rating agencies and the four Cs of credit analysis, so that part three's account of subprime securitization lands.
discussed: Why bond prices rise when rates fall, and why every bond is priced off the treasury yield curve as the risk free benchmark
The curve's shape following lender risk, since thirty year money costs more than overnight money because things go wrong over time
Treasuries remaining the least risky and most liquid bonds regardless of Moody's and S&P no longer rating the United States triple A
Rating agencies not merely influencing bond prices but setting them, as the only subjective input in an otherwise mathematical market, which large institutions trade ahead of
The four Cs of credit analysis, cash flow, collateral, covenants and character, with covenants treated as contract law rather than math
Tax treatment across treasuries, municipals and corporates, and the near total absence of liquidity in a private loan
Amortizing versus non amortizing bonds, using a five year 7% bond at par paying 70 dollars a year against a self amortizing residential mortgage
learned: Learning an industry's lingo is most of the work of understanding it. Jargon is a gate, not a description of real complexity
In fixed income the rating is the price. Understand who assigns it and how slowly they change it before you trust the mark
Covenants decide who gets what when the borrower fails, so a credit view that stops at the numbers is incomplete
Liquidity is a feature markets manufacture. A private loan without a market leaves you contractually stuck for the full term
Distressed debt is an institutional game requiring lawyers, covenant fluency and often a board seat. It is not a retail asset class
notable: His image for the asset class: if the stock market is a slot machine, distressed debt is the craps table in the private room of the most exclusive casino.

summary: Premium goes live with the Conspiracy of Credit masterclass, and he uses the wrap to defend disclosing his FICO short: being short is an opinion backed by research, not a bias. FSK, a $3 billion BDC down 27% this year and cut to junk by Moody's in March, with KKR injecting 150 million of equity and spending another 150 million buying shares

learned: When a sponsor has to inject equity into its own credit fund and buy out exiting investors, read it as a signal about the asset class, not generosity
A workforce cut framed as an AI strategy can lift a stock short term, but it is still a shrinking-cost story, not a growth story
The GFC parallel to private credit has a limit: banks are well capitalized this time, so expect losses and perhaps a recession rather than systemic collapse
Having a position and having a bias are different things; research-driven conviction expressed via a short is still just an opinion
notable: On disclosing his FICO short: I am short because of my research, and I am not trying to convince anyone to join me.

title: Why Energy Stocks Are Down When They Should Be Up with Bob Brackett | The Real Eisman Playbook Ep 60
summary: Bernstein's energy and mining analyst explains the paradox of the moment: the closing of the strait has removed roughly 20% of world oil production, yet prices stay contained because the market keeps betting the war ends soon. Along the way he maps the whole energy stack, from E&Ps to toll-booth midstream to refiners, and makes the case for treating these as trading vehicles, not growth holdings.
discussed: Energy at only 4% of the S&P 500, so generalists buy Exxon and move on; Exxon outperformed in January and February then fell after the invasion
The UAE dropping out of OPEC this year and what it means for the cartel's long-run grip
Exxon and Chevron each returning 30 to 50 billion dollars a year through dividends and buybacks
Why commodity company yields should be compared to TIPS, not treasuries, since the assets are inflation protected
EOG as a great company that is almost transparently great and therefore usually expensive, versus Diamondback as the more attractive stock after levering up for acquisitions
Cheniere trading near an 8% free cash flow yield against 5% for S&P midstream peers, with a pass-through model that takes no price risk
Gas-heavy producers versus oil producers, and refiners capturing margin while selling cigarettes and lottery tickets along the way
learned: Buy deep cyclicals when the commodity has collapsed and nobody will touch them, and sell when everyone is excited; never the reverse
War destroys inventories as well as supply, so restocking should keep oil production strong for a year or two even if peace arrives
A pass-through LNG model with no geopolitical or price risk can be the best risk-adjusted return in the sector without ever being the biggest gainer
These are value and trading vehicles; growth investors do not belong in them, by Eisman's own closing admission
notable: A technical failure killed the video at the 45-minute mark, so Eisman opens by asking listeners to stay for the audio-only back half.

title: Walmart & Target Signal Consumer Stress as the 10-Year Yield Hits 4.6% | The Weekly Wrap
summary: Hot CPI and PPI prints push the 10-year yield to 4.6%, through the 4.5% level he calls his Rubicon, and he explains why that made him lighten up on stocks. A mailbag question also produces his most detailed account yet of how his fund actually closed the Big Short trades in 2008.
discussed: Trump threatening to resume bombing Iran, sending oil higher and pressuring rates
The 10-year at 4.6% versus his 4.5% Rubicon, with upcoming inflation data unlikely to help
NextEra buying Dominion Energy in an all-stock utility merger aimed at data center power demand, including the world's largest data center market
Intuit growing revenue 10%, its slowest since 2024, laying off 17% of its workforce and falling to down 50% for the year
Nvidia's EPS of $1.87, up 95%, with margins still expanding
Home Depot and Lowe's both stuck at 0.6% same-store sales growth, confirming no housing pickup
A mailbag answer on private equity owned software: with ServiceNow down 50% in a year, the 2027 refinancing wall means sponsors must pony up equity or hand over the keys
learned: Have a line in the sand for rates and act when it breaks; his is 4.5% on the 10-year, and he lightened up rather than rationalize
Tight credit spreads do not mean corporate and sovereign creditworthiness have converged; the technicals are doing the work
Private credit's software problem is a 2027 event, not a today event, because that is when the refinancing forces a mark
Exiting a great trade is its own decision: he covered the Big Short positions in spring 2008 because a government bailout, not the fundamentals, had become the risk
notable: The mailbag reveal: covering meant calling the swap desks at Goldman Sachs and Deutsche Bank and accepting their prices, and what they did on their end is not something I thought about much.

title: How Silicon Valley Took Over the Defense Industry with Peter Arment | The Real Eisman Playbook Ep 61
summary: Baird's aerospace and defense analyst traces the industry from the 1993 Last Supper, when the Pentagon forced 60 primes to merge into a handful, to today, when venture-backed drone and space companies are unwinding that consolidation. The primes remain profitable but too big to pivot, and the share shift is running toward cheaper, faster, purpose-built systems.
discussed: The Last Supper dinner at the Pentagon on July 21, 1993, under Defense Secretary Les Aspin, which collapsed roughly 60 prime contractors
The wave of venture capital and private equity money that entered defense between 2020 and 2024
Lockheed Martin's F-35 at a nominal 80 million dollars each, with the program more than a third through its total buy at 156 aircraft a year
Taiwan's dilemma: the shortest distance to China is about 117 miles, which favors affordable drones over expensive fighters
Boeing's economics of spending billions to lose billions to make billions, with the 787 costing double the plan and post-dilution free cash flow potential cut from about $40 to $20 per share
A private equity rollup that consolidated the niche space supply chain the primes had outsourced
Curtiss-Wright and BWX Technologies as nuclear plays, with Curtiss-Wright serving license extensions across the 94 US reactors and growing mid-teens
learned: Forced consolidation created primes too big to pivot; a trillion-dollar defense budget now increasingly flows to nimble newcomers
In defense, the threat geometry sets the product: when the adversary is 117 miles away, cheap drones beat exquisite platforms
Avoid airframe makers at the start of an R&D cycle, because cost overruns are a feature of the model, not an accident
Aftermarket nuclear exposure is the quiet compounder: regulated license extensions on an installed base are recurring revenue with a growth kicker
notable: Eisman's closing verdict: not much to do in the primes, but Curtiss-Wright and BWX are the two names he is going to work on himself.

title: Inside the Hidden Consumer Crisis with Lakshmi Ganapathi
summary: Ganapathi argues the clean bank credit data is the problem rather than the reassurance, because extend and pretend keeps stressed borrowers marked as current. She and Eisman then map the same denial onto private credit's software book and finish on her short book.
discussed: Flat nonaccruals on both consumer and commercial books across every bank, with Jamie Dimon saying there are no issues so far
Extend and pretend keeping borrowers current on minimum payments, which lets lenders avoid marking to market and raising provisions because a provision is itself a panic signal
Buy now pay later reaching roughly 45 million users, with 29% using it for groceries against 14% two years earlier, and 13% using it to pay rent
Banks funding private credit through warehouse lines and direct lending, which then funds buy now pay later books through forward flow agreements
MUFG looking to move 2 billion off its book through a synthetic risk transfer to insurance companies, moving risk in name only
The private credit maturity wall arriving slowly, with roughly 11% refinancing next year and 20% after, against software marks down more than half
Her short book, FICO on VantageScore share gains and banks building internal models, plus AutoZone and Dorman on invoice factoring, GPI in used cars, Wingstop and DoorDash on affordability
learned: Benign data is not the same as a benign situation. Ask what accounting choice is producing the clean number before you trust it
The lender always breaks first and the consumer shows up as the second order effect, so watching consumer data for the first crack means watching the wrong series
Track what a credit product is being used for, not just how much of it there is. Groceries and rent on installment plans is a distress signal a balance total hides
A monopoly ends when a credible second option appears and the customers start building their own replacement, which is the FICO thesis in one line
Risk transfer is not risk removal. Synthetic transfers move the exposure to insurers rather than retiring it
notable: Eisman concedes the bank numbers are the numbers, then accepts they may be measuring something other than the consumer's actual health.

title: The SpaceX IPO: Science Fiction or Serious Investment? | The Weekly Wrap
summary: He dissects the SpaceX S-1 ahead of the June 12 IPO and finds the numbers far less bold than the story: decelerating growth, a 1.9 billion dollar quarterly loss, and only one profitable division. He pairs it with a new recurring theme, that technology's business model builds dependence while subsidizing user costs, and AI tokens are next.
discussed: Nasdaq rewriting its index rules so SpaceX can join with only about a 5% float, on a potential 1.75 to 2 trillion dollar valuation
SpaceX 1Q26 numbers: revenue of 4.7 billion, up 15% versus 33% growth in 2025, with a 1.9 billion loss
The segment split: connectivity at 3.3 billion is the only profitable division, while space revenue of 619 million fell 28%
Salesforce beating on adjusted EPS of 3.88 while GAAP EPS was $2.42, a gap he attributes to stock-based comp he considers ridiculous to exclude
The subsidized-addiction theme: like Uber Eats, AI token costs have been subsidized, and agentic AI is where the real bill arrives
A mailbag on ratings agencies: Moody's and S&P up roughly 24% against a market that doubled, because 2020 and 2021 pulled a decade of debt issuance forward
His answer to the ethical question of owning Moody's given the agencies' AAA stamps in 2008
learned: When an exchange changes its rules to accommodate one company, the deck is being stacked for the launch; read the S-1, not the mythology
A 15% growth, money-losing company at a near 2 trillion dollar valuation prices in multi-planetary dreams, not the connectivity business that actually earns money
Adjusted EPS that excludes stock-based comp is a choice, not a fact; the GAAP gap tells you how big the choice is
Oligopolies can underperform for years for cyclical reasons, issuance droughts, without the moat being impaired; that can be the entry
notable: On SpaceX versus bank stocks: the words we would like to expand our net interest margin just do not generate the same energy as multi-planetary exploration.

title: Is AI a Bubble? Gary Marcus on What Could Break the Story | The Real Eisman Playbook Ep 62
summary: Gary Marcus returns to argue that scaling stopped paying off in December 2024 and that the industry keeps promising more data will fix problems it has never solved. Eisman plays the reluctant bull: he shorted subprime, but he cannot short a story whose biggest company just grew revenue 85%.
discussed: Marcus's 25-year thesis: distribution shift identified in 1998, hallucinations flagged in 2001, still unsolved
Companies privately conceding around December 2024 that bigger models stopped delivering expected returns
CPUs making a comeback (Intel included) because agents need CPU time alongside GPUs, and the case for medium models plus symbolic AI
Token economics: all-you-can-eat pricing at slim or negative margins, with agents deepening losses just as the labs want to IPO
One company spending 180 billion on infrastructure, which both call lunacy driven by FOMO
A Sequoia-based estimate of how much revenue the industry collectively needs to justify the spend
Nvidia's revenue accelerating from 65% to 85% growth over two quarters
learned: What broke subprime was the end buyer refusing the paper; the AI equivalent would be customers refusing token-based pricing once the buffet closes
LLMs are next-word predictors building a model of how people talk, which makes them superb mimics and unreliable generalizers
Unlike a spreadsheet on your laptop, every LLM query has an incremental cloud cost, and that cost structure shapes the whole industry
Marcus frames the AI trade as a bet with a low but nonzero probability of paying off, and Eisman accepts the framing
notable: Eisman admits he could not make the short argument he made on subprime right now, because the biggest company on planet Earth just reported 85% revenue growth.

title: SpaceX's Exploding Capex, AI Addiction Lawsuits, and the Reality of "TokenMaxxing" | The Weekly Wrap
summary: He defends last week's tongue-in-cheek SpaceX takedown by contrasting today's meme-driven IPOs with the institutional dog-and-pony shows he sat through, then turns to business models built on addiction. Kalshi, he argues, has taken gambling out of regulated rooms and put it everywhere, including classrooms.
discussed: The SpaceX valuation assuming conquest of a $28.5 trillion TAM, most of it in AI, where Grok is not yet a world-class product
Kalshi and near-miss psychology: a gambler who almost wins bets again, and more often
Crypto losing its mojo just as Kalshi exploded
Nvidia entering the PC market with a chip in Windows machines from Microsoft, Dell, HP, and Lenovo; over 30 laptops and 10 desktops planned
S&P 500 up over 10% and Nasdaq up 15% for the year, with financials the notable laggard
Partners Group's evergreen Global Value fund receiving 9.8% redemption requests against a 5% quarterly cap
Mailbag: own versus rent in a housing market locked by 3 to 4% COVID mortgages against 7% new ones
learned: Redemption gates spreading from private credit to private equity vehicles signal investors questioning the entire alternatives space
A locked housing market inflates prices artificially: scarce inventory, not strong demand, holds them up
Buy a home below what you can afford so the hidden costs (taxes, maintenance) do not break you, and assume you will merely break even
IPOs once priced in room for investors; meme-era offerings price for the sellers
notable: His housing advice to a high school class: own a home if you want one, but never assume it will make you money.

title: The AI Semiconductor Boom and What Could End It with Stacy Rasgon | The Real Eisman Playbook Ep 63
summary: Eisman says semis are now what financials were in 2008, the center of the universe, and brings back Bernstein's Stacy Rasgon seven months after his last appearance to explain why the boom is accelerating rather than peaking. The one thing that ends it, both agree, is disappointing returns on AI itself, and Rasgon thinks it is far too early for that.
discussed: Nvidia resegmenting its data center business into hyperscale and non-hyperscale customers
The GB300 NVL72 rack: 72 GPUs plus 36 ARM-based Grace CPUs, with agentic AI driving CPU demand per rack higher
Rental prices on even old compute rising because demand outruns exponentially growing supply
Intel: 18A yields near zero at this stage, foundry rumors around Apple, and packaging demand as the real positive
The big five equipment makers: Applied Materials, Lam Research, KLA, ASML, and Tokyo Electron
AI capex at roughly 75% of GDP growth last year, a share Rasgon compares to the railroad buildout
China powering data centers with coal plants at will while the US struggles to add grid capacity, down to restarting Three Mile Island
learned: Investors in a supply-constrained boom chase bottlenecks, which is why memory and CPU stocks (SanDisk, Micron and peers) have beaten Nvidia itself this year
Even in a mania, multiples can contract: the CPU names' earnings rose faster than their stocks
If AI returns disappoint there is nowhere to hide, in semis or out; the buildout is carrying the whole economy
Depreciation of old GPUs only matters in a demand collapse, at which point, as Rasgon puts it, everyone is screwed anyway
notable: Eisman opens by explaining he saw the financial crisis coming because finance was the center of the universe and it was his sector; today the center of the universe is semiconductors.

title: Google Raises $85 Billion and the Market Finally Wakes Up | The Weekly Wrap
summary: A real correction arrives: Broadcom's soft AI numbers plus strong jobs data push the S&P down 2.64% and Nasdaq down 4.18% on Friday. The deeper story is that hyperscalers have become capital-intensive hardware companies now asking public shareholders, not free cash flow, to fund a trillion dollars of capex.
discussed: Google's $85 billion raise, plus SoftBank, Supermicro, and Oracle adding $20 billion, running his tally of equity demands to $360 billion
Hyperscaler AI capex going from about 400 billion last year to close to 1 trillion this year
The moat question: Gemini on top one week, Anthropic the next, despite the spend
OpenAI's S-1 after raising $122 billion at an $852 billion valuation, making a $100 billion IPO plausible
Apple's WWDC and how abandoning the LLM race now looks like a great decision
Private equity technology deals down 70% in Q1 to $20 billion, holding periods stretching past 7 years, $4 trillion unmonetized
The 10-year yield back above 4.5% after employment numbers took Fed cuts off the table
learned: It is one thing to own AI stocks when the companies foot the capex bill, another when they raise the money from public shareholders
Sameness across managers increases the risk that everyone underperforms at once; herd positioning is itself a risk factor
If your active manager is hugging an index, just buy the index; pay up only for genuine stock picking
Massive spend with no durable model differentiation is the signature of an industry without moats
notable: His verdict on manager crowding into the same trades: this is way past FOMO, this is required uniformity in order to stay in business.

title: Is Private Equity Destroying the Life Insurance Industry? | The Real Eisman Playbook Ep 64
summary: After Tom Gober's alarming take on private equity in life insurance, Eisman seeks a second opinion from Tom Gallagher, the Evercore analyst he has known for decades. Gallagher is broadly comfortable: the big alternative insurers take somewhat more risk for an extra 100 basis points, but not an insane amount, and Eisman is surprised by the answer.
discussed: The lineage from Apollo's 2012 annuity acquisition through Athene, taken public and then private again
The player map: Apollo biggest, KKR's Global Atlantic second, Carlyle with 10% of a Corebridge piece alongside a Japanese insurer, Blackstone taking minority stakes
Gallagher's bond-by-bond eye test of the top 30 to 40 private credit positions in alternative insurers' books
Regulators accommodating offshore reinsurance because punitive rules would push companies out of their jurisdictions entirely
Past blowups: 20-year liabilities hedged with three-month options, and secondary guarantee universal life priced for mid-single-digit lapses that ran at 1%
Apollo's net interest margin squeezed by the roll-off of low-cost liabilities plus Fed cuts
The Corebridge-Equitable merger as a scale play in commodity fixed annuities, and Lincoln's roughly 9.5% preferred due out in 2027
learned: Traditional life insurers run a zero-loss expectation model, so conservative that an extra 100 basis points of yield need not signal recklessness
In a commodity product the only way to win is scale, which is the entire logic of annuity consolidation
Decades of long-tail blowups, from long-term care to variable annuities, explain why these stocks sell at three to five times earnings and why the discount persists
At three to five times earnings, buying back your own stock beats any M&A deal, yet the companies still will not go beyond about 8% of market cap a year
notable: Eisman deliberately staged a second opinion against his own earlier guest, and admits he expected the trusted veteran to be more scared than he was.

title: The Lawsuits That Could Change Social Media Forever w/ Ben Zipursky
summary: Eisman brings a Fordham tort professor on to work out whether the wave of addiction lawsuits against Meta and Google can survive Section 230. Zipursky explains how plaintiffs reframe the claim as defective product design rather than harmful content, and why he thinks the strongest looking theory is also the weakest on the law.
discussed: Section 230C of the Communications Decency Act and how broadly courts have read it, including the Sixth Circuit protecting the operator of a gossip site over user submitted defamation
The Los Angeles verdict against Meta, roughly 6 million dollars, with one plaintiff among 1,800 in that filing alone and scores of similar suits nationwide
The New Mexico case split into a consumer fraud jury phase and an injunctive phase heard by a judge, since injunctions do not usually go to a jury
What the injunction actually asks for, namely that Meta redesign its algorithms to be less addictive
Zipursky's negative view of the public nuisance theory, the same theory he is publishing against in the opioid context, which he calls made up but scary enough to force settlements
The product liability route, traced back through the collapse of the privity rule and the exploding Coke bottle line of cases, where a defect is enough without proving negligence
The complete absence of appellate rulings so far, with only two tried cases and every one of them heading up on appeal
learned: The legal question that decides the money is framing. Content claims die under Section 230, design defect claims survive it
A theory can be strong as leverage and weak as law. Public nuisance settles cases precisely because defendants will not risk it going to verdict
Two trial verdicts are not a trend. Until an appellate court rules, nothing about the exposure is settled
Common law does move, and it moves through exactly this kind of repeated litigation, so slow legislatures are not the only route to a rule change
Watch state legislatures alongside the courts. Zipursky thinks statutory regulation of social media is politically achievable where other tech regulation is not
notable: The tort professor turns out to be more optimistic about legislation than about the lawsuits he is being asked to handicap.

title: Anthropic Gets Shut Down By the Government and the AI Story Gets More Complicated | The Weekly Wrap
summary: A short Juneteenth week with two shocks: an Iran memorandum of understanding that the market overcelebrated, and the US government issuing an export control directive that effectively shuts down Anthropic's Fable 5 and Mythos 5 models. He then lays out his fullest side-by-side of the AI bull and bear cases yet.
discussed: The Iran deal being only an MOU to negotiate for 60 days, with the Strait of Hormuz open in the interim; oil fell 5%
Anthropic classified a supply chain risk after limiting DoD usage, then barred from giving foreign nationals, including its own employees, access to Fable 5 and Mythos 5
Kevin Warsh's first Fed meeting: rates unchanged, cuts ruled out, hikes not
The bear case ledger: shareholders now fund capex, and 1 trillion of annual spend has produced no visible moats
The airlines versus TransDigm analogy: hyperscalers as capital-hungry airlines, their suppliers as the great businesses
Europe's top five (ASML, then Roche, LVMH, Novartis, Nestle at 260 to 330 billion) against US top five market caps of 2.7 to 5.1 trillion
Premium interviews with law professor Ben Zipursky on social media addiction suits and with cannabis company Glass House Brands after rescheduling
learned: Watch the difference between a treaty and a memorandum of understanding; markets priced a peace that has not been negotiated
When an industry turns capital intensive, look for its TransDigm: the suppliers, not the platforms, may own the pricing power
Europe is not a hedge against a US recession; its large caps depend on the US economy and carry almost no tech exposure
Addiction-model lawsuits hinge on intent: algorithms designed to addict, not merely engaging products
notable: The week's strangest headline delivered deadpan: the government's export directive shuts down the most sophisticated models of a leading AI lab, and the AI story gets more complicated.

title: The Real State of the American Consumer w/ Three Evercore Analysts | The Real Eisman Playbook Ep 65
summary: Eisman calls in reinforcements: three Evercore analysts covering retail, restaurants and food, and big box, for a full anatomy of the K-shaped consumer. The verdict is a hollowed-out middle, a protein-obsessed eater, and one enormous winner in Walmart.
discussed: Restaurant spending splitting into equal thirds across under 50,000, 50,000 to 100,000, and over 100,000 income cohorts
The barbell in retail: Ralph Lauren and Coach fine at the top, off-price killing it on value, an ocean of struggle in the middle despite the best tax refund season since COVID
Binetti's Murderer's Row of broken stocks: Lululemon, Ulta, Gap, Kohl's, Canada Goose
Nike's rushed direct-to-consumer push, which cost it shelf intelligence and let competitors seize on product weakness
Team protein: LongHorn running 10 to 11% same-store sales while Olive Garden, Domino's, and Wendy's struggle
Legacy food companies (Smucker's, Kellogg's, Kraft Heinz, Campbell) skewed away from protein in a GLP-1 world
Home Depot and Lowe's stuck behind a locked housing market, with pro the only growth avenue, and Walmart's same-day delivery of nearly anything
learned: Walmart's strength is a warning, not just a stock story: it is winning because the middle-income consumer is trading down
A brand that goes direct-to-consumer too fast stops seeing why shoppers pick up the competitor's shoe, and loses the market's early warning system
GLP-1 drugs are quietly repricing the entire food aisle; the losers are the non-protein legacy brands with no end in sight
Experiential retail like the Polo Bar keeps an aspirational brand alive off the shelf
Housing will not unlock through prices: supply scarcity keeps them rising even with sales terrible
notable: Eisman reads out the list of broken retail stocks and christens it Murderer's Row.

title: Why Cannabis Rescheduling Changes Everything for Glass House Brands
summary: Medical cannabis moved from Schedule I to Schedule III in late April, and Eisman brings back Glass House Brands to work out what that unlocks. The answer is geography: the same pound that fetches 200 dollars in California sells for 800 in other medical states and more in Europe, with almost no added cost beyond shipping. Eisman owns the stock and says so repeatedly while insisting he is not selling it to anyone.
discussed: Medical cannabis reclassified from Schedule I to Schedule III on April 23, with an expedited DEA hearing on recreational set for June 29 and a mid July deadline
Glass House producing at roughly 100 dollars per pound and selling into California wholesale at about 200, against 800 to 1,000 per pound in other US medical markets
First quarter revenue of 40.5 million, roughly 80% wholesale and the rest from 11 retail stores
Capacity of about 1.4 million pounds of biomass with the current build out and one greenhouse still vacant, against roughly 700,000 pounds in a normal prior year
Europe as a near empty field, with Germany already a multi billion dollar medical market and almost no European cultivation

The exchange listing problem, with the stock stuck on CBOE Canada and US over the counter, blocking institutional ownership, and precedents where Curaleaf and TerrAscend uplisted to the TSX on a small non Schedule I revenue line
Cannabis and wine farms failing in California, creating land Glass House can buy and convert
learned: When a regulatory cage opens, the low cost producer captures the most, because the price gap between markets falls straight to margin
A listing venue is part of the thesis. A stock institutions legally cannot buy carries a discount that disappears the day they can
Ask what a company can do tomorrow that it could not do yesterday. That question separates real regulatory change from headlines
Disclose your position before you teach the story, then let the listener discount you accordingly
notable: DeCourcy opens by joking that the interview may well be about him getting people to buy the stock, and Eisman lets it stand.

title: The Q2 2026 Report Card: Who Won, Who Lost, and Why | The Weekly Wrap
summary: An early second-quarter report card before he leaves on holiday: a powerful rally off the Q1 bottom, with the S&P up 15% and Nasdaq up 23% for the quarter. Under the surface, investors are chasing scarcity in semiconductors while fleeing anything AI threatens to eat, from software to consulting.
discussed: SanDisk and Micron both up over 200% in the second quarter alone as investors play capex-driven scarcity
Software carnage: Salesforce down 18%, Adobe down 19%, Intuit down 39%
Accenture's ugly quarter: revenue up 3%, bookings down 3%, contracts slipping to fiscal 27, the stock down 18% Friday and over 50% for the year
Three Accenture acquisitions announced in one day, which he reads as buying stuff to hide weakness
Premium subscriptions moving to Substack with a bonus month for existing members
Glass House Brands listing on the NYSE June 30 under ticker GLAS after medical cannabis rescheduling to schedule three
His history lesson on Alan Greenspan ignoring unpayable subprime mortgages, versus Kevin Warsh's close-to-the-vest style
learned: When capex is unstoppable, the market pays for whatever is scarce; the AI report card is really a scarcity report card
Clustered acquisitions announced into weak results are a red flag, not a growth story
Companies are spending more on AI and hiring consultants to help, while cutting everything else; net-net the consultants still lose
Markets are amoral: they do not care about a social safety net, only about dynamism, which is the whole US versus Europe investment case
notable: His epitaph for Greenspan: he saw borrowers who could not pay, decided legal meant acceptable, and history will not be kind to him.

title: The Market's Biggest Warning Signs Right Now with Todd Sohn | The Real Eisman Playbook Ep 66
summary: A chart-by-chart tour with Strategas's chief chartist that keeps arriving at the same place: every flow in the market is a tech flow. Eisman's closing warning is that an index holder is no longer diversified, and if the one theme reverses there will be no place to hide.
discussed: Reading RSI momentum on the semiconductor ETF SOXX, and why overbought is a guideline, not a rule
The boom in leveraged ETFs, including single-stock two-times products that did not exist until 2022
Tech at nearly 40% of the S&P 500, and well over 50% once Google and Amazon are added back in
Flows pouring into tech ETFs while cyclicals and defensives sit moribund; industrials get money only through the power story
No flows into financials, which Sohn reads as unease and, contrarily, as bullish
REITs at roughly 2% of the S&P, an index of about 30 stocks, too small for a portfolio manager to care
Bitcoin's chart described as rough, with money leaving both gold and Bitcoin ETFs and young traders decamping to Kalshi
learned: Owning the index no longer means owning diversification; market-cap weighting has quietly concentrated most funds in the same handful of names
Charts are a summary device: a hundred of them can reconstruct a month of news, and they tell you fastest when you are wrong
Within tech the winners are the groups without AI capital-intensity exposure, semis and tech equipment, while Meta, Oracle, Microsoft and Amazon charts have gone soft
An asset that migrates from counterculture to traditional finance can lose the very audience that drove it; Bitcoin's absorption into TradFi was, in Eisman's word, death
notable: Sohn's parting instruction is pay attention to what you own; Eisman's is darker: if this stuff ever reverses, there will be no place to hide.

title: Steve Eisman Reveals His Personal Portfolio: Every Position Explained
summary: Eisman answers a recurring subscriber request and walks his 16 long positions one by one, sorted into five themes: AI, power and infrastructure, value, great franchises, and unique stories. He explains his method first, buy a story, size it fully, check it every quarter, sell when the thesis breaks, and then names the four conditions that would make him tear the whole thing up.
discussed: Sixteen longs across five themes, with seven of them tech or AI adjacent, which he defends by noting infotech is 37% of the S&P 500 and closer to 50% once Google and Amazon are counted

His guess that at least 50% of all AI spending traces back to Anthropic and OpenAI, both of which lose billions and depend on venture funding, with over 50% of Oracle's data center backlog tied to OpenAI
The Wall Street Journal report that OpenAI may slash prices, which he reads as evidence AI has little or no moat, since the industry already undercharges for tokens
Arista falling 14% for not raising guidance enough, and his admission that failing to also buy the cheaper Cisco was a mistake
Trimming Microsoft over the AI software debate and possible capital raising, noting Chris Hohn sold his entire position
GE Vernova at 45 times 2026 earnings and Quanta at 50 times, both defended on order backlogs that give years of earnings visibility
Charter as a cheap turnaround bundling cable and mobile at 100 dollars against 180 to 200 for rivals, plus Meritage Homes bought near tangible book, both admittedly badly timed
A Glass House valuation exercise producing 40, 49 and 58 dollars per share across three EBITDA margin scenarios against a 13 dollar stock
learned: Concentration is a decision, not an accident. Count your AI exposure against the index weight before calling it aggressive
The discipline that protects a long hold is studying the sell case every quarter, not conviction
Expensive is acceptable when the backlog is long. A business booking orders that fill in years has visibility a multiple cannot see
Write down in advance what would change your mind. He names four triggers, including the 10 year holding above 4.5% for more than a few weeks
When both sides of a debate are so passionate they cannot tolerate each other, treat that heat as a bubble signal
notable: He warns that today's buy the dip reflex belongs to investors too young to have invested through the flat 1970s.

title: Who Wins the Midterms & What It Means for Markets with Dan Clifton | The Real Eisman Playbook Ep 67
summary: The show's first-ever guest returns to handicap the midterms: Democrats likely take the House, the Senate is a 50/50 coin flip, and everything traces back to April 2025, when tariffs turned Trump's economic approval negative for the first time. Clifton then maps how Fed personnel, the 2028 field and the data center backlash all hang off that political arithmetic.
discussed: How the April 3, 2025 tariff announcement, the day before Clifton's first appearance, flipped Trump's approval on the economy negative for the first time
Four political parties in Washington, two inside each formal party, and why a Democratic Congress would choose accomplishment over ambition
Senate math: Democratic pickup chances in four states, a looming nomination error in Michigan, and a prestigious former governor running in New Hampshire
Powell holding his seat through the midterms so a Democratic Senate would force Trump to appoint a mainstream economist rather than a MAGA loyalist
Kevin Warsh's focus on shrinking the Fed's 6 trillion dollar balance sheet by about 1 trillion over time
Data centers as the new fracking: Loudoun County, Virginia data centers paying 40% of the education bill, cutting property taxes about $2,500 a year against a $20 electricity increase
2028 handicapping: Newsom the messy-field Democratic frontrunner; Vance leading Republicans with Rubio and DeSantis alive, and Trump encouraging Vance rather than reining him in
learned: Central bank succession is a political chess game: a chair can protect institutional independence simply by timing his own departure around Senate control
Frontrunner status three years out is nearly worthless; the early leader is rarely the nominee
Local fiscal math can defuse a national backlash: where data centers visibly cut property taxes, the politics flip
Presidents historically muzzle ambitious vice presidents; Trump's encouragement of Vance breaks a pattern running from Reagan-Bush through Clinton-Gore
Large-cap defense stocks have badly underperformed while defense tech has not, a signal of where the new procurement model is heading
notable: Clifton's thesis in five words: data centers are the new fracking, opposed by the same environmental money.

title: The Bearish Case for Oil and Gold with Queen Anne's Gate Capital
summary: Kelly and O'Flynn argue the war disguised a huge and growing oil surplus, and that when the fog lifts prices fall hard. Kelly says the 20s are reachable, with 40 to 50 the likelier landing zone. O'Flynn explains why gold sold off during exactly the crisis it was supposed to hedge, and neither guest nor host can find a reason to own crypto.
discussed: Kelly's view that oil was at 50 and heading to 40 before the war, and that surpluses are larger now, making the 20s reachable
Roughly 5 million barrels per day of new supply arriving next year against demand growth of maybe 2.5 million even on generous assumptions
The UAE adding about 1.5 million barrels now that it sits outside OPEC, plus China pulling back its own demand
Record US exports of distillate and jet fuel propping up apparent demand, with demand itself calculated as a residual plug
The Strait of Hormuz mattering far less than assumed, with Saudi and UAE bypass routes running and Iraq, the most exposed producer, claiming two week restart capability
Gold running from 2,500 to 5,200 over last year in anticipation of catastrophe, then selling off when the catastrophe arrived and holders needed cash
Both guests preferring silver to gold, and Eisman noting he has never owned gold in his life
learned: Oil demand is a residual, backed out from supply, refining runs and net trade. Treat it as an estimate with a plug inside it
A crowded consensus is its own risk. When you cannot find a bear anywhere, the bullish news is already in the price
A war can hide a surplus. Disruption headlines suppress the inventory signal until the shooting stops
Cheaper oil is not automatically disinflationary in a country where electricity, not oil, drives the energy bill
notable: Eisman notes crypto falls on the very days it is supposed to rise, with roughly 75% correlation to the Nasdaq, and O'Flynn suggests young traders left crypto for prediction markets.

title: Why the Entire Market Is Now a Single Bet on AI | The Weekly Wrap
summary: A holiday-week wrap that Eisman uses to step back and structure the AI debate itself, arguing that stocks and bonds have collapsed into one trade. He maps the argument onto his subprime experience: theses develop over time, and the job now is to understand this one well enough to measure its risk.
discussed: Iranian attacks on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, and a premium deep dive flagging the UAE pipeline opening in 2027 that would make the strait matter less
Torsten Slok's estimate that AI data center and energy spending contributes about 1 percentage point of GDP growth, roughly half the total
AI token pricing: subscriptions that never covered token costs, corporations grading employees on usage volume, and what happens as subsidies fade
Chinese AI models as a cheap alternative, raising the possibility of a full-blown price war
The parallel to May 2007, when a tip about a Morgan Stanley internal subprime fund launched a year-long treasure hunt into Wall Street's balance sheet exposure
Nike flat after a disappointing call, plus Circle and stablecoin news
A mailbag on reading: no business books, tons of history, historical fiction like Colleen McCullough's First Man in Rome, and comic books
learned: Diversification has quietly ceased to exist when the stock and bond markets are both expressions of the same AI trade
Investment arguments are built in stages, not delivered whole; the subprime thesis took over a year of digging after the first clue
Subsidized pricing manufactures demand; the real test of AI economics arrives when customers pay the true token cost
Broad, seemingly unrelated reading is an investing edge: history and even dystopian fiction teach that leaders act irrationally and anything is possible
notable: On why his cynicism was right in the GFC when everyone laughed: being well-read is my superpower.

title: AI Dominates Economy and Markets with Torsten Slok | The Real Eisman Playbook Ep 68
summary: Apollo's chief economist decomposes US growth into three unusual engines, with AI spending alone providing about half of it, and shows the K-shaped economy running through wealth, wages and inflation at once. The conversation ends where Eisman wants it: the 60/40 portfolio is now AI-indexed on both sides, so the story had better work.
discussed: GDP growth of about 2% split into roughly 1 point from AI data center and energy spending, 0.3 from the industrial renaissance, and 0.9 from big beautiful bill tax refunds
Housing and autos stalling because the rate-sensitive economy no longer drives growth, leaving rates high for longer
The K shape measured three ways: wealth, Atlanta Fed wage growth by income level, and New York Fed inflation exposure for low-income households
The software maturity wall: 2021 and 2022 vintage debt with 7-year maturities coming due in 2028 and 2029, before the AI disruption debate even starts
US dynamism at possibly an all-time high, with strong job creation among young people despite the layoff headlines
Federal debt at about 100% of GDP heading toward 175%, and why China avoids weaponizing its Treasury holdings
Europe described as sclerotic, waking up on defense but needing strategic financing to compete
learned: Growth built on one sector is fragile in a specific way: no single sector, even housing, has contributed a full GDP point in decades
Tax-refund stimulus creates its own cliff; strip it out and the 2027 growth base falls below 2%
A refinancing wall can kill leveraged software companies on macro grounds alone, whatever AI does to their terminal value
Bond allocations no longer hedge equity AI exposure, because data center debt issuance has AI-indexed the credit market too
A creditor rarely crashes its best customer; China's Treasury restraint is self-interest, not goodwill
notable: Eisman's closing verdict: this AI story better work, because if it does not, the losses will be mammoth.

title: Beyond Ozempic: The Next Wave of Biotech Winners with Boris Peaker
summary: Eisman admits he has never really invested in biotech and spends 74 minutes being taught the sector from the ground up by Jones Trading analyst Boris Peaker. Peaker explains why the pharma and biotech distinction has collapsed, why Phase 1 success so often dies in Phase 3, and where the economics actually reward innovation. The verdict on the business model is blunt: most biotechs exist to be bought.
discussed: The historical split between pharma making small molecules and biotech making complex biologics, dating to Genentech in the late 1970s, now effectively gone
Why Phase 1 results mislead, with carefully curated patients giving way to broad populations where diet, adherence and drug interactions introduce variability
Grapefruit blocking a liver enzyme pathway and disrupting many drugs, offered as the everyday example of uncontrolled patient behavior
Trial cost drivers including university administrative overhead of 30% to 40% on top of study payments, plus screening, imaging and diagnostics
Oncology as the commercially favored field because efficacy reads out fast and safety tolerance is higher for terminal patients
Revolution's pancreatic cancer drug extending median survival from about 6 months to about 13, which Peaker calls scientifically impressive and Eisman calls still only 13 months
Antibiotics as commercially unattractive because a new one is held back as a drug of last resort, and aging as unfundable because the FDA demands a functional endpoint
B cell depletion and immune reset, with a German lupus study keeping B cells undetectable for three to four months and seeing autoantibodies fail to return
learned: Better science does not mean a better business. Antibiotics prove that a genuinely needed drug can have no commercial model
Ask what the endpoint is before believing a therapeutic area is investable. No measurable functional endpoint means no approval path
Early stage trial data is a filtered sample. The curation that makes Phase 1 look good is exactly what Phase 3 removes
In a sector where the exit is acquisition, the question is not can this company commercialize, but will a large buyer want to
notable: Peaker wants to see oncology survival curves plotted next to life insurance actuarial tables, so the real remaining gap is visible.

title: Bank Earnings Just Gave the Market a Much Needed Confidence Boost | The Weekly Wrap
summary: Bank earnings come in with benign credit across the board, which Eisman treats as the single best concurrent read on the US economy. Around that anchor he works through Circle's competitive problem, an IBM pre-announcement that rattles software, and a mailbag that turns into a guided tour of his 11,000-comic collection.
discussed: Large-bank credit trends flat year over year and versus the first quarter; banks trading at 1.3 to 2.1 times tangible book on returns of 13% to 18%
Circle's bank charter weighed against the bigger news of a Visa and Mastercard stablecoin consortium; the stock's round trip from a $31 IPO in June 2025 to nearly 270 to about 63
IBM pre-announcing a disastrous quarter with grim implications for the software sector, while PayPal is reported possibly for sale
UnitedHealth beating and raising on flat revenue, with industry-wide price increases doing the work
GE Aerospace earning $2.02 versus a $1.86 estimate on revenue of 12.63 billion, up 24%, and the stock falling anyway
A mailbag on Bank of New York: a trust bank he has never found worth the attention, and a confession that he owns no banks right now
Twenty-one graphic novel recommendations, heavy on Brian Michael Bendis, plus David Gemmell's Lord of the Silver Bow for The Odyssey's movie week
learned: Bank results are a concurrent indicator with the broadest credit exposure in the economy; when they are benign, the predicted crisis is not here yet
Creating a stablecoin is easy; breaking into the payments system is the hard part, which is why a Visa and Mastercard consortium outweighs a bank charter
A beat means nothing without the pre-positioning: GE Aerospace's excellent quarter still sent the stock down
The most important post-GFC story is how resilient the US economy has become, seventeen years of predicted crises that never arrived
notable: The premium tease quotes Boris Peaker's biggest AI hope for biotech: cutting the probability that a large clinical trial fails.

title: AI Has a Power Problem: Why the U.S. Power Grid Can't Keep Up | The Real Eisman Playbook Ep 69
summary: Baird's sustainable energy and mobility analyst covers the ring just outside the semiconductor center of the universe: the companies electrifying the grid that AI needs. The theme throughout is physical constraint, since turbines, permits and labor all move on timescales the AI buildout does not respect.
discussed: Grid strain predating the data center wave: Midtown Manhattan office towers already getting curtailment notices banning air conditioning from 12 to 4 on hot days
The US adding on the order of 30 gigawatts of power a year, the equivalent of a couple of cities, much of it data center driven

GE Vernova's gas turbines: an order booked this quarter is not installed at a utility until 2030 or 2031, giving visibility deep into the 2030s, with nuclear not material to earnings until at least 2035
Tesla's megapack battery business growing over 30% a year from plants in California, Texas and Shanghai, and Kallo's bet that SpaceX buys Tesla relatively soon
Rivian's R2, a roughly $40,000 to $45,000 smaller SUV that Kallo drove at launch and thinks out-styles the saturated Model Y

Residential solar's brutal economics, door-to-door sales with $10,000 customer acquisition costs, against utility-scale; First Solar and Nextracker discussed, with tariffs souring him on most of the group
Air permits for nitrogen and sulfur oxides taking six months at the state and local level even as federal CO2 concern disappears
learned: The binding constraint on AI is physical: turbines, transformers, permits and skilled labor cannot be scaled at software speed
Long-lead-time equipment makers enjoy a rare kind of earnings visibility; GE Vernova can see its backlog well into the next decade
Hyperscalers still honor their own CO2 targets even where regulators no longer care, which keeps clean generation in the mix
Labor supply may be the last bottleneck standing: the open question is whether the US can staff everything it has decided to build
notable: Kallo, on Musk consolidating control, predicts SpaceX will buy Tesla and soon; Eisman stays a skeptic on the robotaxi promise, noting Elon has been making it for 10 years.

title: Payments Industry - Fear and Reality
summary: Investors have marked down the entire payments complex on fear of agentic AI, and Suchoski's research says the fear runs far ahead of the facts. Agents today mostly do discovery and comparison while humans still press pay, and any agentic commerce that scales will almost certainly run over the existing card rails. Eisman's takeaway is that Visa and MasterCard are the only long term holdings in the group.
discussed: Suchoski's framework of delegation levels, from a recurring subscription at the low end to full agent execution, with today's activity concentrated in search and comparison
Consumer protections, habit and rewards as the reason card rails are sticky, and the requirement that any new rail replicate chargeback protection before adoption
Payments being used as a source of funds, shorted to finance positions in faster growing AI exposed names rather than on company specific bearishness
Bitcoin falling from roughly 120,000 near its October peak to about 65,000, dragging stablecoin volumes that are mostly tied to digital asset trading
The stablecoin bull case shifting away from Circle, with cross border B2B still logically compelling but adoption Eisman calls glacial
Visa and MasterCard partnering with stablecoin issuers to let wallet holders spend over the existing network, leveraging distribution rather than defending against it
PayPal's premium pricing surviving after rivals matched its checkout experience, and Toast hit twice as both a payments and a software name plus rising memory chip costs
learned: Separate the psychology from the mechanics. A sector can be repriced on a fear whose evidence has not arrived
A new payment rail must clear the two sided adoption problem and match incumbent fraud protection. Technical superiority alone moves nobody
Short selling is not always a bearish opinion. Sometimes a group is sold simply to fund a better idea elsewhere
In a hard industry, own the toll collectors and treat everything else as a trade
notable: On stablecoins Eisman answers the logic with a demand for proof: great thesis, show me the money.

title: Google's Negative Cash Flow and the AI Capex Reckoning | The Weekly Wrap
summary: Earnings week shows investors finally punishing ever-mounting AI capex while rewarding almost nothing. Eisman works through his own book, the Equifax read-across to his FICO short, Moody's, and ServiceNow, whose fine quarter loses to the SaaSpocalypse narrative anyway.
discussed: US and Iran trading blows over the weekend as the war grinds on
Equifax results as a window on the FICO short: the Workforce Solutions division, EWS, is really a software business now caught in the SaaSpocalypse debate over AI-powered verification
Moody's earning $4.68, up 31%, with the 2026 multiple now below 30 times; he keeps owning the duopoly and dismisses the AI-disruption fear
ServiceNow: EPS up 10%, revenue of 4 billion up 24%, no visible AI damage, stock down almost 4% and off 38% for the year
A mailbag on Bank of New York and why he owns no bank stocks at the moment despite the group's 30%-plus run
A tutorial on funding shorts: shorting a stock you expect to go nowhere to finance a long you love
Charter reporting Friday, one day after the wrap records
learned: When a narrative hardens, fundamentals stop mattering in the short run; fighting the AI narrative is like fighting a ghost
A quality franchise going sideways is a valuation reset in disguise: Moody's flat since fall 2024 is the cheapest it has been in years
Shorts are not always directional bets; a funding short converts a mediocre stock into capital for a better idea
Watch what investors punish, not what companies report: identical beats now get opposite reactions depending on capex exposure
notable: The ServiceNow line of the week: the irony is that it keeps executing well, but fighting the AI narrative is like fighting a ghost.

title: The AI Revolution: Who Wins, Who Loses & the SaaSpocalypse  | The Real Eisman Playbook Ep 70
summary: Two full-stack tech analysts, the perma-bull newly out on his own and the more measured Davidson voice, argue out how the AI debate turned two-sided in a single year. Even the bulls now concede the live questions: return on the data center spend, whether moats exist, and which incumbents AI eats.
discussed: The two master debates: will the data center buildout earn a return on its capital, and do the model companies have any moat

The Oracle object lesson: backlog jumping from 150 to 450 billion in a day, revealed as one OpenAI deal, from a customer that on September 11, 2025 had little revenue and 1.1 trillion dollars of additional commitments
Open source as the quiet threat: Linux and Apache precedents, frontier models for mission-critical work, free models for everything else
Google graded a distant second in consumer chat and third in enterprise AI, a bureaucracy losing inventors like Noam Shazeer to OpenAI
Gil's winners and losers: Microsoft insurmountable via data centers plus Outlook, Salesforce a loser that stopped investing and just raises prices
Cybersecurity budgets expected to double in two to three years because every AI agent expands the attack surface
Data center moratoriums framed as a gift to China, and AI's self-inflicted PR problem over job-loss rhetoric and electricity bills
learned: A backlog is only as good as its counterparty; one undercapitalized customer can be most of a headline number
Moats may sit in the capex layer, not the model layer: the hyperscaler data center footprint is a barrier even if frontier models commoditize
The doom narrative can be a competitive weapon; incumbents lobbying for safety regulation are also raising rivals' costs
Wealth in a platform shift accrues across the whole supply chain, so the moat question at the top may matter less than it seems
In fast regimes, updating is the discipline: these analysts expect to change their own opinions many times by fall
notable: The panel's message to OpenAI and Anthropic on the wipe-out-white-collar-jobs rhetoric: knock it off, and per Ives, they have been told.

title: The Real Estate Brokerage War, For-Profit Education, & the Art of the Short with Brad Safalow
summary: Safalow walks the residential brokerage ecosystem after the commission settlement, where Compass is trying to route listings around the MLS and Zillow keeps executing while the stock gets re-rated. He then argues the for-profit education group is a structural short, and updates three shorts he pitched a year earlier. Eisman closes by grading each idea himself.
discussed: The MLS as the backbone of residential real estate, roughly 500 of them nationally, and Compass partnering with regional MLSs to build a national equivalent it can steer
State pushback on private listings, with Washington's ban going into effect and Connecticut proposing rules on what a private listing may be
The commission structure holding at 5 to 5.2 percent nationally, split about 2.5 percent each side, with brokers passing roughly 80 percent back to the agent
Zillow as a recommendation that has been, in Safalow's words, a disaster for him personally even though the company has not missed a number
For-profit education stocks rallying hard on a Trump win and then facing the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which kills the Grad Plus program that let graduate students borrow up to cost of attendance
Ghost students, where AI chatbots enroll at schools to harvest aid, plus a shrinking high school population and collapsing cost of educational content

Three short updates: Trupanion's aging pet book raising claims costs, Fresh Pet's human grade marketing retreat against Farmer's Dog while Costco went from zero to over 10 percent of revenue between 2022 and 2025, and Kinsale trading at three and a half to four times book with estimates Safalow thinks are 40 to 60 percent too high
learned: A stock can be right on fundamentals and still lose you money through multiple compression. Safalow's Zillow call never missed a number and still went against him
When an industry's distribution layer is under attack, watch the states, not the incumbents. Legislatures moved on private listings faster than the brokerages did
Aging books kill subscription insurance. Once growth stops, the average pet gets older every year and the loss ratio follows
An insurer that never hires from outside its own ecosystem builds culture and blind spots at the same rate
Marketing claims that cannot survive inspection, like human grade pet food that is not human grade, are a preview of the share loss
notable: Safalow discloses he is short Google in his personal account, directly to a host who owns it, and Eisman waves it off and keeps going.

title: The AI Debate Gets More Complicated: Microsoft Has a Win, Meta Stumbles | The Weekly Wrap
summary: Eisman opens by capitulating on Charter, then walks through an earnings week that split the AI trade in two: Microsoft and Amazon win, Meta burns cash, and credit markets start charging the smaller players real money. He refuses to call the AI endgame, arguing the facts change too fast for anyone to predict it.
discussed: Giving up on Charter after 172,000 second-quarter broadband losses, two bad quarters after his January recommendation
Meta's free cash flow shrinking to 784 million on 28% revenue growth and 55% expense growth, with capex guidance narrowed to 130 to 145 billion
Amazon Web Services revenue growth jumping to 37%, sending the stock up over 7% after hours
The SOX semiconductor index down 23% from its June 22nd peak
CoreWeave raising 2.6 billion of debt priced above 9%, while Google borrows cheaply
Situational Awareness, the 20 billion hedge fund founded by former OpenAI employee Leopold Aschenbrenner, seeking fresh capital after margin losses
A mailbag on the K-shaped economy and the wealth takeoff since the mid-1800s Industrial Revolution
learned: Admit the mistake and move on; two bad quarters in a row on the core metric outweigh a cheap valuation
A credit cycle is forming inside AI: fixed income investors now discriminate between hyperscalers that can repay and newer borrowers that might not
Anyone who claims to confidently predict the AI outcome is kidding themselves; the moats exist, but the story rewrites itself weekly
Even a correct thesis dies on leverage; margin turned a tech correction into a forced capital raise
notable: He opens on Charter without hedging: bottom line, I give up. Simply put, I made a mistake.

title: 250 Years of American Capitalism: Hamilton, the GFC, & the AI Boom | The Real Eisman Playbook Ep 71
summary: For the 250th anniversary of the Declaration of Independence, Eisman interviews Adrian Wooldridge, co-author with the late Alan Greenspan of Capitalism in America, on why the United States out-industrialized everyone. The episode ends in a genuine disagreement: Wooldridge reports that Greenspan blamed the GFC mostly on Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac, and Eisman blames the leverage Greenspan himself allowed into the banks.
discussed: How Wooldridge, an Oxford academic turned Economist writer, came to co-author the book with Greenspan
Hamilton versus Jefferson, and Hamilton's infant-industry tariff argument later copied by Germany
Why creative destruction ran hotter in America: a massive internal market, a culture wired for ambition, and a constitution that constrains government
The Hoover-to-FDR handover taking roughly six months in the middle of the Depression, leaving the country effectively without a government
Greenspan's view that finance had become untethered from the economy, self-serving and absorbing too much talent
Greenspan writing the GFC section solo and blaming Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac, which Eisman rejects in his closing thoughts
learned: Protectionism has a real historical win on its record; infant-industry tariffs helped build dominant American and German industries, which complicates the modern tariff debate
America's edge is cultural churn: rich European families persist for centuries while American wealth turns over, and the mess is the dynamism
Where a clever Frenchman writes philosophy and a clever Brit builds a country house, the American expression of genius is building a company, and that keeps regenerating
The optimist's caveats are political: instability, creeping corporatism, and concentration that innovation does not need
notable: Eisman presses on the GFC chapter, learns Greenspan wrote it alone, and tells the co-author on air that Greenspan got his own crisis wrong.

title: Streaming Hits Hollywood Hard: Here's Why with Producer Peter Hoffman
summary: Hoffman, who produced Terminator 2, Basic Instinct and Total Recall, explains how independents once financed films on presales and why that machinery is gone. Eisman frames it as a margin story: a high margin syndication business traded itself for a lower margin streaming business. Hoffman also recounts the tax indictment that pushed him out of the industry and the film business out of New Orleans.
discussed: Eisman's framing that incumbents happily sold old shows to Netflix and funded their own competitor, quoting the line about capitalists and the rope
Netflix earnings per share growth slowing to 11 percent from 47 percent in the second quarter of 2025, with the stock down 25 percent on the year
Disney's stock sitting where it was in late 2014, roughly 12 years of nothing, and AMC falling from 80 dollars to about 10 over a decade
The major players named as Netflix, Disney, Amazon, Google through YouTube and Paramount, with Prime Video only about 2 percent of Amazon revenue and YouTube about 15 percent of Google

The presale model that let international independents finance films outside the studio talent oligopoly, and why Apple can simply write the check for Neuromancer after Hoffman spent nearly 15 years failing to
Hoffman stopping a James Cameron production 30 days over schedule and telling the director's lawyer he could not remove his name, after which Cameron never spoke to him again
The New Orleans film tax credit indictment, after which the local business fell from about 1.2 billion dollars to 200 million in a year and moved to Georgia, now roughly 2 billion
learned: Selling your library to a distributor is selling the distributor your future. The syndication cash felt free until Netflix used it to fund originals
Streaming is a maturing business, not a growth business. Compare the growth rate to the multiple before assuming the transition is bearable
Prosecutors can destroy an industry cluster without winning a case. The raised eyebrow moved 1 billion dollars of production to another state
Nobody can predict which films work. Hoffman's example is Angel Heart, which he and Eisman both rate highly and which underperformed anyway
When financing depends on presaleable talent rather than material, the range of films that can exist narrows to what the buyer already recognizes
notable: Eisman warns up front that technical problems degraded the audio and video, and runs the episode anyway.

title: SpaceX Disappoints, AI's Free Cash Flow Shrinks, Meta Struggles | The Weekly Wrap
summary: A short pre-break wrap built around a correlation lesson: the Situational Awareness blowup shows what happens when every long and every short in a portfolio is the same bet. He then tours earnings where AI capex keeps eating free cash flow, and closes with his ten TV recommendations.
discussed: His auto-versus-horse-carriage portfolio parable: a thesis can be right in hindsight and still ruin you, because fully correlated longs and shorts amplify every scare
SpaceX reporting revenue of 7.8 billion, up 92%, but capex jumping to 18.4 billion from 10.1 billion, with Musk calling for more; the stock still below its 130 IPO price
Gallop Capital's 10 billion private credit fund seeing redemptions fall below the 5% quarterly cap after 8.5% the prior quarter
His view that private credit's real test arrives when software loan refinancings start next year
Arista beating the whisper number versus AMD, up 246% on EPS but down on in-line guidance
A top-ten TV list, from The Sandman and The Americans to Taylor Sheridan's Lioness
learned: Diversification means uncorrelated positions, not just longs against shorts; if the longs and shorts are mirror images, there is no hedge
Being right over five years is worthless if margin forces you out in five weeks; survival horizon matters more than thesis quality
He holds long-term winners like Arista precisely because trading them quarter to quarter is, in his words, an impossible endeavor
Calm redemption numbers do not end a credit story; the private credit verdict waits on next year's refinancings
notable: He grades his own record twice in one episode, then hands out TV picks like a mailbag victory lap before a two-week break.

title: Private Credit's Clock is Ticking w/ Glenn Schorr & Ken Worthington | The Real Eisman Playbook Ep 72
summary: Two sell-side veterans, Glenn Schorr of Evercore and Ken Worthington of J.P. Morgan, join Eisman on the day Microsoft's blowout lifted the market and a levered hedge fund got liquidated. Both are more positive on private markets than the host, who keeps his doubts and gets Worthington to concede he has no real thesis for owning Bitcoin.
discussed: Recorded July 30th: Microsoft up double digits, Meta down 10% on 28% revenue growth against 55% expense growth, and a 20 billion fund liquidated the same day
Private equity monetization times stretching out, with KKR the exception, posting record monetizations
Sponsors handing back the keys when lenders demand fresh equity to roll financings, and software refinancings hitting early next year at lower valuations
J.P. Morgan internal studies finding AI agents managing money are wrong the majority of the time, telling investors what prompts suggest they want to hear
Stablecoins as a settlement layer for the spread of 24/7 trading that back offices cannot support
Worthington's thesis that blockchains and tokens proliferate together, and Eisman's response that none of it explains Bitcoin
Investment banks humming: equity trading revenue up about 68% on volume up only 9 to 10%, with margin balances up about 50%
learned: Watch the gap between volume and revenue; trading profits are coming from margin balances and volatility, not activity, and that mix is fragile
Disagreement is the trader's friend: Schorr's rule is that trading is bad when everyone agrees and good when they do not
When everything in the investment banks is humming and estimates only go up, that comfort itself is the warning
The private credit reckoning has a date: software refinancings next year, negotiated against valuations that have already fallen
notable: Eisman grants Worthington every premise about blockchains proliferating, then asks flatly: what's that got to do with Bitcoin?

title: Why the Iran War Is Stuck & What Comes Next with Steven Cook
summary: Cook returns to explain why a war that opened with a stunning tactical success has settled into stalemate. The Iranian regime absorbed the decapitation of its leadership, dispersed its missiles and kept firing at Gulf states, and the president backed off once the Strait closed. Cook then tours Syria, Lebanon, Turkey and the region's shifting read on Israel.
discussed: Israel killing 40 of Iran's top leaders in the first minutes of Operation Rising Lion, which Cook says destroyed any chance of the president finding a regime figure to work with
Iran spending the nine months after the June 2025 Operation Midnight Hammer decentralizing missiles and command and control, so damage did not stop the launches
Iranian strikes on Gulf partners including the UAE, Saudi Arabia, Qatar and Oman, hitting Dubai Airport, data centers and Amazon web services facilities
The Strait of Hormuz blockade as the moment the president got cold feet, with the call off coming in early April and the Strait still closed at recording on July 28
The verification problem, with Eisman asking why anyone would believe an Iranian promise to surrender nuclear fuel, and Cook conceding the same doubt that dogged the 2015 deal
A Lebanon framework agreement under United States auspices, with Israeli withdrawal from two villages handed to the Lebanese armed forces and a monitoring mechanism aimed at dismantling Hezbollah

Cook's account of Saudi social change, from seeing no women in Riyadh in 2002 to women everywhere now, and the UAE gratitude for Israeli personnel operating Iron Dome and Iron Beam batteries on its soil
learned: A regime that values survival above the economy cannot be coerced by economic pain. Iran's leadership accepted food on credit and no internet as the price of staying in power
Decapitation forecloses negotiation. Killing the people you would have to deal with removes the off ramp along with the target
Dispersal beats hardening. Nine months of decentralizing command and control preserved the ability to fire under sustained bombardment
Diplomatic normalization usually predates the ceremony. Israeli missions operated in the Gulf for years before the accords put names on them
Public opinion runs on a different clock than governments. Gulf leaders wanted a short war precisely because a long one would be watched on phones
notable: Cook forecasts that if they speak again in three or four months, the picture will look the same, and Eisman tells him he will be back regardless.

title: AI’s Achilles’ Heel: Why Everything Hinges on Anthropic & OpenAI | The Weekly Wrap
summary: With earnings quiet, Eisman steps back and names the single point of failure in the AI trade: if Anthropic and OpenAI ever pull back on compute purchases, the entire chain goes into reverse.
