He pairs that with a shorting lesson, that even a correct bear case a year early is worthless, and declares Bitcoin no longer cool.
discussed: Nvidia partnering with six large asset managers on a 500 billion financing push treating compute infrastructure like commercial real estate or toll roads
The emerging hyperscaler winners, Microsoft, Google, and Amazon, versus Oracle with debt barely above junk and a struggling Meta
The streaming history lesson: incumbents chose margin over growth against Netflix, and it cost them everything
Bitcoin losing young traders to prediction markets, with eToro revenue down 30% on collapsing crypto trading and the stock down 14%
DraftKings facing what he calls the Blockbuster fate as prediction markets encroach
A premium two-part masterclass on analyzing banks coming after Labor Day, with Substack pricing rising to 20 dollars a month on September 7th
learned: Map the dependency chain, not the narrative; the AI trade's real risk is concentrated in two private companies' willingness to keep buying compute
Timing is everything in shorting: a bear case that arrives a year late is indistinguishable from a wrong one, and a year is an eternity for markets
Defending an existing high-margin business against a lower-margin future is how incumbents die; they preserve margin and lose the market
Being early to an asset class guarantees nothing; adapting does
notable: His epitaph for crypto's cultural moment: Bitcoin is no longer the cool toy, prediction markets are, just ask DraftKings.

title: The AI Trade, Rising Rates, and Why the Market Is Still Standing | The Real Eisman Playbook Ep 73
summary: Strategas founder Jason Trennert and strategist Chris Verrone survey a tumultuous year, war, tariffs, an AI capex debate, and a hedge fund blowup, and conclude the market's internals keep improving anyway. Their surprise admission: the 4.5% ten-year yield they long treated as the equity market's breaking point came and went, so the true threshold must be significantly higher.
discussed: Market internals strengthening through the churn: 50% of the S&P above its 200-day average on June 2nd versus 75% now
The hunt for the rate of interest that pulls money out of equities, after their 4.5% call on the ten-year failed to bite
Traditional asset managers, State Street, T. Rowe, Invesco, leading while private equity stocks lag, an industry Trennert calls the biggest beneficiary of near-zero rates
Private equity monetization timeframes stretching to about seven years
Bank stocks at new highs worldwide while private credit worries build, which Verrone finds out of step with any historical crisis setup
Private credit framed as a regulatory arbitrage born of Dodd-Frank pushing lending out of the banks
The end of Fed forward guidance under Kevin Warsh, and why spoon-fed markets now face more volatility
learned: Breadth beats headlines: when internals improve while the index churns, corrections keep resolving upward
Hold a threshold loosely; when the market absorbs the level you feared, the honest move is raising the estimate, not repeating it
Every claimed crisis has a tell, and world-wide bank stocks at new highs is not what the verge of a big problem looks like
Forward guidance was a subsidy to media and hedge funds alike; its removal brings volatility that good companies will survive and lazy positioning will not
notable: Verrone's line on the pattern of tops: leaders roll over only when they rally, fail to make new highs, and fail; and we haven't seen that yet.

title: Why Europe Can't Fix Itself & Why It's Getting Worse with Wolfgang Munchau
summary: Munchau, author of Kaput, returns a year later to report that Europe has gotten worse, not better. His diagnosis is that Germany stopped innovating around the 1990s, built everything on a car industry now losing to China, and chose to regulate technologies it never participated in. Eisman says out loud that the conversation is depressing, because a culture problem has no policy fix.
discussed: German productivity flat for eight years, with Munchau dating the turning point to 2018 and noting industry actually fell over the period
The car industry as the trickle-down engine of the whole German economy, feeding suppliers and the financial system, now losing to China with no diversification strategy
GDPR as the first of the big regulations and the source of the cookie banners, framed as arrogance in regulating an industry Europe does not participate in
Where European tech actually exists: the UK as the most active AI investor with spinoffs around the DeepMind orbit, a small Munich scene, a Paris scene, and almost nothing in Italy or Spain
Munchau's answer for why America has big tech, which is the capital market rather than tax breaks
Energy management as complex optimization, with coal running longer than planned in Germany because nuclear was switched off, and British housing stock too drafty and uninsulated for easy retrofit
Debt piling up everywhere because growth is absent, taxes are maxed, France cannot touch pensions, Germany cannot touch welfare, and defense spending has to rise anyway
learned: Regulating an industry you do not compete in buys you rules and no leverage
A single dominant sector is a trickle-down engine on the way up and a single point of failure on the way down
Capital markets, not tax policy, are the precondition for scale technology companies
Decline reaches a tipping point slowly. Anger and far right support are the visible measure of a system that has stopped working
Gridlock is structural when no executive exists. A confederacy that refuses to federalize cannot decide, whatever its leaders intend
notable: Munchau's analogy lands hard: imagine the United States with a Congress and no president, then make it worse.

title: The Juiciest Corporate Scandals with Becca Platsky
summary: Platsky, a CPA who hosts Corporate Gossip, trades fraud stories with Eisman across Frank and JPMorgan, Paramount and the Ellisons, prediction markets and FIFA. The two disagree on the nature of fraudsters, with Platsky arguing anyone can slip and Eisman insisting people who commit fraud were always doing it. The episode ends on his oldest grievance, that nobody was ever prosecuted for 2008.
discussed: Charlie Javice and Frank, pitched as 400,000 users with socials, incomes, schools, emails, addresses and phone numbers, after other name brand banks passed and JPMorgan bought
The court ruling that JPMorgan's due diligence was not on trial, and Eisman's agreement that being deceived is not a defense for the deceiver
The JPMorgan executive who ran that diligence, once in the conversation to succeed Jamie Dimon, since demoted
Paramount's late-stage governance, described as executives propping up an incapacitated leader, and the Ellison family now using the company to pursue Warner Bros Discovery
Eisman's own view that Paramount and Warner Bros should merge so Netflix does not own the whole business, against Platsky's concern about Larry Ellison also owning TikTok alongside CBS and CNN
Prediction market abuse, including a teleprompter technician betting on which words Trump would say, and the CFTC's unsettled posture toward Polymarket's innovation defense
FIFA sponsorship money flowing to executives, with Chuck Blazer keeping an 8,000 dollar a month Trump Tower apartment for himself and a 6,000 dollar one for his cats and parents
learned: Shorting a fraud is a solvency race. A fraud can persist longer than a short position can survive
The gap between the CNBC appearance and the earnings report is where the story usually is
Insider trading migrates to whatever venue lacks a regulator. Event contracts recreated the problem with none of the enforcement
Whistleblowing is a real option with a real price. Both hosts say it can blow up your life
Missing laws are rarely the problem. In 2008 the statutes existed, the investigation never started
notable: Platsky asks what listeners can actually do and Eisman has no answer beyond screaming, then tells her to keep her circle small and useful.

title: The Art of the Short with Lakshmi Ganapathi: FICO, DoorDash, and AeroVironment
summary: Ganapathi explains how she hunts for shorts, then walks through three: FICO, AeroVironment and DoorDash. Eisman, still short FICO, sorts them into a structural short, a business model short and a consumer credit short.
discussed: Her screen: cocky management, rising ad spend and debt, debt-funded buybacks, and products or warranties that fail customers
FICO's price increases of about 1,600% over four to five years, which pushed FHFA head Bill Pulte to back VantageScore
Her reading that FICO management went from calling Vantage share about 2% to citing roughly 20 to 25% within two quarters
A FICO price target under 500 against a share price a little over 1,000
AeroVironment as a roll-up that bought another roll-up, BlueHalo, selling drones at 50,000 dollars plus while Ukrainian and other rivals sell for 5,000 or less
DoorDash's five or six European lawsuits over Deliveroo, including a French criminal conviction of two former general managers
DoorDash volume leaning on buy now, pay later credit, which would vanish if consumer credit tightens
learned: A monopoly can break when management raises price so far that customers and regulators organize against it
Management statements that shift tenfold in two quarters signal a company caught off guard
A good short thesis can still be untradeable if the stock is too volatile to hold
Consumer demand financed by fragile credit is only as durable as that credit
notable: Eisman admits he is tempted to short AeroVironment but fears the agita of holding a stock that volatile.

title: Is OpenAI the Achilles’ Heel of the US Economy? | The Weekly Wrap
summary: With the ten-year near 4.8%, Eisman argues AI capex now carries US growth and that OpenAI, not Nvidia or the hyperscalers, is the weak link. He is not making a major call yet, but he names safety ETFs for a possible reallocation.
discussed: War in Iran pushing oil up and the ten-year to almost 4.8%
AI capex as the main driver of GDP growth, large enough that a halt would mean near-immediate recession
Nvidia's circular financing, including its potential Perplexity investment and a recent Poolside investment
OpenAI's June quarter: revenue of 6.7 billion, up only 18%, against costs of 12.3 billion, up 3 billion; Anthropic above 11 billion, up over 100%
Oracle's BBB minus rating and 600 billion backlog, about half from OpenAI, recalling its 2025 jump from 230 to 330 on the backlog
Safety ETFs: LVHD, SPLV and KBWP, the property and casualty ETF
Meta's settlement of about 17 billion with state attorneys general, with commentary from law professor Ben Zipursky
learned: When one customer is half a supplier's backlog, the supplier's value rests on that customer's solvency
Revenue growing 1 billion while costs grow 3 billion is a trend, not a rounding error
A late-cycle worry is often a reallocation question, not a stock picking one
Every sector contains a safety subsector; in financials it is property and casualty
notable: He says it is not too early to think through what happens if OpenAI fails.

title: P&C Stocks Worth Owning: The AI Hedge with Ryan Tunis | The Real Eisman Playbook Episode 74
summary: Cantor analyst Ryan Tunis maps property and casualty insurance as a hedge against the AI trade, a sector with its own pricing cycle. The market has softened, so he favours self-help and brokers over buying the whole group.
discussed: The four parts of the sector: commercial lines, personal lines, reinsurance and insurance brokers
New car safety technology cutting accident rates, which lowers auto pricing and shrinks the personal lines market
Progressive's struggle to sell homeowners insurance outside coastal states without independent agent relationships
A commercial soft market about a year old, with softening spreading into casualty lines
Tunis rating Travelers and AIG buy but not Chubb; AIG trades around book value and carries a hard market business mix
Reinsurance brokers as his top subgroup, while reinsurers' pricing discipline remains in doubt
Trupanion's roughly 1,000 dollar policies and free cash flow near 2% of revenue; Kinsale's mid-50s loss ratios and low broker pay
learned: Property and casualty cycles run on their own rhythm, not the economy's
In a soft market, buying on business mix stops working and self-help stories take over
Technology that reduces losses can shrink an insurer's addressable market
A low expense ratio built on paying brokers less can hurt when business returns to the standard market
notable: Eisman leaves more negative on personal lines, which includes Progressive, a stock he holds.

title: Inside AI’s Fragile Ecosystem with Ed Zitron
summary: Ed Zitron, the Substack critic listeners asked for for months, argues AI revenue is tiny next to capex and rests almost entirely on two loss-making labs. Eisman largely agrees and names OpenAI as the problem child.
discussed: Microsoft's fiscal 2026 AI revenue of 34.33 billion, per a Bloomberg estimate, with 24.1 billion from OpenAI
OpenAI losing 20.9 billion on 13.07 billion of revenue in 2025, with a recent quarter operating margin of about minus 183%
Subscriptions that let users burn about 14,000 dollars of compute for a 200 dollar fee
OpenAI's 122 billion raise, 110 billion of it from Amazon, SoftBank and Nvidia
Token maxing, then a turn to cost cutting after Meta pulled its token leaderboard
OpenAI and Anthropic taking about 90% of available compute, and data center buildouts slowed by local pushback in Texas and Pennsylvania
Hyperscaler capex of about 650 billion this year, with about 70% of hyperscaler AI revenue from the two labs
learned: Spending on API tokens is not recurring revenue and should not be annualized
When a supplier's largest customer is funded by that supplier, underwriters should see a concentration risk
Undisclosed segment revenue leaves investors guessing about the core economics
Smart people can run a mania; Wall Street did it with subprime until it blew up
notable: Eisman warns listeners to look past Anthropic's first-half S-1 numbers to second-half revenue after enterprises cut token spend.

title: AI Terminator Fears Grow & Rates Breach 4.9% | The Weekly Wrap
summary: The ten-year breaks 4.9% on war-driven oil, and Eisman concedes 4.5% was not the market's breaking point. He also dismisses AI extinction talk, doubts Tesla's robotaxi valuation and says FICO's monopoly will break badly.
discussed: Oil above 100 dollars and the ten-year above 4.9%, the highest since November 2023
Bessent's treasury buybacks failing to impress; the ten-year rose from 4.80% to 4.845% that day
Fed Chair Warsh wanting to shrink a 6.7 trillion balance sheet, with markets pricing about a 60% chance of a September hike
Tesla at 220 times 2026 earnings of 1.66, down 59% from peak EPS of 4.07, against GM at 6.5 times
OpenAI cutting prices and claiming a tenfold rise in usage; Qualcomm granting Amazon warrants on 25 million shares at 161.26, worth over 4 billion
Pulte attacking FICO again as VantageScore opens to all lenders
GameStop's revenue falling to 790 million from 972 million, with collectibles now bigger than video games
learned: A rate threshold is a guess; the market sets the real one
Falling earnings do not guarantee a falling stock when investors buy a story
Rising yields can lift gold when the yield rise comes from inflation fear
Warrants to a customer are not circular financing, but they deserve scrutiny
notable: Asked about gold against a 5% treasury, he takes the treasury: the government is stretched but not yet overstretched.

title: The Big Short Partners Reunite: Rates, AI, Gold and Two Stock Picks | The Real Eisman Playbook Ep 75
summary: Eisman sits down with two of his Big Short partners for a lightning round on Scott Bessent's bond buying, the deficit, gold, AI nerves and why shorting has become harder. The partners make the case for precious metals as the endgame of a debt problem Washington will not fix, and pitch a cannabis long alongside a shared FICO short.
discussed: Porter Collins arguing interest expense plus entitlements equal about 110% of tax receipts, leaving printing as the only exit
Gold as a debt-free central bank asset, with central banks close to holding more gold than Treasuries
Bessent's long-bond purchases of at least 4 billion dollars, mocked as an attempted Draghi moment
How a multi-manager fund such as Citadel runs a near-zero net book levered about five to one
All three being short FICO, and Carvana at 30 to 40 times earnings as a short that has failed for eight years
A cannabis producer selling at about 200 dollars a pound in California that could earn 50% to 65% EBITDA margins abroad, with progress seen as a 2027 event
SpaceX's S-1 promises, including asteroid mining, as a sign of how far AI and space narratives have run
learned: When debt service plus entitlements exceed revenue, markets start pricing monetization, and hard assets benefit
A market-neutral book can carry high gross leverage because its volatility is engineered low, which hides how much capital is really at work
A short can be right on the numbers and still lose for years if the stock has a buyer of its paper and a devoted base
notable: The partners credit Eisman's habit of asking how a fund levers its book as the question they now use on their own calls.

title: How to Analyze Bank Stocks (Part 1): Leverage, Accounting, and Loan Losses
summary: Part one of a paid lecture on bank analysis. Eisman builds from a zero-leverage bank to explain why banking is a low-margin business that only works through leverage, then covers risk-weighted capital and how loan loss reserves drive the stocks.
discussed: The identity ROE equals ROA times leverage, shown with a bank earning a fine 1% ROA but a pathetic 1% ROE unlevered
Deposits treated as debt, and leverage defined as assets divided by equity
Risk-weighted assets rewarding banks that pile into low-weighted assets, and risk weights resting on loss history that underwriting can change
Large-bank CET1 ratios falling since the fourth quarter of 2024 as regulators loosen capital rules
JPMorgan provisions of 8.3 billion and 10.5 billion in the first two quarters of 2020 under CECL, then 611 million in the third
Non-accruing loans at JPMorgan of 9.4 billion in 2Q26, down 5% year on year, and at Bank of America of 5.8 billion, down 4%
Michael Burry's point on stretched chip depreciation schedules as an example of judgment hidden in accounting
learned: Read a bank's returns through leverage: a small change in ROA becomes a large change in ROE
Capital ratios built on historical loss rates are only as good as current underwriting standards
A reserve true-up forces guidance down and often marks the contrarian moment to buy
Watch year-on-year and sequential non-accruals at the four biggest banks for the broadest read on credit
notable: He predicts private credit losses will surface first in investor redemptions, not in bank non-accrual data.

title: Why Dario Amodei and Sam Altman Are Faking the AI Doomsday Crisis | The Weekly Wrap
summary: Oil near 110 dollars pushes the ten-year above 5% and the Fed hikes. Eisman concedes his 4.5% line was wrong, then argues Anthropic and OpenAI talk up AI doom as cover while their business models cannot afford any slowdown.
discussed: The Fed raising rates 25 basis points to 3.75% to 4%, defying President Trump, and penciling in another hike this year
Bessent's long-Treasury buying program rising from 4 billion to 6 billion dollars and working for only one day
FICO raising prices about 1,600% over five years, with pressure now spreading to credit bureaus and mortgage insurers
Senators blocking the crypto Clarity Act after the industry spent hundreds of millions on it, a blow to Circle
OpenAI representing about 300 billion of Oracle's 600 billion plus backlog, and an Anthropic IPO expected within a month or two
The Kevin Mitnick prison story as a parallel for fear of poorly understood technology
Mailbag: most S&P sectors correlate with AI; staples and healthcare are only 14% of the index; LVHD, SPLV and KBWP as diversifiers; shorting Nvidia against the box
learned: When a rate threshold breaks without a selloff, move the line rather than defend it
Judge a CEO's warnings against what his financing commitments require him to do
Diversification from a dominant theme may require going inside sectors, such as property and casualty insurers within financials
notable: He admits outright that his 4.5% ten-year threshold was wrong.

title: Stock Picking in Difficult Times with George Noble | The Real Eisman Playbook Ep 76
summary: Former Fidelity portfolio manager George Noble returns to argue the macro has flipped from tailwind to gale: Treasury cannot repress rates on 40 trillion of debt, Japan's yields threaten US demand, and AI returns look weak. He closes by laying out his shorts in SpaceX and Tesla.
discussed: Bessent cast as Norman Lamont defending sterling against Soros, with Noble noting Bessent was a junior who did not make that trade
A regime change away from the post-GFC world where money printing carried no cost, and disdain for fixation on monthly CPI decimals
Japan's ten-year crossing 4% for the first time in about 30 years, which Noble says should be near 7% given debt to GDP of 240%
Japanese and Chinese selling of Treasuries while US policy discourages foreign buyers
An AI ecosystem that depends on OpenAI, framed through related-party and VIE accounting
SpaceX valued at 1.7 trillion against Noble's estimate of roughly 200 to 500 billion, and Tesla US sales down 26% in July
Tesla's share price roughly unchanged over five years, and doubts on robotaxis
learned: Stock picking works best when the macro factors are neutral or behind you; fighting rising rates in rate-sensitive groups is hopeless
A country's sovereign yield should roughly track its debt burden, as a subprime borrower's rate tracks its credit
In a momentum mania, avoiding the few overvalued giants and indexing the rest can win when the worm turns
notable: Eisman says Noble may be more negative on AI than he is, judging it on return on investment.

title: How to Analyze Banks (Part 2): Deposits, Valuations, and Silicon Valley
summary: Part two of the bank lecture uses Silicon Valley Bank to show how a bank can fail with no credit problem, then walks through the bank income statement, valuation and the choice between large and plain-vanilla banks. Eisman ends by explaining why he owns no banks today.
discussed: Silicon Valley Bank rising from 50 dollars in 2010 to 760 in November 2021 and failing on 10 March 2023
SVB's 212 billion in assets sitting below the 250 billion stress-test threshold, with a deposit base drawn entirely from venture capital
Unrealized bond losses hitting book value but not earnings, and Bank of America's roughly 100 billion of such losses being an earnings problem, not a solvency one
Net interest income as margin times average earning assets, with loans producing about 70% of interest revenue and Citi's thin deposit franchise hurting its margin
Goldman re-rating from 1.3 times to about 3 times tangible book
Bank OZK's 32.6 billion loan book, 50% commercial real estate, trading at one times tangible book
First Horizon's CEO calling his bank a buyer, not a seller, on the 3Q25 call
learned: Deposits are only as stable as their diversity; many depositors who are all the same act as one
A bank that funds long bonds with short money is surfing the curve and can fail without a single bad loan
Buy banks after recession fears have killed them and lighten up at peak valuations
An M&A thesis needs a willing seller; impeccable logic does not make a CEO sell
notable: He treats buying large investment banks today as an indirect AI bet and declines to add to his AI risk.

title: The Enron-Era Tricks Are Back in AI: How These Companies Are Hiding Their Debt | The Weekly Wrap
summary: With the ten-year at a multi-year high above 5.10%, Eisman calls 5% the market's Rubicon and a correction probably imminent if yields stay there. The core of the wrap compares off-balance-sheet AI data center financing, above all Meta's Beignet vehicle, to Enron and the GFC's SIVs.
discussed: Oil and the ten-year as the only two variables moving the market, with strong data pushing yields above 5.10%
S&P cutting Oracle to BBB minus, one notch above junk, and troubling news at Blue Owl Capital
Paramount cleared after a California settlement requiring a CNN oversight board and 30 theatrical films a year; Netflix at a growth wall
SoftBank borrowing in the junk market to fund an equity investment
Meta's Louisiana data center financed through Beignet Investor LLC, 20% Meta owned with Blue Owl and Pimco, under a 20-year lease with Meta bearing overruns
Ernst & Young's critical audit matter on the VIE, which Eisman reads as auditor nervousness
Meta's Muse agent in household use, and a mailbag correction on the Section 1259 constructive sale rule for shorting against the box
learned: Disclosure is not the same as sound accounting: Enron disclosed its SPVs and the auditors signed off
When a company guarantees the lease and bears the overruns, the debt is economically its own wherever it sits
Read a critical audit matter as a signal of where the auditor is uneasy
notable: He details his own tax-compliant hedge: close the short within 30 days of year end, hold the long 60 more days, and retake the risk in 2027.
